PREFACE 

HIS book represents the first attempt to collect all the Maryland statutes and case law applicable to corporations generally.

For many years past local enterprises have, with few exceptions, been incorporated under the Maryland law, and corporate firms in the leading financial centers outside the State have frequently recommended the incorporation of new or reorganized enterprises in Maryland. Thus about seven thousand corporations, including many well-known companies doing business throughout the United States, are operating under Maryland charters.

No attempt can be made to state, except in the most general terms, the apparent reasons for increasing use of the Maryland law as a medium for incorporation. The legislature, influenced by a conservative local Bar, has not tried to outrun other states in "liberalizing" the law. Nevertheless, the statute has consistently kept pace with legitimate business requirements, and the policy of the State to welcome incorporation of national or out-of-state enterprises has been recognized in the opinions of the Court of Appeals. The statute and its amendments have been carefully and properly drafted. Many of its provisions have been taken over in recent revisions of the corporation laws of other states. Professor Ballantine, in writing of the new California law, of which he was the principal draftsman, states that the Maryland law was one of the models used by his committee. The trend toward incorporation in Maryland may, therefore, be said to result from the conservative tone of the law, which must primarily serve the needs of the State's own industrial and financial communities, and also from its excellent draftsmanship. 

Owing to the readjustments and liquidations of the present period, most general practitioners have been called upon to engage in corporate litigation. Such cases often present quesiii

iv 

PREFACE 

tions of great complexity and importance. A lawyer engaged in corporate litigation or in any phase of modern corporate work must be fully acquainted with every relevant case decided in the state of incorporation as well as with the widely separated sections of the corporate statute or code which may have some bearing on the questions presented to him. It is the purpose of the present book to fulfill this need for a complete reference work on the Maryland corporation law. 

The material has been presented in the form of a discussion of each subject, referring to and abstracting all the statutes and all the cases likely to throw light on that subject. This method is a departure from the customary plan of local corporation textbooks, which for the most part follow the form of a reprint of the statutes with extensive annotations. 

The reason for the adoption of the "treatise" method is that unless a practicing attorney is familiar with the entire corporation statute, an examination of sections of the law dealing primarily with the point under consideration may afford an incomplete answer to his specific problem. There may be other sections of the law appearing in a different part of the book which may affect or completely change the answer. For example, Sections 12 to 16 of the Maryland law deal primarily with by-laws, but references to optional by-law provisions are scattered throughout the law from Sections 5 to 86. 

An effort has been made to include in the text a statement of methods and practices frequently employed by specialists in the corporate field. These practices embrace many points not specifically covered by the statutes or referred to in the decisions of the courts. In many cases they have been sanctioned by the officials of the State Tax Commission who administer the law. The general practitioner cannot be expected to be familar with such methods and practices, and no other printed statement or discussion of them is available. 

In the chapter on Corporate Taxation the material is presented in the form of a reprint of sections of the law, with annotations, first, because the law itself was enacted at one time, in 1929, and is arranged in logical sequence, and second, because abstracts of a taxing statute would for the most part be too incomplete to be of service.

PREFACE 

V Numerous local forms are included in Part II. The full text of the "General Corporation Law" (a term explained in Chapter I) appears in Part III, together with the so-called "Blue Sky Law" and other relevant statutes. The forms are annotated with references to sections of the text and to sections of the Corporation Law; the latter, in turn, are annotated with references to sections of the text. 

Legislation enacted by the General Assembly of Maryland in 1933 (effective June 1 except in the case of "emergency laws") and decisions of the Court of Appeals published in Volume 163 of the Atlantic Reporter and in the Advance Sheets of Volume 164 through March 13, 1933, as well as in 

The Daily Record (Baltimore) through March 18, have been included.

Grateful acknowledgment is extended to W. Ainsworth 

Parker, Esq., for valuable aid in the original study and classification of material, and for his specific contribution of the chapters on Dissolution and on Issuance of Stock and the 

Sections dealing with Preferred Stock. I wish also to thank my partners and other friends for helpful advice in both the preparation and revision of the manuscript.

§ 1. History of the General Corporation Law.—Incorpora tion under general laws began in Maryland with the "Vestry Act" of 1798, an enactment of limited scope available only for the creation of certain religious corporations. While this Act was broadened somewhat in 1802,2 the first general law of any importance was the Manufacturing and Mining Companies Act of 1838. During the succeeding thirty years general laws were enacted for the creation of various classes of corporations -building associations, cemetery companies, telegraph companies, oil companies, and universities and colleges. The 

Code of General Laws of 1860 brought together the various provisions then in force as separate subtitles under one article dealing with corporations." 4 Following the adoption of the State Constitution of 1867," the first comprehensive General Corporation Law was drafted and in 1868 was enacted by the General Assembly." This law, with only minor amendments, continued in effect until 1908, when it was thoroughly revised and modernized.8 

The new law was based to some extent on the old, and the

great body of judicial decisions rendered during the past century is, therefore, often available to aid in the construction of the present law.

Since 1908 amendments to keep pace with changes and refinements of corporate practice have been made at nearly every session of the Assembly, which now convenes in January of the odd years.⁹

§ 5. Scope of discussion in subsequent chapters. Since this book is concerned chiefly with the Maryland General Corporation Law and its construction by the courts, it has been found necessary to omit the great body of statutory provisions dealing with special classes of corporations and judicial decisions rendered thereunder. An exception has been made in the discussion of corporate taxation, where statutes and decisions relating to various classes of corporations have been included because of the difficulty and the practical importance of the questions involved. Non-stock or membership corporations are seldom differentiated in the law from share corporations, and for that reason both stock regulating these companies were contained in Art. 23 until 1922 (See L. 1922, Ch. 492).

§ 6. Constitutional provisions.-The State Constitution prohibits the creation of corporations by special act, "except for municipal purposes and except in cases where no General Laws exist, providing for the creation of corporations of the same general character as the corporation proposed to be created." Any act passed in violation of such provision is declared to be void.2 There is also a broad provision to the effect that the legislature "shall pass no special law for any case for which provision has been made by an existing 

General Law."

These Constitutional provisions have been strictly construed. Accordingly, it has been decided that an amendment to the charter of a corporation, even though of a kind permitted by the General Law, is not within the scope of such provisions and may be made by special act. It has also been held that a charter of limited duration which had expired might be revived by special act. Other cases indicate that a corporation which is to have a limited existence or powers

otherwise unobtainable may now be created by special legislation. Probably any special act of incorporation is valid if the exact result cannot be attained under General Law.8 § 7. Formation by special act. As just indicated, there are still cases in which a corporation may properly be created by special act. No particular form of act would be necessary, provided the intention to create a legal entity were clear, 10 and the grantee or grantees of the franchise properly indicated.¹¹ 

Acceptance of a charter granted by special act is essential to the creation of a corporation,12 and it has been held that such acceptance will not be presumed if there are no corporate meetings or other acts of exercising the corporate franchise within the State.13 The only safe course would be to hold a meeting of incorporators or members within the State as soon as organization had been effected, and to pass a specific resolution accepting the charter. 14 

The partial invalidity of a charter granted by special act does not render such charter wholly void.15 But acceptance of part only of the terms of a special act is in fact rejection.16 

§ 8. Corporations formed under General Corporation Law.- 

All corporations, except (a) those excluded from the operation of a general corporation law by the State Constitution, and (b) those for which special and inconsistent provisions as to formation are made in Article 23 of the Code, are formed under the provisions of the General Corporation Law." § 10. Definitions and general considerations.-The present chapter deals with the positive requirements of the General Corporation Law applicable to the formation of corporations by the preparation and filing of a certificate of incorporation. 

These provisions, as previously indicated, are available for the formation of all corporations except banking institutions, municipal corporations, railroad companies, religious corporations, and coöperative associations.¹ 

The "certificate of incorporation," as referred to in subsequent sections, constitutes the "charter" of the corporation to the same extent as a special act of incorporation. The statutory definition of "charter" is as follows: "The word 'charter' shall include charter granted by special act, certificate of incorporation and agreement of consolidation, either as originally passed or filed or as amended, unless such construction would be inconsistent with the context."2 

The following general provisions applicable to charters are of sufficient importance to be reproduced here, as introductory to the specific requirements of the statute with respect to the contents of the certificate of incorporation:

No charter or other paper, which is not in conformity with law, shall be received by the State Tax Commission for record.³ 

Every corporation formed under this article shall have, until forfeiture, the right of perpetual succession; and all provisions in the charter or certificate of any existing corporation or imposed upon it by any act in force at the time of its creation or formation limiting its duration, are hereby annulled and repealed.* 

Every corporation formed under the provisions of this article shall be subject to any and all provisions and regulations which may hereafter, by any change in or amendment of the laws of this State, be made applicable to such corporation." 

§ 11. Contents of certificate of incorporation. (a) Incor porators or subscribers.—“The incorporators, being any three or more adult persons, shall sign and at least three of them shall acknowledge a certificate of incorporation, in which shall be stated: (a) That the subscribers thereto (giving their names and postoffice addresses) associate themselves with the intention of forming a corporation." 

The State Tax Commission interprets this provision as requiring that the Christian or given name in addition to the surname be inserted in the case of each incorporator, and has formed the practice of rejecting certificates in which only the initials and surnames of the incorporators appear." 19 office of such corporation in this State for the transaction of business is actually situated. "31 

As to change of agent or address, it is provided as follows: 

No amendment of the charter of any such corporation shall be necessary to change the location of the principal office of such corporation from one place in a county or the City of Baltimore to another place in such county or city, or to make any change whatsoever in the names or addresses of any resident agents. Every such corporation shall notify the State Tax Commission promptly of any change (not made by amendment) in the location of its principal office, or in the name or postoffice address of any resident agent, (giving in each case the county and city, town or place, street and number, if number there be).32

It will be noted that the statutory provision as to change of resident agent's name or address without amending the charter includes "any change whatsoever"; but that the principal office may thus be changed only within the county or city. 

In case of an intended change of principal office from one county to another, or from the city of Baltimore to a county, or vice-versa, an amendment of the charter, duly authorized as in the case of any other charter amendment, is essential to effectuate such change.33

The distinction between changing the principal office and changing the postoffice address of the resident agent is a clear indication that the two need not be the same, and there is, in fact, no positive statutory requirement that the principal office and the address of the resident agent shall be in the same county or city. It is the practice of the Commission to accept charters designating a principal office in one county and an agent residing in another county.34 § 15. (e) Authorized capital stock. The recording fee is Ten Dollars ($10) except in the case of a certificate providing for two or more classes of stock. 

In such case the recording fee is Fifteen Dollars ($15). The 

State Tax Commission is charged with the duty of transmitting a certified copy of the certificate, as recorded, to the clerk of the Circuit Court for the county in which the principal office of the corporation is to be located (if in Baltimore, to the clerk of the Superior Court).46

The Commission has adopted the practice of requiring the filing with it of only the original of each certificate of incorporation, and of transmitting such original, after copying and recording the same, to the clerk of the court as a certified copy from its records. No provision is made for the Commission to file and preserve the originals in its office after recording has been completed. The statutory requirement that a copy be filed with the original at the office of the Commission dates from the period (prior to September 30, 1920) when certificates were recorded in the office of the Secretary of State as well as with the State Tax Commission.47 

The Attorney General has ruled that no copy need be filed.48 

The statute further provides: 

A duly certified copy of a certificate of incorporation, from the records of the Secretary of State, the State Tax Commission, or the Clerk of the Circuit or Superior Court, shall be evidence of the existence of the corporation and of its right to exercise the powers therein mentioned. The recording by the State Tax Commission of the certificate of incorporation shall be conclusive evidence of the payment of the recording fees and the bonus tax, if any, required by law to be paid to it, and of the existence of the corporation, except in a direct proceeding by the State.49

§ 20. Statutory provisions.-Certain general powers are explicitly vested in corporations by Section 9 of Article 23. 

These powers, which will be enumerated in the succeeding sections, are granted not only to corporations created since the enactment of the section in its present form,' but also to corporations previously formed. It is necessary to discuss the statutory powers as preliminary to an understanding of the importance and effect of various clauses as to purposes and objects which may be inserted in the certificate of incorporation.3

§ 23. Use corporate seal.-This power is expressed in the statute as follows: "To make and use a common seal and alter the same at pleasure. 9910 The old rule that the corporate seal was essential to the due execution of a contract by a corporation is obsolete in Maryland, as elsewhere.¹¹

Whether or not the use of the corporate seal makes a specialty of an instrument which would otherwise be a simple contract has been discussed in several cases. The mere addition of a corporate seal, with no reference thereto in the body of the instrument, does not create a specialty, 12 but it has been held that a negotiable certificate of indebtedness to bearer, executed, issued, and delivered pursuant to resolutions of the board of directors of the issuing corporation, and signed by the treasurer and by the secretary attesting the corporate seal, is a specialty.13 

§ 24. "'14

contracts, incur liabilities and borrow money for its corporate purposes; and to issue bonds, notes, and other obligations and secure the same by mortgage or deed of trust of all or any part of its property, franchises and income; provided any such issue of bonds, notes, or other obligations secured by mortgage or deed of trust of any of the franchises of the corporation shall have been authorized at any meeting duly warned, as provided for in sections 19 or 20 of this article, by the affirmative vote of a majority of all of its members or a majority of all of its stock (or if two or more classes of stock have been issued, of a majority of each class), outstanding and entitled to vote thereon."'16

Since the power to make contracts is limited to the corporate purposes, any case involving the power to contract depends on the corporate purposes as stated in the charter. 

Under this section a corporation has power to contract to do anything which it is authorized to do. Conversely, a corporation ordinarily is not empowered to contract to do that which it is not authorized to do in the line of its corporate purposes.' 17 

Contracts of guaranty offer some difficulty, in that the performance of the guaranty involves payment of money or loss on the part of the corporation which it can validly suffer only by virtue of having entered into the contract. Under the 

Maryland decisions, it is probable that a contract of suretyship or guaranty is not within the powers of a corporation, unless the guaranteeing of obligations, under some circumstances, is stated as among its corporate purposes. 18

Stock retired has the status of authorized but unissued stock.40 

Acquisition of its own stock by gift or bequest does not release the shareholder from liability for any unpaid subscription, and the corporation may not release such liability unless its assets remaining immediately thereafter "shall be not less. than the debts of the corporation plus the amount of its issued capital stock."41

Acquisition by redemption.-Stock may be made subject to redemption by provision of the charter. 42 Stock which is redeemed is automatically retired. 43 A corporation may also, without express charter power, purchase for retirement and thereby retire any shares of its stock then subject to redemption, at not exceeding the redemption price.44 Stock so retired, or retired by redemption, thereafter has the status of authorized but unissued stock, unless the charter provides that it shall not be reissued.45 The powers above mentioned as conferred on the corporation may be exercised by the board of directors unless expressly reserved to the stockholders. 46

A purchase of redeemable stock for retirement is placed in all respects on the same basis as a redemption of such stock, and in neither case may the stock be so acquired if after its retirement the assets of the corporation shall be less than the debts of the corporation plus the amount of its issued capital stock remaining after such retirement.47

In the statute and hereinafter in this discussion a purchase for retirement of redeemable stock at not less than the redemption price is regarded as a redemption and not as a purchase, and is not intended to be included in the word purchase.48

Acquisition by purchase.-As above stated, this paragraph does not include a purchase for retirement of redeemable stock at not exceeding the redemption price.

A corporation may purchase shares of its own stock out of surplus if so authorized (a) by its charter or (b) by the vote of two-thirds of its stockholders of each voting class.49 Unless so authorized it may not purchase shares of its own stock,50 and the law expressly prohibits any such purchase unless thereafter the assets of the corporation shall be not less than its debts plus the amount of its issued capital stock. 51 Prior to consummation of such purchase, however, the corporation may, through proper proceedings, reduce its issued capital stock, and the surplus so made available may be used to purchase stock if the assets of the corporation thereafter shall be not less than its debts plus the amount of issued capital stock as reduced.52

Stock lawfully acquired by purchase may be held by the corporation or sold or otherwise disposed of by it from time to time53 or it may be retired by proper proceedings. 54

The liabilities of stockholders for payments received by virtue of unlawful purchases or redemptions, or in event of unlawful releases of liability, are discussed in a subsequent chapter. 55

tion v. Rosenthal (1927),57% it was decided that such a contract is valid since. the enactment of the above section, though the actual purchase could not be carried out until the statutory requirements had been fulfilled. 

The court said, in part: "It is true that . . ... a corporation can purchase shares of its own stock only when authorized to do so by its charter or by the vote at a meeting duly called and held of the holders of two-thirds of the shares of each class of stock outstanding, and unless one or the other of these conditions precedent had been complied with, the purchase of its own stock by a corporation would be an invalid or ultra vires act... There being what on its face is a valid contract of the corporation to purchase, upon certain contingencies, shares of its own stock, we must, without any showing to the contrary, presume that the necessary condition precedent to the making of a valid contract had been complied with." 

Under the statute and this decision, it is desirable, in most cases, to include in the charter of a corporation a provision expressly authorizing the purchase of its own stock; for, as the court points out in summarizing the statute, a vote of the holders of two-thirds of each class of stock must be obtained in the absence of charter power. The vote need no longer include any classes of non-voting stock.58 As subsequently pointed out, the proportionate vote required may, by a suitable charter provision, be reduced to a bare majority of all voting stock in the aggregate. 59 § 29. Exercise charter powers.-Finally, a corporation is given power "generally to exercise the powers set forth in its charter and those herein enumerated, and also to do every other act or thing not inconsistent with law which may be appropriate to promote and attain the objects and purposes set forth in its charter. "64

With respect to the construction of railroad charters, the power of making branch lines does not arise by necessary implication;73 but where the charter of the Baltimore & Ohio 

Railroad included the power to construct lateral roads, an amendment to the charter of another railroad, stating that it should have the same powers as those granted to the Baltimore & Ohio by its charter, was held to include the branching power. 74 In the leading Maryland case on construction of corporate powers, the Western Maryland Railway sought to repudiate a contract which it had made to pay "commissions" on its receipts from certain stations sufficient to make up to the bondholders and stockholders of the Blue Ridge Hotel Company any amounts needed to pay interest and dividends due them if the earnings of the Company were not otherwise sufficient. The Court construed the contract as a guaranty of interest and dividends, made in consideration merely of the increased traffic over the lines of the railroad due to the operation of a resort hotel. The railroad had power, by its charter, to construct its railroad, warehouses, or other works necessary to the road, buildings, stations, other works, and accommodations necessary or convenient for the operation of the road; to aid any other railroad company by subscriptions to stock or otherwise; to consolidate with any company owning a railroad, 70 State v. A company formed to build and operate a canal was held to be authorized to make a contract to construct, on land conveyed to it for the canal, a basin for loading and unloading, such contract being similar to an agreement by a railroad to erect and maintain a station on land conveyed to it; but an agreement by such canal company to maintain the basin as a source of water for a mill on the grantor's property was decided to be beyond its powers.78

An express provision of statute is required to authorize a corporation to act as administrator or executor.79 Charter power to "accept and hold all such trusts as shall or may be committed to it by any person or by the order and direction of any judge or any court or tribunal," is not, however, sufficient to authorize a corporation to act as executor.80

In approaching the Maryland decisions the first point to be understood is that the language of the various opinions is confusing and irreconcilable,88 and that the key to the problem lies in an analysis of the decisions themselves rather than in the statements made by the court. For example, in Heironimus v. Sweeney,89 the court quotes two of its inconsistent prior statements to support its decision: (1) "When a party makes a contract with a corporation which is simply beyond the powers of the latter, he may recover back the money paid thereon whether the contract be executed or executory";90 and (2) “It is inequitable to permit one who has received the proceeds and benefit of the contract to repudiate it on the ground that the corporation from which he has obtained the benefit, had no power to make the contract."91

The first of the above statements, though quoted with approval by the court as late as 1896, is clearly not the law at the present time. The decision in Maryland Hospital v. 

Foreman, 92 which first laid down the principle that an executed ultra vires transaction might be reopened, may now be regarded as impliedly overruled on that point.93 

Nor is the second quotation to be accepted without qualification as a statement of the law at the present time. It has been decided that a railroad corporation may altogether repudiate its obligations under an ultra vires contract which has been fully performed on the other side.94

CHARTER-POWERS, PURPOSES, AND OBJECTS 39 

If a contract or transaction is more than merely ultra viresthat is, if it is illegal, as subversive of public morals or some other strong public policy, or as in violation of express statutory prohibitions-the question is not one of ultra vires. It is important, therefore, to distinguish between illegal transactions and those which are merely beyond the charter powers or purposes of the corporation, as the two kinds of transactions are governed by different rules. 95 

Since corporations are held accountable for torts and crimes, the ancient doctrine of special or limited capacity, though it has at times been asserted by the Maryland Court and by the Supreme Court of the United States, furnishes an inadequate and unsatisfactory explanation of the decisions on ultra vires. Other reasons for refusal to enforce ultra vires contracts must be sought. 

There are two substantial reasons why ultra vires contracts and transactions must be denied validity under certain circumstances: (1) the State has an interest in confining the activities of the corporation to its granted powers;96 (2) the stockholders have an interest in confining its activities to those which are fairly within the scope of the purposes for which such stockholders have invested their money.97 

In the case of public service corporations, banks and the like, the interest of the State may well be sufficient to require that ultra vires transactions be regarded as void unless fully executed on both sides, and that no private estoppel shall be permitted to nullify such protection given to the public interest.98 "Maryland Trust Co. vs. National Mechanics Bank, (1906) 102 Md. 608, 63 Atl. 70. See France, op. cit. 122. 

"International Fraternal Alliance v. State, (1893) 77 Md. 547, 26 Atl. 

1040 (charter of beneficial association may be forfeited for unauthorizedly engaging in insurance business; corporation given opportunity to amend charter as better protection to policy holders than dissolution). The peculiar protection accorded creditors of a corporation, as distinguished from those of a partnership, does not, it is said, arise until insolvency. Bartlett v. Smith, (1932) 160 Atl. (Md.) 440. Unusual facts involving ultra vires acts might, however, present a proper case for injunctive relief or for a receivership of a solvent corporation at suit of creditors. See Hagerstown Furniture Co. v.

But in the case of ordinary business corporations, if the ultra vires act is one which could have been authorized by charter amendment without the consent of any public authorities, the only substantial interest is that of the stockholders.99 

In so far as the State has an interest, it is amply protected by the power of the Attorney General to proceed for forfeiture of the charter.¹ 3 The suggested distinction is supported by recent textwriters of standing. A consequence of its acceptance is that in an ordinary business corporation a stockholder who has acquiesced in an ultra vires act will not be heard to complain of it. The corporation is treated as if it were an association of persons similar to a partnership. The shareholders are protected to the extent that the directors, corresponding to the managing partners in a partnership, may not undertake any transaction which is beyond their implied or apparent authority. The fiction that third persons study the charters of corporations with which they deal is entirely discarded; and if the corporation has openly engaged in an ultra vires business for a period of time, its stockholders, if they do not object, will be held to be estopped and to have waived their right to do so when the business turns out badly and the right to engage in it becomes the subject of litigation."

Construction of preferred stock clauses.-The corporation law, as above quoted, 10 permits the creation of stock of one or more classes having preference over other classes of stock: (a) as to the payment of fixed annual dividends (which may be cumulative) payable quarterly, half-yearly or yearly; (b) as to its distributive share of the assets of the corporation on dissolution. The same right to create classes of preferred stock likewise exists with respect to non-par stock.12 Preferred stock, like all other classes of stock, represents pro tanto the capital of the corporation, and the holder of preferred stock is on the same footing as the common stockholders in all respects except those in which the charter provides otherwise. 13 11 Obviously the expression "preferred stock" is in no sense a definition of the precise nature of the preferences granted thereto. These preferences are, in any particular case, those conferred upon the stock by the corporation, at least so far as they are not inconsistent with statutory provisions. The 

Maryland statute permits a wide latitude in the creation of preferred stock. The precise preferences granted in any case are primarily a matter of contract evidenced by the charter, the stock certificate, and other relevant documents. The terms of the contract are to be determined as in the case of other contracts. For example, evidence is admissible to show the situation of the parties and the purposes to be accomplished, but negotiations preceding the final agreement are inadmissible. 

These principles were stated and applied by the Court of 

Appeals in the case of Scott v. Baltimore & O. R. Co.¹

question there presented for decision was whether the holders of preferred stock of the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad, issued pursuant to a reorganization agreement, were limited to the four per cent dividend as to which they were expressly given a preference, or were entitled to share with the common stockholders in earnings available for distribution after payment of the dividend of four per cent. The stock certificate did not expressly provide that the preference of the preferred stockholders was limited to four per cent, but the court held that the circumstances under which the certificates were issued and the language therein used indicated that the preferred stock was so limited. 

Preferred stock being, as above stated, a part of the corporate capital, it follows that, if the corporation becomes insolvent, holders of the stock are entitled to nothing in distribution until after the creditors of the corporation are paid.

In Heller v. National Marine Bank15 the Court of Appeals was required to determine the rights of holders of a so-called preferred stock issued pursuant to L. 1880, ch. 474 (Code 

1888, Art. 23, Sec. 294; Code 1904, Art. 23, Sec. 408), which according to this statute should, on being recorded as therein provided, "constitute a lien on the franchises and property of such corporation and have priority over any subsequently created mortgage or encumbrance."16 The Court in differentiating between this statutory so-called preferred stock and what is ordinarily called preferred stock discussed the characteristics of the latter at some length. It said (p. 610): 

The law is perfectly well settled that as between creditors and ordinary preferred stockholders, the latter, as owners of the property of an insolvent corporation, are, upon a distribution of its assets, entitled to nothing until its creditors are first fully paid. There is a palpable difference between the relation of a stockholder and a 

15 (1899) 89 Md. 602, 43 Atl. 800, 45 L. R. A. 438, 73 Am. St. Rep. 212. 

16 This provision was repealed by L. 1908, Ch. 240, which enacted (as Code 

1904, Art. 23, Sec. 34) the provisions for the creation of preferred stock substantially as they now appear in Art. 23, Sec. 38. L. 1880, Ch. 474 was construed also in the following cases: Rogers, Brown & Co. v. Citizens Bank, (1901) 93 Md. 613, 49 Atl. 843; Leviness v. Consolidated Gas Co., (1911) 

114 Md. 559, 80 Atl. 304, Ann. Cas. 1913C 649; Baltimore, C. & A. Ry. Co. v. 

Godeffroy (1910) 182 Fed. 525 (C.C.A. Md.).

creditor to the corporate property. Stock, whether preferred or common, is capital; and, generally speaking, a certificate of stock merely evidences the amount which the holder has contributed to or ventured in the enterprise. Such a certificate, representing nothing more than the extent of his ownership in the capital, cannot well be treated as indicating that he is, by virtue of it alone, also to the same extent a creditor who may compete with other creditors in the distribution of the fund arising from a conversion of the corporation's assets into money. He cannot, if he is simply an ordinary preferred stockholder, in the nature of things, so far as third persons are concerned, be at one and the same time and by force of the same certificate, both part-owner of the property and creditor of the company for that portion of its capital which stands in his name. His certificate, therefore, in such circumstances, merely measures the quantum of his ownership. As his chance of gain throws on the stockholder, as respects creditors, the entire risk of the loss of his contribution to its capital, it is a fixed characteristic of capital stock that no part of it can be withdrawn for the purpose of repaying the principal of the capital until the debts of the corporation are satisfied. 

The statute in accordance with this principle states that, "In case of insolvency, the debts and all other liabilities of the corporation shall be paid before any payment or distribution is made to the holders of any class of stock."17 

In Heller v. National Marine Bank (above referred to) the court, in connection with the definition of preferred stock above quoted, went on to say, "To be strictly accurate, we ought to say there is a sense in which a shareholder is a creditor. 

In that sense every corporation includes its capital stock amongst its liabilities, but it is a liability postponed to every other liability. And as to the matured and unpaid guaranteed dividends due on preferred stock, the relation of creditor undoubtedly exists. Baltimore & O. R. Co. v. State, 36 Md. 

541."'18 The court here is no doubt speaking of dividends already set aside and declared but not paid, as appears from the case cited. The question whether the provision above quoted postponing stockholders to other creditors of an insolvent corporation would apply to such unpaid dividends has not been presented for decision in Maryland.

§ 38. Voting rights.-The statute permits the regulation of voting powers of stock in the charter.20 If not otherwise provided, each stockholder is entitled to one vote for every share of stock standing in his name, unless an installment payable thereon or duly called is overdue and unpaid.21 A denial by the charter of the right to vote to any class of stock is valid for the purpose of issuance of bonds, notes, and other obligations secured by mortgage of franchises, 22 amendment of the charter, 23 consolidation, 24 sale, lease, exchange, or transfer of corporate property as an entirety, 25 issuance of stock and convertible securities, 26 authorizing a purchase by the corporation of shares of its own stock,27 and dissolution.28 

Such denial is not valid in case of a vote to amend the charter so as to change the terms of non-voting stock which is outstanding.29 Where it is proposed, by charter amendment, to change the terms of outstanding stock, whether voting or non-voting, unanimous consent of the holders of such stock (by vote at a meeting or in writing) must be obtained unless the charter reserves the right to make such an amendment.³0

§ 39. Convertible stock and securities; warrants and 

The charter may provide that shares of stock of any class shall be convertible into shares of stock of any other class upon such terms and conditions as may be therein stated. For the purpose of the bonus tax imposed by the laws of this State, 32 the authorized amount of stock of any class which by the terms of such charter is convertible into stock of another class shall be taken to be either the amount of such stock authorized by such charter or the aggregate amount of the stock into which such stock is convertible, whichever is the greater, except that if the charter provides that, out of the stock of the corporation then or thereafter to be authorized, stock shall be reserved for issuance upon such conversions, the bonus tax shall be calculated and paid upon the amount of stock authorized by such charter without reference to the amount of stock into which any of such stock is convertible.33

The concluding proviso of this section affords the means of authorizing convertible stock without paying the bonus tax, at the time of incorporation, on the stock into which such stock is convertible, if larger in amount than the convertible stock. The stock required for such conversions may be authorized by subsequent charter amendment when and as the convertible stock is issued, or thereafter. 

The proviso permits the use of a desirable method of preserving the value of the conversion privilege; that is, by changing the ratio of conversion in case a greater or less amount of the new stock is issued. This method of protecting the conversion privilege was often preferred to that of restricting the amount of the new stock which could be issued, though

The privilege thus conferred of reducing the requisite number of votes for corporate action is exceptionally valuable in the case of a large corporation whose stock is widely held, when it may be impossible to obtain the attendance, in person or by proxy, of a large number of shareholders. Inactive shareholders are protected by the fact that, in large corporations, the stock in attendance at meetings normally affords a fair sample of the sentiment of the entire body of shareholders. At a recent stockholders' meeting of one of the large investment trusts, a highly desirable charter amendment increasing the capital stock would have failed of passage for want of the two-thirds vote required by law, if the charter had not contained a provision authorizing any corporate action (including charter amendments) to be taken by the vote of a majority of all voting shares."

§ 44. Provisions empowering directors to issue stock.- 

In issuing stock or convertible securities, the procedure provided by any one of four statutory methods must be complied with. 10 These methods will be fully discussed in a subsequent chapter,¹¹ and need not be taken up here except in so far as they indicate the desirability of including appropriate provisions in the charter of a corporation conferring power on the directors to issue stock. In the absence of such provisions, a vote of stockholders, if any, must be obtained to authorize any proposed issuance of stock,12 except in case of an issuance of par stock for money at not less than par, which may be done by the directors. 13 

With the same exception—that is, in the case of an issuance of par stock for money at not less than par,14-a stock issuance statement must in all cases be filed with the State Tax Commission if there are no appropriate charter provisions. 15

On the other hand, by the inclusion of suitable charter provisions the following advantages can be obtained: (1)

No-par stock may be issued by action of the board of directors alone, for any lawful consideration, and without filing for record a stock issuance statement;16 (2) any stock may be issued by action of the board of directors alone, for any lawful consideration, provided a stock issuance statement is filed;¹7 and (3) any stock may be issued by action of the board of directors alone, for lawful considerations fully described in the charter. 18 These optional methods are also applicable to the issuance of securities convertible into shares of stock.19 

To secure the advantages enumerated in (1) and (2) above, a single clause authorizing the board of directors to issue any stock, from time to time, including securities convertible into shares of stock, for "such considerations as they deem advisable," should be inserted in the charter. 20 It will be noted that a stock issuance statement will then be required in case of an issuance of par stock for a consideration other than money at not less than par, but will not be required in case of an issuance of no-par stock, a resolution of the board of directors being, in that event, sufficient under the statute. 

Where the consideration is actually specified in the charter, under option (3) above, no further charter provision is required, and in this case no stock issuance statement need be filed, for the effect of the charter provision is to include the stock issuance statement in the charter itself. 21 This method is rarely used in practice, because of its rigid requirement that the consideration for the stock be fully determined and described in advance of filing the charter. However, it is sometimes convenient in cases in which a corporation is formed to take over a specific piece of property or business.

57 § 45. Reserved powers in charter affecting method of amending the charter and transfer of assets pursuant to charter amendment.-If the charter is silent as to the power of amendment, (a) a vote of two-thirds of the outstanding shares of voting stock of each class is necessary to effect any charter amendment;23 (b) an amendment changing the terms of outstanding stock requires unanimous consent of the holders of all of such stock;24 and (c) in case an amendment is adopted authorizing sale, lease, exchange, or transfer of the corporate assets as an entirety, any dissenting stockholder has the same right to demand compensation which he would have if the sale, lease, exchange, or transfer were carried through pursuant to the statutory procedure prescribed in case charter authority is lacking.25

The following advantages can be obtained by appropriate charter provisions: (a) If so provided by the charter, an ordinary charter amendment may be authorized by the vote of less than twothirds of the outstanding shares of voting stock of each class, but not less than a majority of the total number of votes to which all voting shares in the aggregate are entitled. 26 (b) An amendment changing the terms of outstanding stock may be authorized by the proportionate vote required for an ordinary amendment, if the charter suitably reserves to the corporation power to make amendments changing such terms.27 (c) A sale, lease, exchange, or transfer may be carried through pursuant to an amendment conferring authority therefor, without compliance with the statute granting compensation to dissenting stockholders, if the charter reserves to the corporation power to make such amendment.28

59 It holders," and "not contrary to the law of the State." may be pointed out in this connection that the common-law rule granting the stockholder a preëmptive right is not a strict rule of law, based upon public policy, but is a rule of intention resting upon a fair implication from the contract between the stockholder and the corporation.36 As such, it should give way to evidence of a contrary intention, as by a charter release of the right, at least with the aid of a statutory provision such as that contained in Section 4 (g). Discrimination between shareholders of the same class would, it is believed, be condemned irrespective of the charter clause releasing preemptive rights.37

There are no decisions or dicta bearing upon the question whether, pursuant to charter provisions, the preëmptive right may be denied to one class of stockholders but reserved to another. In the ordinary case in which preferred stockholders have invested capital for a fixed return, and the common stockholders are, in substance, the owners of the business, a provision denying to such preferred stockholders the right to subscribe to new issue of common stock but reserving such right to the common stockholders, seems a fair and reasonable discrimination.38 Even in the absence of a charter release or waiver, it has been held, though not uniformly, that a corporation may issue additional common stock to common stockholders for cash without offering a proportionate share thereof to non-voting and non-participating preferred shareholders, 39

of a bank by the issuance of shares of its stock in exchange for the stock of the bank. The trust company was formed by the consolidation of preëxisting trust companies, the charter of one of which expressly granted preëmptive rights to stockholders. In denying the preemptive right with respect to the proposed issue of stock, the court laid down the following propositions: (1) preemptive rights granted by the charter of one of two consolidating corporations do not pass to the stockholders of the consolidated corporation; (2) independently of charter provisions, the stockholders of a corporation have such privilege when it can be exercised consistently with the object which the issue of stock is designed to accomplish; and (3) in the case of an issue of stock to be used only to buy the stock of another corporation, the privilege could not be exercised consistently with the object of the issue, and it is, therefore, properly denied.40 

§ 48. Transactions with officers and directors.-The Mary land law with respect to transactions of a corporation with its officers or directors, participated in by them as agents of the corporation, which will be discussed subsequently,¹¹ may be summarized by the statement that such a transaction is not void, but is voidable if unfair and, if called in question, will be set aside unless the director or officer successfully sustains the burden of showing the fairness of the transaction.42 

A customary Maryland charter provision that contracts of the corporation with its directors or officers, or with another corporation having an interlocking directorate, shall not be set aside except for actual fraud, is of doubtful validity43 but may nevertheless be of some assistance in a close case by reason of the warning thereby (theoretically) given to stockholders.

§ 49. Statutory provisions affecting charters of non-stock corporations.-The charter of a non-stock corporation may provide for the holding of meetings of members thereof outside the State.45 Such a corporation may provide by its charter (or by-laws) who shall constitute the members thereof, within the meaning of statutory regulations. If neither the charter nor the by-laws of such a corporation provides for members thereof as such, or there are in fact no members, the members of the governing body or board for the time being are to be regarded as the members.46 In drawing the charter of a member corporation, it is customary to list the original members and to provide that changes in the membership may be made as provided in the by-laws.47 

In place of the clause relating to capital stock, the charter of such a corporation states that it "shall have no capital stock."'48

Another clause frequently employed in order to stamp the corporation (for income tax purposes) as not organized for profit is inserted as a preamble to the clauses relating to powers. This clause states that the object of the corporation is to organize and operate a club (or society, association, foundation, etc.) exclusively for recreation (or social intercourse, education, etc.) and other non-profitable purposes, and that "no part of the net earnings of the corporation is to inure to the benefit of any member." It is then stated that "for the purposes aforesaid the corporation shall have the following powers," and the usual clauses as to corporate powers follow.49

As in the case of a stock corporation, the charter may require for any purpose an affirmative vote different from that required by law for such purpose. 63 charter unless there is statutory authorization for it, or unless it is clear that the clause is for the purpose of "defining, limiting, and regulating the powers of the corporation and of the directors and stockholders" and that it is not in conflict with any provision of law.62

Charters are frequently rejected by the State Tax Commission because of some clause granting powers in excess of what is permitted by the statute. Among these are clauses granting unlimited power to discount papers or unlimited power to guarantee obligations."4 So also a clause stating that the directors shall have full power to make, alter, and repeal by-laws, even if the charter should be passed by the Commission, may lead to difficulty when acted upon.65 The same is true of a clause providing, without any limitation, that meetings of stockholders may be held outside the State.66

§ 52. Scope of discussion.-The conception of a corporate charter as constituting a contract between (a) the corporation and the State,¹ (b) the corporation and its shareholders, or each shareholder and the other shareholders, and (c) the corporation and its creditors³ is so fundamental that it is easily left out of consideration when dealing with the seemingly unlimited powers of amendment granted by modern statutes. It is impossible, therefore, to deal as a practical matter with the essentials of a valid charter amendment under the Maryland law without going into some detail as to limitations on the power of amendment imposed not only by the statutes themselves but by principles of law existing independently of the statutes and operating, to some extent, in spite of them." 

§ 53. Methods of amendment.-Maryland charters may be amended in the following ways: (1) In the case of a stock corporation, before any stock subscriptions have been accepted, the incorporators may make any desired amendment." (2) In the case of all corporations, whether created by special act or under the General Law, an amendment may be made by special act of the legislature, accepted by the corporation, even though the amendment is one which might be adopted under the procedure provided by the General Law.8 (3) In the case of all corporations, the charter can be amended by following the statutory procedure, which in most cases requires a vote of two-thirds of each class of voting stock.⁹

CHARTER-AMENDMENT 

67 These methods will now be separately discussed. Under what circumstances, if any, a minority of shareholders or members may obstruct an amendment by special act or by two-thirds vote under the General Law will then be taken up.10 

It is clear that there can be no minority group to object in case of an amendment by the unanimous action of the incorporators, as mentioned in Paragraph (1) above. § 54. Amendment by incorporators before any stock subscribed. The privilege of amendment by action of the incorporators applies only to stock corporations. The statutory conditions and procedure are as follows:

It shall be lawful for all of the incorporators of any corporation having capital stock, before any subscriptions to stock have been accepted by the board of directors, to amend the certificate of incorporation in the following manner:

An amended certificate of incorporation shall be signed by all of the incorporators who signed the original certificate of incorporation. 

Such amended certificate of incorporation shall be executed, acknowledged, delivered and recorded in the same manner, as in the case of an original certificate of incorporation, but no bonus tax shall be payable except in respect of any increase in authorized capital stock, and upon receipt for record by the State Tax Commission, such amended certificate of incorporation shall take the place of the original certificate of incorporation. Such amended certificate of incorporation shall contain only such provisions as it would be lawful and proper to insert in an original certificate of incorporation.¹¹ 

§ 55. Amendment by special act and acceptance.-The constitutional prohibition of the creation of corporations by special act when a General Law exists providing for creation of corporations of the same general character¹2 has been held by the Court of Appeals to be inapplicable to the amendment of a corporate charter, whether such charter was obtained by special act or under the General Law. 13 Hence, any corporate charter may be amended by seeking action on the part of the legislature. It is necessary, however, that the amendment be accepted by the corporation in order to be valid. 14 If

the legislature is acting within a reserved power of amendment,15 acceptance has already been given or will be presumed. 16 But if the special amendatory act is outside the 

State's reserved power of amendment, no such presumption will be indulged." While the point has not been presented in 

Maryland, it seems that a majority of cases elsewhere hold that a general power of amendment reserved by the State can be exercised for the benefit of the State alone, and cannot be conferred upon or exercised for the benefit of a majority of the stockholders or members as against a minority." 

Acceptance of an amendatory act by the corporation, so as to bind a minority, will always be inferred from action by the corporation under the terms of the amendment and acquiescence in its provisions for a reasonable time without protest on the part of such minority.19 The requirement of corporate action in accepting an amendment by special act is coextensive with the requirement of corporate action in initiating a similar amendment under the General Law. For example, in the case of a corporation formed at a time when the General Law permitted unlimited freedom of amendment by the majority, a dissenting minority would not be prejudiced by an amendment made by special act and accepted by the majority. 

Therefore, the limitations to be subsequently stated as to the power of amendment under the present General Law by twothirds vote²º are applicable with equal force to the power of acceptance of amendments made by special act.

§ 56. Statutory power of amendment without consent of minority; scope of power.-The statute in terms provides that "every corporation of this State, heretofore or hereafter incorporated, may **** amend its charter and thereby accomplish any one or more of the following objects," listing certain objects,23 and then adding, "and the making of any other amendment of the charter that may be desired, provided that such amendment shall contain only such provisions as it would be lawful or proper to insert in an original certificate of incorporation made at the time of making such amendment."24

This is, in terms, an unlimited freedom of amendment. The procedure, requiring two-thirds vote of stockholders or members, is described in the next section. 

Certain statutory restrictions and provisions, as to amendments changing the terms of outstanding stock, or authorizing the corporation to sell, lease or exchange its assets as an entirety, will be taken up later. 25 Limitations on the statu- ⚫tory power of amendment as applied to corporations created before the general revision of the incorporation laws in 1908 will also be discussed subsequently." 

In making any amendment the statutory provisions must be fully complied with; and, since an increase in capitalization may be made only as provided by statute, an amendment changing par to no-par stock without following the special statutory provisions applicable to an increase of capital must be held not to capitalize any surplus of the corporation.27

§ 57. Method of procedure.-Amendments are made accord ing to the following procedure prescribed by the statute: 

The board of directors shall pass a resolution declaring that such amendment or amendments is or are advisable and calling a meeting of stockholders or members to take action thereon. The meeting of the stockholders or members shall be duly warned in the manner provided in section 19 of this article. If two-thirds of all the shares (or, if two or more classes of shares have been issued, two-thirds of each class), outstanding and entitled to vote, or two-thirds of the members vote in favor of such amendment or amendments, articles of amendment setting forth such amendment or amendments and stating that the same has or have been duly advised by the board of directors and adopted by the stockholders or members shall be signed and acknowledged in the name and on behalf of the corporation by the president or a vice-president with the corporate seal attached, attested by the secretary or an assistant secretary, and the matters and facts set forth in said articles of amendment shall be verified under oath by the chairman or the secretary of the meeting of the members or stockholders at which such amendment or amendments was or were adopted.30

The charter of a corporation may validly authorize a vote less than that above required, but in no case less than a majority of all the votes to which all voting stockholders in the aggregate are entitled.³¹ 

The articles of amendment are delivered to the State Tax Commission for record,32 together with the recording fee and the bonus tax, if any. The recording charge, as in the case of a certificate of incorporation, is Ten Dollars ($10.00) unless the articles provide for more than one class of stock, in which event the fee would be Fifteen Dollars ($15.00).33 There is no bonus

Whether charter restrictions on the amending power are permissible and valid is a question on which there might well be a difference of opinion. One of the leading text-writers would deny validity to such restrictions, in the absence of statutory authority. It may be suggested that statutory authorization can be found.36 

§ 58. Increase of authorized capital stock.- 

If an increase of the authorized capital stock of any corporation shall have been duly authorized, as in Sections 28 and 29 provided, the articles of amendment shall set forth: (a) the total number and par value of the shares of the capital stock theretofore authorized and, if more than one class, the number and par value of the shares of each class; (b) the total number and par value of the shares of the authorized capital stock as increased and, if more than one class, the number and par value of the shares of each class; and (c) the preferences, voting powers, restrictions, and qualifications of each class of the authorized capital stock as increased or a statement that such terms thereof are as set forth in the charter.37 

The same procedure applies in case of an increase of stock without par value.38

An increase of outstanding stock may not be made by amendment. For this reason, an amendment changing par stock to no-par stock does not have the effect of capitalizing surplus, though the articles of amendment omit to state that capitalization of surplus is not intended.39

§ 59. Decrease of authorized capital stock.- 

If a decrease of the authorized capital stock of any corporation shall have been duly authorized as in Sections 28 and 29 provided, the articles of amendment shall set forth: (a) the total number and par value of the shares of the capital stock theretofore authorized and, if more than one class, the number and par value of the shares of each class; (b) the total number and par value of the shares of the capital stock issued and, if more than one class, the number and par value of the shares of each class; (c) the total number and par value of the shares of the authorized capital stock as decreased and, if more than one class, the number and par value of the shares of each class.41

The number of shares of authorized but unissued stock without par value may likewise be decreased.42 

If the charter provides that stock which has been redeemed or redeemable stock which has been purchased for retirement may not be reissued, the authorized capital stock is automatically decreased by such redemption or purchase for retirement.43 

§ 60. Reduction of amount of issued capital stock.-Prior to the 1931 amendments it was necessary to execute and file "Articles of Amendment" in order to reduce the issued capital stock, even though no change was to be made in the wording of the charter. By the 1931 amendments, however, "Articles of Reduction" are provided for,44 and if the reduction is to be made by changing the wording of the charter, "Articles of Amendment and Reduction," setting forth the matters required to be set forth in Articles of Amendment and in Articles of Reduction, must be prepared and filed.45

CHARTER-AMENDMENT 

73 

The pertinent provisions of the new statute are as follows: 

Every corporation of this State, heretofore or hereafter incorporated, may from time to time reduce the amount of its issued capital stock in the following manner and subject to the following provisions: (1) If such reduction is to be made without changing the wording of the charter, it shall be advised by the board of directors and authorized by the stockholders in the manner and by the vote required for the adoption of an amendment to the charter, except that the board of directors, without a vote of the stockholders, may authorize a reduction which is to be effected by retiring shares held by the corporation. Articles of reduction setting forth such reduction and stating that the same has been advised by the board of directors and authorized by the stockholders, or authorized by the board of directors as the case may be, shall be executed, acknowledged, verified and recorded in the manner, including payment of the same recording fees, prescribed with respect to articles of amendment. (2) The articles of reduction shall set forth: (a) the method of effecting the reduction; (b) the amount of issued capital stock prior to the reduction and, if divided by classes, the amount of each class; (c) the amount of the reduction of the issued capital stock, and, if the amount of issued capital stock is divided by classes, the amount of the reduction of each class, and (d) the amount of issued capital stock as reduced and, if the amount of issued capital stock is divided by classes, the amount of each class as reduced. (5) Any shares of stock retired by reduction of the issued amount of capital stock shall thereafter have the status of authorized but unissued capital stock of the corporation and, until the classification thereof shall have been changed shall retain the classification obtaining before such retirement; provided, however, that, if under the charter the shares so retired may not be reissued, the authorized capital stock of the class to which such shares belong shall be deemed to have been reduced by the number of shares of such stock so retired. (6) A reduction in the amount of the issued capital stock heretofore or hereafter made may be made the basis of distributions or payments to stockholders and of releases of the liability of stockholders whose shares have not been fully paid, to the extent of any surplus thereby created, provided the assets of the corporation remaining immediately after such distributions or payments or releases shall be not less than the debts of the corporation plus the amount of its issued capital stock as reduced. If any such reduction is made the basis of distributions or payments which reduce the assets of the corporation to an amount less than its debts plus the amount of its issued capital stock as reduced, the stockholders shall severally be and remain liable to the

corporation or its receiver, trustee or other person winding up its affairs to the extent of the excessive distributions or payments to them respectively for the debts of the corporation existing at the time of such reduction. (7) Except in the case of shares subject to redemption retired by purchase for retirement under paragraph (2) of Section 50 or by redemption, no reduction of the issued amount of capital stock shall be made except in the manner provided and subject to the provisions of this section. (8) Nothing in this section shall be taken or construed as limiting or affecting the liability of stockholders in banking, safe deposit, trust or loan corporations.46 

On purchase of redeemable stock for retirement, or on redemption thereof, the issued capital stock is automatically reduced.47 A corporation may purchase shares of its stock out of surplus created by a reduction of issued stock, if so authorized by its charter, or by two-thirds vote of each class of stock.48 Similarly, stock which has been acquired by gift, bequest, or purchase may be retired by execution and filing of Articles of Reduction.49 

All of the above provisions are made applicable to a reduction of issued stock without par value.50

A further requirement of the statute is that no amendment changing the terms of outstanding stock shall be valid without unanimous consent of the holders of such stock, in the absence of a reservation in the charter of the right to make such amendment.53 When such an amendment is adopted, the articles must recite the fact that the holders of such stock have duly authorized the change.54 The word "terms," as used in the statute, is defined as "the contract rights of the holders as expressed in the charter."55 § 62. Effect of reservation in charter of powers of amendment. The following reserved powers of amendment are expressly authorized by statute to be inserted in corporate charters: (a) A reservation of the right to make an amendment changing the terms of outstanding stock. 56 With such reservation appearing in the charter, an amendment of this kind can be made according to the usual procedure without the necessity of obtaining unanimous consent of the holders of such shares. 57 (b) A reservation of the right to make an amendment authorizing sale, lease, exchange, or transfer of the corporate 

53 Id. The statute is silent as to whether such reservation must specify what vote shall be required for adoption of an amendment changing the terms of outstanding stock. The practice has been to assume that the usual vote as for other corporate amendments is intended when the so-called reservation merely states, "the corporation reserves the right to amend its charter so as to change the terms of outstanding stock. The further question arises whether the statute intends that the particular respects in which the terms of outstanding stock are to be changed must be set forth in the reservation. The solution of these questions may well depend upon whether the clause of the statute authorizing changes in the terms of outstanding stock without consent of such stock is to be strictly or liberally construed-apart from a strict or liberal construction of the reservation itself. In a contest between the management of a corporation, backed by majority stock, and the individual investor, it would seem that doubtful questions of construction (as far as the reservation is concerned) would be resolved against the management as being responsible for the draftsmanship of the charter, when such responsibility can in fact be shown. The statute itself, in so far as it is thought to permit a change in or denial of fundamental rights, would, it seems, also be strictly construed.

As stated, there is substantial authority for the view that the State's power of amendment "is not reserved in any sense for the benefit of the corporation, or of a majority of the stockholders. The power of a majority of the stockholders to bind a dissenting minority by accepting an amendment of the charter does not depend at all upon whether the State has reserved to itself the power to alter or amend the charter, but depends 'essentially upon the question whether the change is of such a character that it may be deemed so far in furtherance of the original undertaking, and incidental to it, as to be fairly within the power of the corporation to bind its individual members by its corporate assent, or whether it is such a departure from the original purpose that no member should be deemed to have authorized the corporation to assent to it for him.'"'66

The Act of 1868, making corporations subject to changes thereafter adopted in the General Laws,67 would unquestionably have the effect of binding the stockholders of a corporation to accept minor changes in the procedure of amendment or in the corporate government, as well as changes not of a fundamental character made in the charter by virtue of a General Law broadening the powers of amendment.68 But, as stated by a leading text-writer in referring to the power of the Legislature to authorize a company to amend its charter over the dissent of a minority by legislation passed subsequent to the organization of the company, "it is submitted that no mere generalities should ever be held to sanc-

Chronologically, the general incorporation laws of Maryland developed as follows: 

1798-The Vestry Act.70 1802-The Religious Corporations Act."¹ 1838-The Manufacturing and Mining Companies Act.72 1846-The Member Corporations Act.73 

1838-1868-Acts providing for the formation of building associations, cemetery companies, telegraph companies, oil companies, and universities and colleges.74 

None of the above acts contained any provision for charter amendments. In 1852, following the adoption of the new 

State Constitution of 1851, several of the above acts were repealed and re-enacted, and two of the new acts contained general provisions for amendment. These were as follows: 

1852-The Manufacturing Companies Act.75 Under this 

Act a two-thirds vote would authorize an increase or reduction of capital stock, or a change or extension of the business.76 

1852-The Member Corporations Act." This Act allowed amendment "by authority of the corporation."'78

Member corporations still might amend "by authority of the corporation."'81

In 1868 the General Corporation Law was revised. The title of the amendatory statute indicated an intention to repeal the corporation law as contained in the Code of 1860, but no section expressly did so.82 The Court of Appeals held, however, that the new law, being intended to be in lieu of the old, repealed it in its entirety, even where no inconsistency appeared.83 The new law provided (Section 42) that any "alteration or amendment *** made by the authority of the corporation" should be acknowledged and recorded in the same manner as an original certificate, and should then become a part of the charter. This provision, taken from the Member Corporations Act of 1852, was in force uninterruptedly until the revision of the General Corporation Law in 1908.84 It is clear that authorization would have to be voted by the stockholders rather than the directors;85 but it will be noted that the law is silent as to whether a majority vote or a unanimous vote of the stockholders would be required. Attention is called to the opinion of some writers that in the absence of an express statutory provision authorizing amendment by a majority or other designated proportion, any charter amendment would require unanimous consent.86

The Act of 1868 required only a two-thirds vote for increase or diminution of capital stock,87 or for reincorporation of thenexisting corporations under the new Act.88 Similarly, a manufacturing company might extend or change its business within the manufacturing field by a two-thirds vote.89 

These provisions of law remained virtually unchanged until 1908. The Code of 1888 (superseding all previous laws,⁹0) contained the added provision, (originally enacted in 1870) that a change in the par value of stock might be made by a two-thirds vote.⁹1

By Chapter 240 of the Acts of 1908, from which the modern corporation law of Maryland dates, it was provided that amendments changing the powers, name, business and principal office of the corporation, and classifying or re-classifying, increasing or reducing its capital stock, might be made by majority vote of the stockholders of each class entitled to vote.92 

The Act of 1916, Chapter 596, added the general clause, "and any other amendment that may be desired * * * but changed the majority vote provision to a requirement of two-thirds. . 99 By Chapter 545 of the Acts of 1920, the restriction, previously referred to, as to amendments changing the terms of outstanding stock, was added. 93

Finally, it was also enacted by Chapter 307 of the Acts of 1922 (now Art. 23, Sec. 23) that the corporate charter might validly provide for a majority vote of all shares in the aggregate to authorize any corporate action.94 

This extended history of the amending provisions of the Maryland corporation law has been deemed necessary because the careful practitioner, called upon to amend a Maryland would involve great uncertainty, and that it is essential for the practitioner to know under what circumstances such uncertainty can be eliminated.

81 charter, should know under what circumstances he must go into the question whether the proposed amendment is a "fundamental change." In the following cases the question need not be raised:

I. Any amendment, made for a proper business purpose, to the charter of a company incorporated after June 1, 1908.95 

II. An amendment to the charter of a manufacturing company increasing or reducing the capital stock, or changing or extending the corporate business within the manufacturing field, if the company was incorporated after May 29, 1852.96

III. An amendment reducing the par value of the stock of a company incorporated after April 4, 1870.97 

IV. An amendment increasing or reducing the authorized capital stock of a company incorporated after February 14, 1860.98 

V. An amendment extending or changing the business of any company incorporated between 1860 and 1868.99 

On the other hand, it is probable that the vote of a majority or two-thirds to reincorporate under the provisions of a general law would not change the situation as regards the right of a shareholder who did not approve the reincorporation to object to a "fundamental change" by amendment under such general law.

In all cases, therefore, except those enumerated above, the amendment should be determined to be not a fundamental change, or else unanimous consent should be obtained.¹ 44

As to what constitutes such a "fundamental change," the reader must be referred to the general works on corporation law.2

Thus far the question has been assumed to be one of construction only. There is, however, a growing body of legal writing which asserts that there are equitable limitations upon the power of the majority to amend a charter or change the corporate enterprise, fundamentally and radically-in effect impairing so-called "property rights" of the dissenting minority. Any amendment or other change of this character must, it appears, not only be adopted in strict accordance with the statutory and authorized charter provisions, but must be intended to serve a proper business purpose of the corporation as such. 2a 3

Charter as contract with State.-The conception of a corporate charter as a contract between the State and the corporation, declared by the Supreme Court of the United States in the Dartmouth College case, imposes upon the State the duty to pass no law impairing the obligation of such contract. There are certain well-defined exceptions to these rules, or cases which fall outside their operation:

I. A municipal corporation's charter is not a contract and may be amended by the State at will." 

II. The exercise of the police power is paramount to the obligation of an irrepealable charter.³ 

III. The exercise of the power of eminent domain by the 

State or by a corporation under power granted by it is likewise paramount to the obligation of an irrepealable charter." 

IV. The State may impair the value of a charter or franchise by granting similar privileges to other corporations intending to compete with the corporation first chartered.10 

V. A corporation may validly waive or release any of its charter rights or accept an amendment offered by the State either at or subsequent to incorporation, and the shareholders will be bound if they acquiesce in such waiver, release, or acceptance.11
