State's reserved power of amendment; surrender of exemptions from taxation.-As heretofore stated, since the adoption of the Constitution of 1851 the State has reserved the right to amend or repeal every corporate charter granted or adopted thereafter.15 The effect of the provision is that every such charter must be read as if the constitutional provision were incorporated therein.16 An amendment made by the State under this reserved power is valid without the subsequent consent of the corporation." The reservation is not exhausted by one amendment, but will sustain successive amendments.18 Moreover, the wisdom of the legislature in making an amendment under the reserved power is not open to question.19 Where the power to amend exists, regulation of a corporation, not otherwise valid, may be upheld as a charter amendment.20 A release of charter rights by a corporation under an agreement with the State is as effective as a reservation of power to permit the State to amend the charter in respect to such rights.21

§ 66. Limitations on State's reserved power of amendment. 

It has been pointed out that, according to the weight of authority, the State's reserved power is to be exercised for the benefit of the State alone and cannot be set up by a majority seeking to justify a "fundamental change" made under subsequent general legislation against the dissent of a minority.29 Other limitations on the scope of the reserved power are as follows:

I. The State's reserved power is to be read into those charters only which were granted or adopted since 1851.30 

II. Even where the reserved power exists, an amendment changing the "fundamental character" of the corporation would be outside such power,31 and would be valid only if accepted by the corporation, unanimous acceptance or acquiescence being in that event required.32

III. The reserved power would not authorize an arbitrary, unreasonable, and oppressive amendment, nor any amend-

Power to make, alter and repeal by-laws.-The scope of the power of a corporation to make by-laws is thus expressed in Section 9 of Article 23: a corporation shall have power "to make by-laws not inconsistent with law or with its charter for regulating the government of the corporation and for the administration of its affairs." 

Under Section 15 the by-law power is vested generally in the stockholders or members, but under certain conditions and to a limited extent may be vested in the directors. 89 adopt and alter by-laws is vested in the directors prior to the issuance of voting stock, but in the case of a non-stock corporation the power is vested in the members from the time of creation of the corporation. In all cases the directors may be empowered by the by-laws adopted by the stockholders or members (or by the directors of a stock corporation prior to issuance of stock), to make, alter, and repeal additional or supplementary by-laws, not inconsistent with any of the "by-laws adopted as aforesaid," but such supplementary by-laws may be altered or repealed by the stockholders or members.2

With the exceptions above stated, the statute does not authorize delegation to the directors of power to make by-laws. 

The statutory provisions as to "additional or supplementary by-laws" adopted by the directors have not been construed by the courts.³ 5 While the by-laws may be amended only at a general meeting, or at a special meeting convened for the purpose,4 meetings called at regular intervals for a specific purpose, such as the election of directors, may become, by force of custom, general meetings at which action on the by-laws may be taken. A custom regulating the manner of proposing candidates for office has also been regarded as binding, and as having the force of a by-law. Any custom is, however, invalid if in conflict with the charter of the corporation."

93 the powers of the board in the management of the business and affairs of the corporation may be delegated to the executive committee to the extent authorized by the by-laws. (d) Officers.-A corporation may prescribe by its by-laws "the powers, duties and tenure of its officers and agents."36

The statute requires that every corporation shall have a president, a secretary, and a treasurer, of whom the president shall be chosen from among the directors, and the by-laws may provide for one or more vice-presidents, assistant secretaries, and assistant treasurers. All the officers are chosen by the board of directors unless the by-laws otherwise provide, and vacancies among the officers are filled by the board unless the by-laws otherwise provide.37 Any two offices, except those of president and vice-president, may, if provided by the by-laws, be held by the same person.38 

The by-laws may provide that the annual report of the corporation shall be prepared by an executive officer other than the president.39 § 72. (e) Stock.-The by-laws may incorporate any desired limitations or restrictions as to the issuance of stock under statutory and charter provisions.40

(g) Amendment of by-laws.—As previously stated, amendments to the by-laws may be made only by the stockholders or members, except in the case of a stock corporation which has no voting stock outstanding.48 In any event, reasonable restrictions may be imposed by the by-laws on the power of amending such by-laws.49 Moreover, the board of directors may be given power, in the by-laws, to make, alter, and repeal additional or supplementary by-laws, not inconsistent with the by-laws adopted by the stockholders or members (or by the directors of a stock corporation prior to the issuance of stock).50 § 75. Copy of by-laws to be kept at principal office in State; evidence of by-laws.-The original or a certified copy of the by-laws, with all amendments thereto, is required to be kept at the principal office in Maryland for inspection by stockholders or members.51 A copy of the by-laws, certified "to be a true copy, under the seal of the corporation by the president or a vice-president, and the secretary, or an assistant secretary, or the treasurer, or an assistant treasurer," is made prima facie evidence of such by-laws in courts of the State.52 § 76. By-laws as to order of procedure are, as a rule, directory rather than mandatory, so that an election of officers is valid though made in violation of a by-law that officers' salaries shall be fixed before election.75 A by-law of a non-stock corporation dividing its membership into classes, of which only the "active" members shall be entitled to vote, does not govern in case of a special election, held by virtue of a special act of the legislature which does not distinguish between different classes of membership.76 Fraud of judges in counting ballots for election of officers and in accepting and rejecting proxies may be attacked despite a by-law authorizing the directors to appoint judges of election and making their decision final.77 

§ 78. Authority and duties of officers and agents.-Corpora tions are expressly authorized to regulate in their by-laws the powers and duties of their officers and agents.78 The effect of such regulations upon the stockholders or members, and upon third persons without notice, has already been referred to.79 

A by-law conferring full control of the business upon the president of a corporation, subject to the approval of the board of directors, does not empower him, after the corporation has become insolvent, to transfer all its assets to one of its creditors, without obtaining the assent of the board.80 Where a by-law of a corporation engaged in the brokerage business authorized it to buy produce for its own account "when deemed necessary by the executive committee to avoid loss," such by-law was admissible to negative the defense that the general manager of the company had no authority to contract to buy a shipment of pears.81 A by-law defining the powers of the president and general manager of a brewing company was inadmissible, as against a third person, to show that such officer lacked of any corporation may require a vote for any purpose greater than that otherwise required by law (Secs. 5, 21), but only certain non-stock corporations may regulate the quorum at members' meetings in their by-laws.

§ 79. Compensation of officers and agents. Since by statute the directors may exercise all of the corporate powers, except those conferred upon the stockholders by law or by the charter or the by-laws,85 it follows that the compensation of officers and agents is to be fixed by the board of directors unless otherwise provided. A by-law provision granting such power to the directors is customary, however, and such provision has been held to prevent the president of a corporation, who had entire charge of its business, from increasing the salary of the treasurer as fixed by the board of directors, even though he and the treasurer owned a majority of the stock.87 Despite a by-law providing that compensation shall be fixed before election, action of the board in electing officers and subsequently fixing their salaries is not invalid.88 § 80. BY-LAWS 

103 A business association may validly provide in its by-laws that its members shall have no dealings with a person engaging in "proceedings inconsistent with just and equitable principles of trade."10 A by-law of a grocers' association is also valid which provides that members shall cease to be such on retiring from the grocery business.11

A by-law of a savings bank which provides for special deposits having a prior lien but not sharing in profits or surplus is within the powers of the bank.12 

Shareholders in a building association are not creditors until they have given notice of withdrawal, as prescribed by the by-laws, and therefore are not entitled to a receivership on the ground of insolvency, without giving such notice, where the association is not insolvent unless their claims are counted as liabilities. 13 Fines on members, as imposed by the by-laws, are enforcible in equity.14 Borrowers are not stockholders, regardless of by-law provisions declaring them to be such.15 They cannot vote at meetings, nor are they entitled to notice thereof, even though the by-laws expressly require it.16 By-laws of which borrowers have no express notice are not binding on them, since they are not stockholders." Entrance fees must be fixed in the charter in order to be valid, and no discrimination in this respect between borrowing and non-borrowing "members" is permitted. 18 

10 McCarter v. Baltimore Chamber of Commerce, (1915) 126 Md. 131, 94 Atl. 541 (Chamber not liable to third person for loss of employment contracts due to notice by Chamber to its members to have no dealings with plaintiff, acting pursuant to by-laws).

Incorporators, directors, and stockholders; incorporation complete without meeting.-The modern idea of a corporation as a creature of business convenience rather than an association of persons is carried, under Maryland law, to the extent of regarding incorporators as mere signatories having no connection with the company other than appearing as the subscribers to its certificate of incorporation. No meeting of the incorporators or of any other group is prerequisite to the creation of the legal entity. There are, however, a few concessions to the group theory: (1) the incorporators of a stock corporation may amend its charter before any subscriptions have been accepted; (2) the incorporators of any company which has no assets or liabilities and has issued no stock may petition for dissolution; and (3) the incorporators are doubtless responsible for matters of fact stated in the charter-though their valuation of the con- 

1 See §§ 16-18, supra. See also Art. 23, Sec. 7.

sideration for which stock is issued, as stated in the charter, is "conclusive for all purposes in the absence of actual fraud."4 5 It is suggested by a leading text-writer that the incorporators are the actual members of a corporation and can act "as the supreme authority" until stock has been issued. Even if this is true, theoretically, under the Maryland law, the statutory provisions granting full power to the directors as to adoption of by-laws and issuance of stock before the corporation actually has stockholders, leave it a matter of slight practical importance to determine the exact status of the incorporators." 

Since the incorporators have virtually no powers under the Maryland law, and since there can be no stockholders until the issuance of stock has been authorized by the proper body, it follows that the complete organization of a stock corporation requires a meeting of the directors named as such in the charter, who, as just pointed out, may exercise the powers of the corporation to issue stock and thus create the stockholders. 

A corporation may continue in existence indefinitely without issuing stock and without exercising any powers, unless the State asserts a right to forfeit the charter by judicial proceedings for "non-user of franchises."

Adoption of by-laws.-The power to adopt by-laws, as indicated before, 23 is conferred on the directors of a stock corporation prior to the issuance of stock. 24 It is of vital importance, therefore, that the directors should adopt by-laws before any resolutions are passed relating to the issuance of stock, because (1) as soon as stock has been issued, the corporation can adopt no by-laws until it holds a meeting of stockholders; and (2) the difficult question may be encountered as to whether or not an offer on the part of subscribers, followed by resolutions of the board, has resulted in the creation of stockholders, 25 so that those guiding the corporation might then be in doubt as to which group had the power to adopt valid by-laws.

§ 87. Election of officers; qualifications.-The directors elect the officers, in the absence of a by-law provision to the contrary.28 The president must be a member of the board, but no other officer need be chosen from among the directors.29 

If it is desired that more than one office should be held by the same person, the by-laws should contain a provision to that effect.30 The officers are ordinarily elected to serve until the first annual meeting and thereafter until their successors are duly chosen and have qualified.31 Subordinate offices may be created, but there must in any event be a president, a secretary, and a treasurer. 32 § 88. Agents; compensation of officers and agents.-If a general manager or other agents are to be selected, they or some of them may well be appointed by the board at the organization meeting.33 Salaries of officers and agents are to be fixed by the board, in default of by-law provisions, 84 and it is often desirable to fix such salaries at the organization meeting or soon thereafter. It is a general principle that officers are not entitled to compensation for their services as such, in the absence of an understanding to the contrary.35

Resignations of temporary directors; increase in board; filling vacancies.-Where it is desired not to name the final directors of the corporation in the charter, and to have the routine matters of organization attended to by a meeting of temporary directors, the by-laws should include a provision empowering the directors, by vote of a majority of the entire board, to increase the membership of the board to not exceeding a certain number and to fill the vacancies created by such increase.43 Toward the close of the meeting the temporary directors tender their resignations "to take effect at the end of the meeting," pass a resolution accepting such resignations, and fill the vacancies thereby created. The board is next increased to the desired number and the additional directors elected by virtue of the by-law provision above discussed.44 

The result may be that the meeting will no longer contain a quorum, so that the increase of the board should not take place until all other business has been transacted. Furthermore, the election of officers should be postponed to a subsequent meeting if the intended president cannot be made a member of the board prior to the election at the first meeting. 45

The above description of a meeting conducted by temporary directors will be better understood by reference to the form of minutes of the organization meeting included in Part II. further certify that said by-law provision (or resolution) is in force (or, that the above officers are still in office) at this date. § 93. Necessity for two separate meetings.-Because of the fact that no power is given to the directors of a non-stock corporation to adopt by-laws,¹ it is necessary to hold a meeting of the members of such a corporation in order to complete organization. Under the best practice the first members are named in the charter, and it is then possible to have the meeting of members prior to any meeting of directors. Otherwise the meeting of directors must precede in order to have the directors elect the first members, unless the charter contains no provision for members as distinct from directors, when the directors are, by statute, constituted the members for purposes of taking corporate action as members. In such event there must nevertheless be two separate meetings.5 

Routine matters in connection with the organization should normally be transacted at the directors' meeting rather than at that of the members. 4

§ 94. Meeting of members. At the members' meeting, when held first, a waiver of notice, as in the case of the directors' meeting, should be signed by all members named in the charter. Following organization of the meeting, the charter is accepted and the form of by-laws adopted. The procedure is the same as in the case of the directors' meeting discussed in the preceding chapter. Any temporary members may present their resignations to take effect at the end of the meeting, provided the by-laws clearly make provision for the directors to elect members and fill vacancies. Meetings of members of a non-stock corporation may be held outside the State if the charter so provides." 

§ 95. Meeting of directors. 10-The meeting of directors in the case of a non-stock corporation is conducted in the same manner as the meeting of directors of a stock corporation.11 The acceptance of the charter and adoption of by-laws, having been attended to at the members' meeting, are, of course, omitted, as are resolutions relating to issuance of stock. There is usually no provision for an executive committee, and the officers are seldom paid salaries. In other respects, however, the suggestions made in the preceding chapter can be followed. Frequently the by-laws provide for election of officers by the members, and in that event the election minutes may simply be transferred to the earlier meeting of members. If the directors' meeting must be held first because it is not clear who the members are, it is essential for the directors to resolve the doubt by electing members, if empowered to do so.12

121 122 § 96. Authorized capital stock; issued stock; stock certificates. The corporation law provides separately for the authorization of stock and for its subsequent issue. Stock may be authorized only by the terms of the certificate of incorporation, original or amended. This is required to state "the total amount of capital stock, if any, of the proposed corporation, and the number and par value of the shares." If there are non-par shares the certificate is required to state that such shares are without par value and the number authorized.2 Authorized but unissued stock is not capital, but only potential capital convertible into actual capital by its issuance for value. It has existence in the sense that an agreement to issue it can be specifically enforced in equity notwithstanding the rule that equity will not enforce specifically an agreement to deliver non-existent property.4

In the case of convertible stock rather than obligations, it is, however, provided that "the authorization of the issuance of stock of any class which is by the terms of the charter convertible into stock of another class shall constitute the authorization of the issuance, in accordance with the terms of the charter, of the stock into which such stock is convertible."21

They are as follows: 

I. Issuance of par stock or securities convertible into such stock for money at not less than the par value of such stock.-The board of directors may, subject to charter or by-law restrictions, authorize such issue.22 

II. Issuance of non-par stock or securities convertible into such stock by directors under power conferred by charter.-If empowered to do so by the charter, the board of directors may, subject to charter or by-law restrictions, authorize the issuance of non-par shares of any class or securities convertible into such shares, stating by resolution the value of any consideration other than money for which it authorizes such shares to be issued unless such value shall have been fixed by the charter.23

III. Issuance of stock of any class or securities convertible into stock of any class, for any consideration not stated in charter. 

Section 43 of Article 23 provides a method by which stock of any class or securities convertible into stock of any class may, subject to charter or by-law restrictions, be issued for any consideration not stated in the charter. Any stock which may be issued under either Section 42 (Paragraph I, above) or Section 45 (Paragraph II, above) may be issued under Section 43, although the requirements of this section are more exacting. 

Section 43 requires the following as prerequisite for issuance: (a) The issuance must be authorized by the corporation. 

If no stock is outstanding and entitled to vote or if the charter or certificate of incorporation so permits, the board of directors may authorize the issuance, stating the value of the consideration by resolution. 

If there is stock outstanding and entitled to vote, the authorization must be by resolution of the board of directors advising issuance for a certain specified consideration (stating the value thereof, if other than money) approved at a meeting of stockholders by the vote of two-thirds of each class of stock outstanding and entitled to vote. 

22 Art. 23, Sec. 42. 

23 Art. 23, Sec. 45.

(b) A sworn statement must be filed with the State Tax Commission (with the recording fee of $5.00) showing in detail in the form prescribed by the statute: (1) The corporate authorization of the issue; (2) The nature of the stock or convertible securities and the character and amount of the consideration paid or to be paid therefor; (3) The terms of conversion of any convertible securities. 

A form of stock issuance statement is given in Part II. 

IV. Issuance of stock of any class or of securities convertible into stock of any class, for considerations stated in charter.— 

Section 44 provides an alternative method of issuing any stock or convertible securities for any consideration. By this method the directors may (if the charter permits) issue stock of any class or securities convertible into stock of any class, subject to charter or by-law restrictions, without filing the stock issuance statement required by Section 43, provided the certificate of incorporation states the consideration to be received and/or the terms of conversion with the same particularity with which they are required by Section 43 to be stated in the stock issuance statement. 

It will be observed that the methods of issuance summarized in Paragraphs III and IV permit fully paid and non-assessable par stock to be issued for less than par and permit convertible securities to be issued for less than the par value of the stock into which they are convertible. This is also specifically permitted by Section 41(8).24

In reference to Methods I, II, III, and IV, it is provided that: (1) "Consideration other than money" includes a consideration partly in money;' .25 

24 A statute prohibiting, in general terms, the issuance of stock except for money, labor done or property actually received, forbids issuance of par stock for less than par. Trent Import Co. v. Wheelwright, (1912) 118 Md.

§ 101. Limitations on liability. The liability of stock holders, in all except banking corporations,¹ is limited to the unpaid portion of the stock subscription under the terms of the subscription contract. When the agreed consideration, of whatever nature, has been paid for stock, it becomes fully paid and non-assessable. Moreover, as previously stated, the valuation placed by the directors or incorporators, as the case may be, on considerations other than money for which stock is issued, is conclusive for all purposes in the absence of actual fraud.4 3 

§ 102. Conflicting rights of stockholders and creditors.- 

The effect of the statutory provisions and decisions thereunder is to afford absolute protection to a subscriber or transferee who in good faith receives stock for which the agreed con- ¹ Including safe deposit, trust and loan corporations. While a transferee is ordinarily liable for calls and assessments, on the theory of a novation, he is entitled to rescind the transfer of stock to him, upon discovery that the agreed consideration has not been paid therefor, and he is not subject to calls or liable to the receiver suing for the benefit of creditors. Likewise a stockholder whose subscription has been induced by fraud is entitled to rescind such subscription upon discovery of the fraud. A corporation is estopped to make any assessments or calls upon stock which it has issued as fully paid. For the protection of creditors, upon insolvency, a provision of statute expressly empowers the receiver of a corporation to enforce the liability of the stockholders to the corporation. Assets other than the liability of stockholders must be exhausted before such liability is resorted to,¹0 but the "insolvency" referred to in the statute is that resulting from insufficiency of the assets exclusive of liability of stockholders. ¹¹

Conditions of liability.-The liability to creditors as represented by the receiver in the event of insolvency, and the liability for calls and assessments made by the corporation are virtually coextensive, both being limited to the unpaid portion of the purchase price according to the terms of the subscription contract and both being subject to approximately the same conditions and defenses.32 An outline of such conditions and defenses follows.

§ 106. Enforcement of calls and assessments.-Unpaid subscriptions may be called at any time by the board of directors (unless otherwise provided) on thirty days' written notice, which may, however, be waived by the stockholder.78 If any installment is not paid when due, the directors may bring an action therefor, or may sell at public sale a sufficient number of shares to pay assessments and expenses then accrued.79 

Advertisement for three weeks is required, and twenty days' notice of sale must be given the shareholder.80 If there is no bidder, and an action at law has been brought against the shareholder, the stock and all payments theretofore made are forfeited to the corporation within six months after the institution of the action, 81

Liability of stockholders to the receiver of an insolvent corporation on unpaid stock subscriptions or for dividends paid during insolvency may be enforced either by a single suit in equity, to avoid a multiplicity of suits, or by separate actions at law. 82 The fact of insolvency, the ascertainment of debts, and the proportionate amount of assessments necessary may be adjudicated by order of the equity court in the receivership proceeding, and such order is binding on all permitted, though in an action by the creditor at law under the old statute he was required first to pay his own subscription in full). § 107. General considerations.-Every corporation directed by statute to "hold annually a stated or regular meeting for the election of directors and for the transaction of general business."1 Other meetings, which may be called at any time on ten days' notice by the president or a majority of the board of directors,' are known as special or extraordinary meetings. The annual meeting is open to the transaction of any business, unless otherwise provided by the by-laws." 3 ¹ Art. 23, Sec. 17. The entire board of directors must be elected at every annual meeting (Art. 23. Sec. 10), unless the by-laws provide for a division of the directors into classes (Sec. 14; and see §§ 69, supra, and 115, infra). 

The existing board continues in office, however, on failure to hold the annual election (Sec. 25). 

Art. 23, Sec. 19 (1). Special meetings may also be called by a majority of the executive committee, if the by-laws so provide (Sec. 19), or by the holders of a majority of the voting stock or a majority of the members (special provisions as to notice-see the following section). Borrowers from a building association need not be counted in determining whether the requisite proportion of stockholders joined in calling a meeting. First 

Mortgage Bond Homestead Assn. v. Baker, (1929) 157 Md. 309, 145 Atl. 876.

Art. 23, Sec. 19 (1). 

Art. 23, Sec. 17. An amendment to the by-laws cannot be made at the annual meeting without notice of intention to make such amendment, if the charter requires such notice. Mutual Fire Ins. Co. v. Farquhar, (1898) 86 

Md. 668, 39 Atl. 527. 137

While the by-laws may regulate the time and place of holding such meetings, and the notice to be given thereof," the statute allows no freedom as to time and manner of notice of special meetings, and the business which may be transacted thereat is limited to that specified in the notice." Stockholders' meetings may be held outside the State, under certain conditions, though meetings of the members of a non-stock corporation may be held outside the State merely if the charter so provides.⁹ An individual stockholder has the right to compel by mandamus the holding of a regular meeting at the time required by the corporate regulations.10

While a presumption of regularity attends corporate proceedings, especially after the lapse of time,¹¹ action taken by the stockholders or members individually or not at a duly called and constituted meeting is ineffectual.12 Even if the shareholders and the directors are the same persons, action taken by the directors may be invalid when stockholders' approval is required unless a separate and distinct meeting of stockholders is held. 13 Ratification by the stockholders may, however, be presumed if the stockholders meet and take no action,¹4 unless, at least, the statute requires an affirmative vote of ratification.

§ 109. Time and manner of giving notice.—In the case of special meetings, ten days' written or printed notice must be "given to each shareholder or member by leaving the same with him or at his residence or usual place of business, or by mailing it, postage prepaid, and addressed to him at his address, as it appears upon the books of the corporation."23 

The same notice must be given of each annual meeting, unless the by-laws otherwise provide;24 but entire freedom is given to regulate by the by-laws the time and manner of giving notice of annual meetings. 25 The provisions just discussed apply to regular meetings and to special meetings called by the president, or by a majority of the board of directors or executive committee. Power to convene a special meeting, however, is also conferred upon the holders of a majority of the voting stock, or a majority of the members. Upon request in writing of such majority delivered to the president, the secretary or a director, it is the duty of such president, secretary or director to call a meeting for the purpose stated in the request. If the officer or director so requested fails within three days to issue a call for the meeting, the majority stockholders or members may do so by giving fifteen days' notice of such meeting by advertisement inserted in a newspaper published in the county or city in which the principal office of the corporation is situated.26 

§ 110. Contents of notice.-Unless otherwise provided by the by-laws 27 the notice of the regular annual meeting need not contain a statement of the purposes of the meeting, and any business may be transacted thereat,28 except extraordinary business for which the law specifically requires notification.29 At a special meeting, however, no business except that named in the notice may be transacted."

§ 112. Quorum.-The proportion of stock or membership which shall constitute a quorum may be regulated by the charter. In the absence of such regulation, a majority of the voting stock or membership is required. 43 Certain member corporations may provide by their by-laws what shall constitute a quorum.44 It is frequently provided by the bylaws of a corporation that a majority of the stock or membership in attendance at a meeting may adjourn such meeting from time to time, although a quorum is not present, and such provision is no doubt valid as a reasonable and generally sanctioned practice.45 The adjourned meeting requires no notice.46 Even though the minutes of a meeting do not state that a quorum was present, it is so presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary.47 § 113. § 116. Acts requiring vote of stockholders or members.-

§ 117. Election of directors.-The directors are elected by the stockholders or members at the annual meeting for a term of one year, unless the by-laws divide the directors into classes, one class being elected in each year. The subject of election of directors has already been discussed in connection with by-laws¹ and stockholders' meetings.2 3 § 118. Powers and authority of directors. It is expressly provided by statute that the board of directors may exercise all corporate powers except such as are by statute, charter, or by-laws reserved to the stockholders or members. A list of corporate acts for which the statute expressly requires a vote of stockholders or members is given elsewhere. While such a vote is required in case of a mortgage or deed of trust of any of the "franchises" of the corporation," the directors, it would seem, may authorize a mortgage of corporate property not including franchises. As to a matter within the powers of the board of directors, a resolution passed by stockholders or members does not control their discretion, unless it can be regarded as a validly adopted by-law." § 119. Declaration of dividends.-There being no statute expressly providing for the declaration and payment of dividends out of surplus or net profits, the board of directors is vested with full power and discretion with respect thereto, as at common law. 20 Numerous cases have arisen in which the issue was whether a particular dividend (cash or stock) should be regarded as income or as corpus. The rule established is that, as between two persons such as life tenant and remainderman, a dividend or portion thereof representing earnings of the corporation during the period of the life tenancy will be regarded as income, but a dividend or portion thereof representing earnings prior to the life tenancy will be taken to be corpus, and the declarations of the directors as to the source of the dividend will be controlling.21 While a stock dividend capitalizing earnings is, in general, regarded as income to the same extent as a cash dividend,22 it has, however, been held that a stock dividend representing proceeds of sale of certain securities which had been purchased out of accumulated net profits is corpus and not income as between

155 An issuance of stock to members of the board of directors for the sole purpose of enabling them to control the corporation, though made with all formalities required by law and by the charter and by-laws, is, according to a recent statement of the court, void as not carried out in the interest of the stockholders as a whole.57 

§ 122. Personal liability. The statute imposes personal liability on directors for (a) improper declaration of dividends and (b) losses resulting from loans to stockholders or directors. (a) The first liability is imposed upon any directors who shall "knowingly or without making reasonable inquiry vote for, or assent to, the declaration of any dividend when the corporation is insolvent, or any dividend, the payment of which would render it insolvent, or would diminish the amount of the capital stock." In event of such payment, such directors become liable, jointly and severally, to the extent of such payment, "for all the debts of the corporation then existing."'58 

The above wording of the statute is contained in the 1931 amendment. Prior thereto, every director was liable in event of improper payment of dividends unless before such payment he placed a certificate of his objection on record. A further important limitation included in the statute by the 1931 amendment is the following: "A dividend from the surplus or the net profits of the corporation as determined in accordance with good accounting practice shall not be deemed to diminish the amount of the capital stock."59 Liability for the payment of dividends out of net earnings when the capital assets of the corporation had shrunk in value, so that there was no surplus, was not clear until the amendment. The 

Maryland Court of Appeals had not passed upon the question. 

It was raised in a recent New Jersey case involving a Maryland corporation, but was not decided, the court assuming for the purposes of its opinion that such a dividend would be illegal, 7 First Mortgage Bond Homestead Assn. v. Baker, (1929) 157 Md. 309, 145 Atl. 876, citing Punt v. Symons & Co., Ltd., [1903] 2 Ch. 506, 515; 

Elliott v. Baker, (1907) 194 Mass. 518, 523, 80 N.E. 450; Luther v. Luther 

Co., (1903) 118 Wis. 112, 94 N.W. 69, 99 Am. St. Rep. 977. See also Street, Ultra Vires (1930 ed. of Bryce's Ultra Vires), p. 360. 

50 Id.

Art. 23, Sec. 87, as amended by L. 1931, Ch. 480.

but expressly stating that only the Maryland Court could determine the question.60 Prior to the amendment, also, the liability of participating directors extended to debts thereafter contracted "while they should respectively remain in office," but this additional liability was omitted from the amended section. (b) The liability in case of loans is imposed on the officer or officers or directors who make any loan to a stockholder or director or who assent to the making of such loan. It is a joint and several liability "for all debts of said corporation," and is limited to "the extent of the loss that may result from such loan."61 There is no specific requirement that the creditor asserting the liability shall have become such while the director or officer sued continues in office. The provision as to loans does not apply to "any homestead or building association, or any corporation whose principal business under its charter is to loan money on real or personal property, or to any corporation receiving or authorized to receive money on deposit, or to any life insurance company lending money to any of its policy holders on their policies."'62 The 1931 amendment eliminates the previous prohibition of loans to stockholders and directors, but leaves the liability of directors and officers unchanged.63

In the event of the insolvency of the corporation, the liability in respect of improper dividends and loans is collectible by the receiver or other person winding up its affairs, as an asset of the corporation.64

Upon the dissolution of a corporation "otherwise than by judicial proceedings," the directors take title to and become trustees of its assets for the creditors, stockholders, and members, and become "jointly and severally liable to the creditors, stockholders and members to the extent of its

§ 123. Election of officers.-Unless otherwise provided by the by-laws,¹ officers are chosen by the board of directors for the term of one year. The statutory provision as to officers and their election is as follows:

Every corporation subject to the provision of this article shall have a president, a secretary and a treasurer, all of whom shall be chosen by the board of directors unless the by-laws otherwise provide. 

The president shall be chosen from among the directors. The corporation may have one or more vice-presidents, assistant secretaries and assistant treasurers, if the by-laws so provide, all of whom shall be chosen by the board of directors, unless the by-laws otherwise provide. 

Any two of the above offices, except those of president and vicepresident, may, if provided by the by-laws, be held by the same person, but no officer shall execute, acknowledge or verify any instrument in more than one capacity, if such instrument is required by law or by the by-laws to be executed, acknowledged or verified by any two or more officers. Except when otherwise provided the directors and officers hereinbefore mentioned shall hold office for one year and until their successors are chosen and qualified. The manner of filling all vacancies occurring in the board of directors or among the officers hereinbefore mentioned shall be as provided in the by-laws; 

1 As to by-laws, see § 71, supra. 159

and in default of such by-laws such vacancies shall be filled by the board of directors.2

Though ordinarily a vote of shareholders or directors is necessary to elect or appoint officers, it has been held that the appointment of an officer may be "inferred." Persons acting as officers are presumed to be such and rightfully in office in the absence of proof to the contrary. A custom requiring notice of the names of candidates for office has been regarded as constituting a valid and effective by-law. 5 § 124. Authority of officers; general manager. The liability of a corporation for the acts of its officers and agents is governed by general principles of the law of agency, provided the acts done do not exceed the charter powers of the corporation. Acts of officers which are within the scope of general powers ordinarily exercised by such officers are binding on the corporation. Similarly, a corporation taking the full benefit of a transaction entered into by officers is presumed to have authorized or ratified it,' and a company having treated a contract made by officers as valid is estopped to deny their authority. Greater familiarity with the duties and authority of officers is expected of a shareholder or member than would be required of an outsider. For example, it has been held that the payment of dues by a member to an officer who had

President.-Powers incidental to the discharge of duties delegated to the president of a corporation are within his authority, and he is permitted to choose his own method of performing such duties. Thus it has been held that a president authorized to purchase stock of another company may employ an agent to do so and render the corporation liable for the compensation of such agent, even though the facts as to the employment of the agent were misstated to the corporation.10 

A corporation is estopped to deny the authority of the president to borrow money and execute a chattel mortgage of corporate property, where he has been accustomed to borrow money for the corporation whenever needed without the express authorization of the board of directors.11 The fact that the president ordered work done and that the work was done and accepted, is sufficient to justify a finding that the corporation authorized or ratified the contract. 12 On the other hand, extraordinary powers may be vested in the president only by express action of the board of directors. 

Where the by-laws provided that the president (subject to the approval of the board of directors) should have full control of the business, he was not authorized, on the insolvency of the corporation and without the consent of the board, to transfer all the corporate assets to one creditor as against another creditor subsequently attaching part of them.13

§ 126. Liability of corporation for wrongful acts of officers.- 

The mere fact that a person engaging in a wrongful act or an illegal transaction is an officer of a corporation does not render the corporation liable therefor; the act or transaction must have been in furtherance of the business of the corporation or intended for its benefit and advantage.41 In accordance with the converse of this rule a corporation selling a lot under water as dry land was held liable in deceit to the purchaser thereof, where the sale was made by means of a false plat sent by the president of the corporation to the president of another company acting as sales agent. The president of the latter company knew of the falsity of the plat, and the court stated that both corporations and both presidents individually could be sued by the purchaser.42 On the other hand, where the purchaser of bonds sold by a bank on commission sued the bank for misrepresentation, no liability was imposed because the sale was an ultra vires transaction. 43 

It has also been held that a bank cashier has no implied authority to represent the bank in ordering an arrest, and that in the absence of express precedent authority or subsequent ratification a bank is not liable for malicious arrest and false imprisonment at the request of its cashier.44 And

§ 127. Liability of corporation for wrongful acts of agents.— 

Liability for the wrongful acts of agents is governed by the same principles as liability for the wrongful acts of officers. 

The act must have been performed for the benefit of the corporation and as part of its business and must have been within the scope of the agent's authority. 48 The principal's liability is tested by the apparent scope of the agent's employment and is not limited by secret instructions. Thus, where an agent brought an unsuccessful foreign attachment suit, the liability of the corporation for malicious prosecution was not defeated by written instructions to the agent prohibiting attachments unless expressly authorized.49 Generally speaking, a corporation is responsible for the wilful tort of an agent within the scope of his employment even though unknown to the corporation or forbidden, and irrespective of whether the corporation actually benefited. 50

§ 129. Personal liability for acts performed or contracts made in own name for corporation. Whether an officer or agent, in making a contract, is acting on his own responsibility or as the representative of the corporation, so as to impose liability on it, is ordinarily a question of fact. For example, where the president of a corporation ordered a survey made of land owned by it, the question whether he was personally liable for the cost of the survey was in doubt on the evidence and was therefore left to the jury.68 And where the general manager of a company ordered an employee to take another employee to a street car in such manager's personal automobile, the manager did not thereby relieve himself from responsibility for the driver's negligence and place such responsibility on the company.69 But where demand for the transfer of stock was made on the secretary and treasurer of a company and wrongfully refused, the president, who knew nothing of the matter, was not personally liable for conversion of the stock.70 

Where an agent signs a written contract in his own name, ordinarily both the agent and the principal are bound to the third party;"¹ the agent, however, if the third party understood he was contracting on behalf of a corporate principal, may, when sued, recoup for damages incurred by such principal.72 

In case of ambiguity as to whether the contract on its face is that of the agent or the corporation, parol evidence may be admitted.73

A contract signed by the president of a corporation in his own name was nevertheless the contract of the corporation

§ 134. Majority and minority stockholders.-The courts have repeatedly stated that, in the absence of fraudulent, illegal, or ultra vires acts, minority stockholders of a corporation have no standing in court to control the actions of the majority. The latter, it has been said, are not trustees or quasi-trustees for the minority and may exercise their control for any purposes they desire so long as ultra vires acts or fraud or illegality are not committed. § 136. Illegal or ultra vires acts as ground for relief. 

Relief to minority shareholders on the ground of illegality is granted only if acts illegal in themselves have been done or threatened; mere mismanagement or the doing of a lawful thing in an unlawful manner, it has been said, does not justify interference by a court of equity.23 Ultra vires acts also afford ground for relief. A stockholder is entitled to enforce the provisions of a corporate charter by injunction 24 or by mandamus.25 

§ 137. Methods of relief. Where the right to judicial interference has been established, as in the case of fraud or illegal or ultra vires acts, various methods of relief have been sought and granted, in accordance with the particular circumstances involved. Mandamus has been allowed to enforce compliance with charter provisions relating to the holding of an election,26 and to require officers or directors fraudulently declared elected to yield up their positions to those who were actually elected. 27 Minority stockholders may also protect their rights by an injunction against the commission of ultra vires, fraudulent, or illegal acts. 28 In an unusual case relief was granted in the form of a decree for an accounting by the agent of a foreign corporation to a resident minority stock-

The question under what terms and conditions a minority stockholder can maintain or defend a suit on behalf of the corporation is of some importance. In the case of a beneficial society it was held that members who had left the corporation could not maintain a suit to recover corporate funds.33 

Shortly afterwards the question was presented more directly. 

The court decided that shareholders ordinarily cannot file a bill on behalf of the corporation in the absence of proof that the directors or officers have refused to institute proceedings or are not the proper persons to prosecute, but that demand on the directors is unnecessary where they themselves are guilty of the wrongs complained of.34 On a second appeal this

It was decided that the corporation, representing the minority stockholders, might recover their proportion of the excess payments, to be turned over to them, but that no right of recovery existed with respect to the remaining proportion of such payments. 88 Since suit was brought in the name of the corporation by the new management, no question was presented as to the right of the minority to sue directly, or to file a bill in the name of the corporation without the coöperation of the management. In a later case it was held that equity has jurisdiction of a suit by a stockholder to prevent the collection of promissory notes of a corporation issued ultra vires. 39

It would seem, therefore, that the Court is not at all committed to the doctrine that the only relief which a stockholder can have against third persons dealing with the corporation " Davis v. Gemmell, (1891) 73 Md. 530, 21 Atl. 712. This case also holds that a minority stockholder, in such a suit, cannot plead limitations on behalf of the corporation. A stockholder cannot appeal from a judgment against the corporation. Preston v. Poe, (1911) 116 Md. 1, 81 Atl. 178. If a corporation is dissolved by judicial proceedings, defenses to claims, including limitations, may be interposed by any stockholder. Art. 23, Sec. 97.

If the stockholder's right to relief is clear, and if the directors, upon demand, refuse to act, or if they are concerned in the wrongful acts complained of, the stockholder should be permitted to litigate in equity the narrow questions which affect his rights without acting through a receiver. The overwhelming weight of authority in other jurisdictions permits such suits.40 

Where, however, a bill was filed by majority stockholders, in their name, to enforce a right of the corporation, it was held that the bill was not maintainable; the stockholders should have proceeded through and in the name of the corporation, obtaining proper corporate action as their control would enable them to do.41 § 138. In considering the attachment of stock in a domestic corporation, the controlling provisions are those of the Uniform Stock Transfer Act, applicable to certificates issued after 

July 1, 1910. These provisions are as follows: 

63. No attachment or levy upon shares of stock for which a certificate is outstanding shall be valid until such certificate be actually seized by the officer making the attachment or levy, or be surrendered to the corporation which issued it, or its transfer by the holder be enjoined. Except where a certificate is lost or destroyed, such corporation shall not be compelled to issue a new certificate for the stock until the old certificate is surrendered to it. 

64. A creditor whose debtor is the owner of a certificate shall be entitled to such aid from courts of appropriate jurisdiction, by injunction and otherwise, in attaching such certificate or in satisfying the claim by means thereof as is allowed at law or in equity, in regard to property which cannot readily be attached or levied upon by ordinary legal process.57

The Uniform Act was enacted by L. 1910, Ch. 73, which repeals "all Acts or parts of Acts inconsistent with this Act."58

The remaining enactment regulating the procedure in making attachments is Section 80 of Article 23, which was enacted in 1908,59 two years before the Uniform Stock Transfer Act.

Section 80 provides for attachments of stock in domestic corporations and in national banks located in the State. 

It provides that the sheriff shall leave at the principal office of the corporation a notice that he has seized the stock of

The Uniform Stock Transfer Act provides that nothing therein contained shall be construed as enlarging the powers of a trustee, executor, or administrator, or other fiduciary, to make a valid endorsement, assignment, or power of attorney.84 

It also expressly calls for application of the law of principal and agent, executors, administrators, and trustees in cases not specifically provided for:85

Assignments by trustees, executors, administrators, guardians, holders of limited or restricted interests and cotenants are regulated by Section 73% of Article 23, enacted in 1927.86

The Uniform Fiduciaries Act, however, was enacted in 1929, and repeals "all Acts or parts of Acts" inconsistent therewith.87 

It provides as follows:

If a fiduciary in whose name are registered any shares of stock, bonds or other securities of any corporation, public or private, or company or other association, or of any trust, transfers the same, such corporation or company or other association, or any of the managers of the trust, or its or their transfer agent, is not bound to inquire whether the fiduciary is committing a breach of his obligation as fiduciary in making the transfer, or to see to the performance of the fiduciary obligation, and is liable for registering such transfer only where registration of the transfer is made with actual knowledge that the fiduciary is committing a breach of his obligation as fiduciary in making the transfer, or with knowledge of such facts that the action. in registering the transfer amounts to bad faith.88

While a corporation is protected against liability by this section in registering transfers made by fiduciaries, nothing in this section or in the Fiduciaries Act expressly requires it to register such transfers unless Section 73½ has been complied with. This section provides that an assignment or power of attorney executed by a fiduciary directing the transfer

Stock certificates issued to "Robinson, Agent," and "Allen, in trust," were lost. It was held in a series of cases that the words "agent" and "in trust" implied that the stock was held for another, and that the corporation might refuse to issue new certificates to the representatives of Robinson and Allen in the absence of evidence either that they owned the stock in their own right or that, if there were trusts, the period of limitations had run on them.90

Following these decisions an Act was passed providing that in such cases the personal representative of the deceased stockholder should be entitled to a new certificate, and the corporation should be relieved from liability to the principal or beneficiary if he should subsequently assert his claim, but that the administrator should be allowed to distribute the proceeds of the stock only after giving notice by advertisement and obtaining a bond from the distributees. § 145. Deceit in sale of stock.-A transferee who has been induced to purchase stock through fraudulent misrepresentations may have the sale rescinded on application to a court of equity.39 Limitations or laches does not begin to run against such transferee until discovery of the fraud, or of facts putting him on inquiry.40 Where no misrepresentation of fact was made to or heard of by the complainant prior to his purchase, there was no ground for relief, even though misrepresentations were made to other purchasers.41 A misrepresentation as to the value of stock as established by other sales thereof, may afford the remedy of rescission. 42 

It has been decided that a misrepresentation that the stock to be purchased was treasury stock, when it was in fact that of the individual making the sale, constitutes fraud and may if relied on, furnish ground for relief.43 In a later case in which the court found no actual representation, the statement was made that such a representation might not be material. The fact, however, that the representation has been repeatedly used as an inducement by those selling stock, would seem to indicate that the matter is generally regarded as material. Since the more recent dictum of the court does not refer to its prior decision, the later statement should be confined to the particular circumstances of the case then before the court. 44 The failure to keep corporate books as required by statute is not in itself ground for allowing an action for deceit in selling stock,45 though on the issue of the truth or falsity of certain representations, evidence is admissible of the absence

§ 146. Dealings between promoters or underwriters.-Pro moters or members of an underwriting syndicate stand in a fiduciary relation to each other. A member of such a syndicate who makes profits through his position not disclosed to his associates must account therefor. Each member is entitled to a share in such profits, and the promoter seeking to withhold profits is not entitled to retain the shares of members not joining in the claim for an accounting, as such shares belong to the syndicate as a whole.2 The usual principles of construction apply in the case of contracts between promoters.³ 

Where two promoters, A and B, entered into a contract for the transfer of patent rights from A to B, which were then to be transferred to a corporation in exchange for shares of its stock, to be sold by B to the public, and where A was to be paid by B for his patent rights in "cash from sale of securities of the corporation," it was held that A was entitled only to the proceeds of sale of stock issued to B for the patent rights, and could not claim the commissions which B received for

Indefinite contracts between promoters will not be enforced. 

Plaintiff and defendant agreed that the former should form a corporation, transfer his canning plant to it in exchange for all of its stock, and then transfer four-sevenths of the stock to defendant in consideration of the latter's agreement to furnish money to remodel the plant and $100,000 a year "if necessary," and to retain plaintiff as president and as one of three directors. Defendant advanced certain sums of money, then ejected plaintiff as president, and the company went into bankruptcy. It was held that the agreement as to retaining plaintiff and as to advances was too indefinite to enforce." § 147. Accounting by promoters to corporation or stockholders.-Promoters do not stand in a fiduciary position to a corporation which they form and to which they transfer assets in exchange for all of its stock. Even when they do not continue as sole stockholders, the receiver of the corporation cannot require them to account for profits which they have made through assembling the assets and turning them over to the corporation at a price greatly in excess of cost. Where a consolidation of businesses is effected by promoters, and each separate proprietor is to be paid by the promoters in stock of the corporation issued to them, no relief may be obtained by one of the vendors against the promoters by reason of their profits through obtaining additional stock of the corporation by revaluation of the business, unless express provisions of the contract with such vendor have been violated. § 150. Validity and construction of corporate mortgages.— 

The power is granted to every corporation subject to the provisions of Article 23 to "incur liabilities and borrow money for its corporate purposes; and to issue bonds, notes and other obligations and secure the same by mortgage or deed of trust of all or any part of its property, franchises and income."¹ 

Any issue of bonds, notes, or other obligations "secured by mortgage or deed of trust of any of the franchises of the corporation" must be authorized by a majority of each class of voting stock (or a majority of all members).2 Chattel mortgages have in some cases been made by officers without a vote of directors or stockholders and sustained because of unusual circumstances of estoppel or ratification. Mortgage covering after-acquired property; future advances. The validity of a clause in a mortgage covering after-acquired property has been left in some doubt as a result of the case of First National Bank v. Lindenstruth. In that case a mortgage of real and personal property (in form a conveyance) included stock in trade, and provided that in case of sale of some of the stock and substitution of other articles, the lien should cover such substituted stock. After-acquired stock was mingled indistinguishably with the original stock, and a judgment creditor levied on some of the stock. It was held that the lien on after-acquired stock was ineffective, and that the creditor might levy on and sell any part of the mingled stock. The court points out that under some conditions such a covenant would be effective in equity. Although this decision has not been overruled and would probably be followed in a case at law, it is generally assumed that the afteracquired clause creates a valid equitable lien, which would be promptly enforced upon application to a court of equity, and in local practice the clause is frequently employed in corporate indentures. • State v. Brown & A. & E. R. Co., (1885) 64 Md. 199, 1 Atl. 54, 6 Atl. 172. 'Swift v. Smith, Dixon & Co., (1886) 65 Md. 428, 5 Atl. 534, 57 Am. Rep. 

336. The following comparatively early cases deal with the construction and effect of corporate mortgages: Green v. Conkling, (1852) 3 Md. 384; Northern

§ 158. Preferences and priorities. In determining priori ties between different classes of bondholders, it was held in one case that second mortgage bonds should be given priority over those under the first mortgage by reason of fraud on the part of the holders of the prior lien bonds. 52 Holders of income bonds may not enjoin sale of a subsequent issue of bonds unless the issuance thereof would be in violation of rights secured to them by the indenture governing the income bonds. 53

Holders of income bonds of the C. & O. Canal, issued when the State as prior mortgagee waived its claim on tolls and revenues, obtained a receivership over the opposition of the State with the object of having the property put into earning condition instead of being sold. When the question arose whether the trustees should have an extension of time, the State again resisted, but the extension was granted. One of the judges wrote a separate concurring opinion in which the point was made that a mortgage of rents and profits was equivalent to a mortgage on the fee simple estate, and that the State therefore had waived its entire lien. The majority, however, declined to accept this proposition. Three judges dissented from the decision allowing the extension.54

In the case of a public or quasi-public corporation, a creditor for necessary supplies, such as coal, furnished to carry on the business when in receivership and immediately prior thereto has an equitable lien on earnings. Such lien is preferred to that of bondholders under an income mortgage. Bondholders intervening to ask sale of the property are entitled to claim for their deficiency on a parity with unsecured creditors as regards distributions of earnings made by the receiver before their intervention.57

A "business trust" operating a public service business is treated as an incorporated utility in determining priorities in funds in hands of receivers. As to current income, creditors for current necessaries are preferred, but the bondholders are preferred to claims for services by the trustees or managers of the trust, and to claims for coal furnished more than nine months before the receivership. Those lending money to pay overdue dividends rank as unsecured creditors. 58 

Though in the case of a private corporation bondholders are preferred to creditors furnishing ordinary supplies to the receiver to run the business, they are not necessarily preferred to creditors rendering services or furnishing supplies actually needed for preservation of the mortgaged property. Such creditors, however, have priority only "under proper circumstances" or where the services or supplies were furnished at the request of the bondholders.59

§ 159. Status of bondholders' committee.-A protective committee is often formed to represent bondholders in negotiations leading to reorganization of an unsuccessful company. 

Where such a committee purchases the mortgaged property at foreclosure sale, the members are individually liable for the purchase price.63 A statute providing that the old corporation should be dissolved on sale and creating the committee as a new corporation would not have the effect of releasing the members of such committee from personal liability.64

Trustee under indenture.-The usual clause of a corporate mortgage waiving liability of the trustee except for its own gross negligence or wilful default is a proper and valid provision. The trustee is not liable to bondholders in the absence of conduct amounting to a breach of trust. 

The certification of bonds by the trustee merely identifies them, and the fact that the security does not measure up to expectations of its value is no reason for imposing liability on the trustee for certifying such bonds.68 

The trustee is not liable for the expenses of a sale set aside for its failure to give bond, where its failure to do so was not negligent. Nor is its failure to obtain a discount on taxes any ground for imposing liability in the absence of proof of negligence. The trustee may retain a contingent expense fund; and it is proper for it to charge the bondholders' committee with the expense of an audit stated by auditors at their request. If the trustee has banking powers, it is privileged to deposit with itself funds received pursuant to the indenture, and is then charged with interest received, that is, the rate which it customarily pays on similar accounts rather than the full legal rate."9

Installment bonds.-The status of the holder of a bond to be paid for in installments, or of an installment certificate, exchangeable when paid up for a bond, would depend upon the rights secured to such holder under the contract. In the only case thus far decided in the State, "coupon bonds" were issued, entitling the holder, after he had made monthly payments for ten years, to the repayment of a specified sum, together with an interest in a certain surplus and in delinquent fees on similar bonds. The corporation went into the hands of receivers, and the court decided that the holder of such a bond was not a "creditor" until he had made all his payments; that he was in the position of one entering into a subscription contract; and that the case was similar to that of a building association where a member is not a creditor until he gives notice of withdrawal.72 

A slight variation in the facts might well produce a different result.

Corporations which "have been or shall have been duly authorized by law to carry on in whole or in part any kind of business of the same or similar nature" are authorized to consolidate and thereby to form "one new corporation." 

The first step is to draw up an agreement of consolidation; second, to have such agreement submitted to and approved by the respective boards of directors; third, to have the agreement approved at separate meetings by the stockholders of the respective corporations; fourth, to have the agreement executed by the corporations; fifth, to have attached thereto affidavits of the chairmen or secretaries of the stockholders' meetings that the required corporate action was taken; sixth, to have the agreement delivered to the State Tax Commission together with the bonus tax, if any payable, plus a recording fee of twenty dollars ($20.00) and additional recording fees of two dollars ($2.00) each for every county in which any one of the corporations owns property, the title to which may be affected by land records, to cover the expense of preparation and transmission of a certificate of consolidation

The agreement of consolidation must contain: (a) The terms and conditions of the proposed consolidation; (b) The mode of carrying the same into effect; (c) The name of the new corporation; (d) The postoffice address of the place at which the principal office of the corporation in this State will be located as in the case of a certificate of incorporation and the name or names and postoffice address or addresses of the resident agent or agents who will be in charge thereof, as in the case of a certificate of incorporation; (e) The counties in this State in which any of the consolidating corporations own property, the title to which could be affected by the recording of an instrument among the land records, and if any of the consolidating corporations own such property in the City of Baltimore, the agreement of consolidation shall so state; (f) The number, names and addresses of the directors and the names of the officers, who shall act as such until their successors are duly chosen and qualified; (g) The amount of authorized capital stock of each consolidating corporation and the total amount of authorized capital stock of the new corporation and the number and par value of the shares; (h) The total amount of capital stock of the new corporation to be issued for stock of the consolidating corporations; (i) The restrictions, if any, imposed upon the transfer of the shares or of any of them; (j) If the capital stock is classified, the amount, par value, preferences, restrictions and qualifications of each class, specifying the amount of each class authorized and the amount of each class to be issued for stock of the consolidating corporations; (k) The manner of converting the capital stock of each of the consolidating corporations into stock of the corporation; (1) All such other provisions and details which shall be deemed necessary to perfect the consolidation.³

The agreement may also contain "any amendment or amendments which may be desired" (i.e., to the charters of the respective consolidating corporations). If so, the agreement must contain "all matters and things required to be stated in articles of amendment." No amendment which cannot be made in the usual manner is authorized to be made in an agreement of consolidation, except that it is permissible

Where a consolidation of businesses is effected by promoters through transfer of such businesses to a new corporation in exchange for stock of such corporation, the fact that the promoters retain for themselves additional stock of the new corporation, through assembling the businesses in their own name and revaluing them as an entirety, issuing all the stock to themselves and transferring the agreed shares to the sellers of the separate businesses, does not indicate an unlawful overissue of stock, nor is it in violation of any rights of the vendors unless expressly granted to them by contract.13

Rights of dissenting stockholders.-Any stockholder who has voted against an agreement of consolidation may, within twenty days after it has been filed with the State Tax Commission, serve upon the consolidated corporation a written demand for payment for his stock. If the stockholder and the corporation fail to agree upon the fair value of the stock, or if, having agreed, the corporation fails to pay or tender the amount, the stockholder may, within thirty days after his demand was served, apply to a court of equity for the appointment of three disinterested commissioners to appraise the fair value of the stock without regard to the effect of the consolidation, the award of a majority of the commissioners, when confirmed by the court, to be conclusive, except that either party may appeal to the Court of Appeals from the action of the lower court in confirming such award. The stock, when paid for and transferred to the corporation, has the status of authorized but unissued stock. If the award is not paid within thirty days from the confirmation thereof

Since consolidation of corporations has been permitted under the general law since it was first enacted, there is little likelihood that a stockholder could successfully prevent any proposed consolidation at the present time on the ground that it represented a fundamental change in the charter to which he had not agreed. § 166. Sale, lease, or exchange of assets. The statute permits any stock corporation (except a railroad company) to sell, lease, or exchange its property and assets as an entirety, including its good will and franchises, to or with any other domestic or foreign corporation authorized to acquire and hold such property. An agreement must be drawn up, approved by the directors, and submitted to the stockholders at a specially notified meeting. If approved at such meeting by the vote of two-thirds of each class of stock outstanding and entitled to vote, the agreement is then executed and performed by the proper officers. 33

A dissenting stockholder has the same rights as in case of consolidation.34 The agreement is, however, carried out without waiting for the determination of proceedings brought by stockholders. The grantee takes the property of the grantor corporation subject to its debts and liabilities, including the claims of dissenting stockholders. The right of stockholders to obtain payment for their stock ceases upon rescission of the agreement.35

Restrictions on the assignment of municipal franchises imposed by ordinances granting such franchises are not abrogated or impaired by the statute.36 

A minority stockholder, having at his disposal a fair statutory remedy of payment for his stock, has no right to block an agreement for transfer of assets in the absence of proof of

The statute provides that "a corporation may acknowledge any instrument required by law to be acknowledged, by its attorney appointed under its seal, and such appointment may be embodied in the deed, or such instrument may be acknowledged by the president or any vice-president of such corporation without such appointment."33 Acknowledgments and affidavits required by the corporation law may be made "before any notary public or other officer competent to take acknowledgments of deeds for land situated anywhere in this State."34

The use and effect of the corporate seal in pleading has already been discussed.35 Whether an instrument having the corporate seal affixed is thereby made a specialty has been the subject of a decision by the Court of Appeals. It was held that the written promise of a corporation to pay money, signed by its president and secretary and having its corporate seal affixed, but making no reference thereto in the body of the instrument, is not a specialty.38 The test is, therefore, whether the instrument by its language purports to be under seal.

PAGE 238 239 242 § 176. General rule as to observance of corporate entity.- 

The question is frequently raised whether the position of a corporation as an independent legal person standing between its shareholders and outsiders with whom it deals, can be disregarded so as to give rise to direct rights and liabilities between the shareholders and such outsiders. The general rule is that the corporation will always be regarded as an independent person, distinct from its shareholders and having rights not limited by disabilities or liabilities which would be imposed on its shareholders. This rule is subject to exception only when necessary to prevent fraud or to enforce a paramount equity.¹

Creditors of subsidiary corporations.-A subsidiary corporation is a "one-man corporation" in the sense that it is owned and controlled, wholly or predominantly, by a single stockholder. Thus, liability will be imposed on the parent corporation for torts of its subsidiary where the latter is so closely controlled or managed by the former that it is in fact the agent or instrumentality, or, as it is sometimes termed, the "mere puppet"15 of the parent or master company. § 178. Limitation on rights of shareholders as affecting right of corporation. In a few cases where it was deemed necessary to prevent fraud or enforce a paramount equity, the courts have looked behind a corporation to its shareholders for the purpose of determining the rights of the corporation. 

Thus, in setting aside preferences made to officers and directors of an insolvent bank, a payment to a corporation of which one of the defendants was president, has been regarded as a preferential payment to an officer or director. 20 Similarly, where the payee of a note made by a corporation was himself a director therein, and the other directors were his dummies, a resolution of the directors authorizing such note was held to be evidence neither of its valid execution nor of the payment of consideration therefor.21 And in a suit by a corporation against former directors and officers to recover alleged excessive salaries paid, equity will look behind the corporation to its shareholders for the purpose of determining whether they should receive relief. Where the majority were not so entitled, it was held that the relief granted the corporation should be reduced to the proportion receivable by the minority who were not precluded from asserting their rights.22
