What books and records must be kept; requirements as to where books should be kept.-The original or a certified copy of the by-laws is directed to be kept at the principal office of the corporation in Maryland.¹ Original or duplicate stock ledgers must also be kept at the principal office "or at any other office or agency of the corporation in such city or town as may be specified in the by-laws."2 The directors are required to keep "full and fair accounts of their transactions," and the president or some other officer specified in the by-laws must "annually prepare a full and true statement of the affairs of the corporation, which shall be submitted at the annual meeting of the stockholders or members and filed within twenty days thereafter at the principal office" in Maryland.³

A duplicate of any voting trust agreement must also be filed in the principal office of the corporation.¹

The books of the corporation must be "kept so as to show at all times what money or other consideration was received by such corporation for the stock issued by it and the number and par value of the shares of each class issued for the same," together with similar entries as to convertible securities. Annual reports of domestic corporations.-"Every corporation subject to assessment on its property or any part thereof by the State Tax Commission, and any corporation the shares of whose stock are subject to assessment by the State Tax Commission, and any corporation. against whom any tax is to be calculated by the State Tax Commission" must file an annual report with the Commission on or before March 15 in each year. The only corporations which might be relieved from reporting under this statute are membership corporations having no capital stock. Domestic ordinary business corporations must in all cases report because the commission is required to calculate the annual franchise tax on capital stock, and all other domestic stock corporations are under the same duty because of the tax on their shares of stock. It is customary, also, for membership corporations to report under this section.2 

The statute continues by prescribing a corporation report "in such manner and containing replies to such interrogatories as may be determined upon by said Commission, including a list of its stockholders, with their addresses and the number and/or class of shares held by each, in order that it may perform any duties imposed upon it." The Commission 

1 Art. 81, Sec. 178. See § 215, infra. 

2 The Commission has adopted the policy of requesting and accepting such reports, the alternative being that the Commission will suggest that the local taxing authorities send questionnaires to corporations not reporting.

REPORTS AND ANNUAL REQUIREMENTS 247 

4 has ruled that it will dispense with the filing of a list of stockholders if that is unnecessary to the performance of any of its duties. Accordingly, a domestic ordinary business corporation having no tangible personal property within the State need not file its list of stockholders. In cases in which the list must be filed, non-resident stockholders need not be listed; it is sufficient to give the total number of shares of each class held by non-residents. The Commission may require the report to be "under oath of such officer or officers as it may determine."

The report, though filed March 15, is prepared as of January 1, and taxes and assessments are calculated by the Commission as of January 1.6

If the report is not filed, the Commission may compel the filing thereof by mandamus, or may "proceed to determine or assess such tax, or take such action, upon such information as it can obtain." Penalties are imposed at the rate of $5.00 for any delay; $1.00 additional for each ten-day period of delay, or fraction thereof; and $10.00 additional for delay of more than eighty days. Penalties may be waived for good cause. § 186. Method and scope of treatment.—A complete state ment of the tax law of Maryland as applied to corporations and corporate securities would be impossible without extensive quotation from the statutes. In dealing with these questions, therefore, a change of method from earlier portions of the book has been adopted. In the sections immediately following there is given an outline or general survey of the system of taxation as codified in 1929 in the revised Article 81 of the Code of General Laws. This is followed by the text of those sections of the law which apply particularly to corporations or which are necessary to an understanding of problems of corporate taxation. Where sections of the law are omitted, the fact of omission is noted, and the contents, if sufficiently important, are briefly summarized. Judicial decisions are given in the form of annotations to the sections of the law to which they apply.

PART I-SUMMARY OF TAX LAWS 

§ 187. Ordinary and special taxes; no income tax.-Taxes ´in Maryland are divided into ordinary taxes, by which is meant direct taxes on real and personal property, and special taxes. 

The latter include the organization or bonus tax on domestic corporations, franchise taxes of various kinds on domestic and foreign corporations, certain taxes on commissions and a collateral inheritance tax. There is also an estate tax, applicable so far as credit may be obtained on the Federal Estate Tax, and there are various occupational or license taxes. 

The estate tax is provided for by Article 62A of the Code.¹ 

1 Since this Article applies only to estates of residents, it is inapplicable to stock in Maryland corporations owned by non-resident decedents.

CORPORATE TAXATION 

253 State licenses are prescribed by Article 56, and local license fees are imposed by city or town ordinances, or by public local laws, applicable to one or more counties or to the City of Baltimore. There is no Maryland income tax. 

The general tax laws were revised in 1929 and collected as a new Article 81 of the Code of General Laws. Inasmuch as the tax and licensing provisions not found in Article 81 have no particular application to corporations, they will be omitted from the subsequent discussion. 

In the case of the ordinary taxes on real and personal property, levies are made for State, county and municipal purposes. The City of Baltimore ranks as a separate county, but every other incorporated city or town is within the limits of one of the counties. Certain intangible property is subject to limited rates of taxation, but other property may be taxed at the full State, county and/or city rate. Assessments of shares of stock of corporations and of their tangible personal property (when subject to taxation) are made by the State Tax Commission. Other assessments are made by the local authorities.

The various "special taxes" are levied for the use of the State alone, except in the case of the annual franchise tax on domestic ordinary business corporations, one-half of which goes to the county and/or city in which the corporation has its principal office,2 and the franchise tax on deposits of savings banks, three-fourths of which goes to the county and/or city in which the bank is located. § 188. Classification of corporations for purposes of taxation. The principal classification of corporations under the tax laws is that of (1) "ordinary business corporations."³ 

The shares of stock of such corporations are not taxed, and they pay an annual franchise tax on the amount of stock issued or subscribed for. Intangible personal property of such corporations is exempt from taxation when they do no business within the State. Other important classifications are those of (2) "finance" corporations; (3) domestic companies other

Actual principal office, and not necessarily that named in the charter. 

Art. 81, Sec. 1(20). See § 196, infra. 

Defined by Art. 81, Sec. 2(9). For a summary statement of this defini tion, see the next section.

than ordinary business corporations, and national banks situated in Maryland, whose shares of stock are taxable; (4) railroad companies, banks, title and trust companies, and certain public service corporations, domestic and foreign, which pay a franchise tax measured by gross receipts; (5) savings banks which pay a franchise tax on deposits; and (6) foreign corporations as such. Special exemptions are also granted to various classes of corporations. § 189. Taxes payable by domestic ordinary business corporations; definition thereof.-The definition of an ordinary business corporation excludes public utilities, surety and insurance companies, building associations, banking institutions and finance corporations. It includes all other stock corporations, and it also expressly includes any domestic stock corporation doing no part of its business in the State. An ordinary business corporation pays the usual taxes on Maryland real estate, where situated. It is also assessed on its tangible personal property where its stockholders respectively reside, non-residents being counted at the principal office." 

Its interest-bearing bonds and its mortgages on property outside the State, as well as its dividend-paying shares in foreign corporations, are assessed at the principal office at the same rate paid by individuals-15 cents per $100 for State purposes and 30 cents per $100 for county and/or city purposes. The above intangible property is exempt if the corporation does no business in the State. Finally, the corporation pays an annual franchise tax based on the amount of its capital stock issued, outstanding and/or subscribed for as of January 1. It pays no other franchise tax, such as the tax on gross receipts imposed on certain corporations, and it pays no tax for account of its stockholders on its capital stock, as is the case with other domestic corporations. 

The bonus tax based on the amount of authorized capital stock must be paid at the time of organization. This tax is the same as in the case of other domestic corporations. 

4 See note 2, § 187. "Residence" as used in the statute is elsewhere defined as "principal 

See note 1. office."

CORPORATE TAXATION 

255 § 190. Taxes payable by other domestic corporations except railroad companies and finance corporations.-Domestic corporations not of the ordinary business classification are required to pay a tax on their shares of capital stock for account of their stockholders. This tax is in lieu of the tax on tangible and intangible personal property, from which such corporations are exempt. Finance corporations pay a modified form of share tax. All other domestic corporations, even those subject to the gross receipts tax (the sole exception being railroads), are required to pay the share tax, which, though collected from the corporation, is assessed against the stockholders and may be passed on to them. The tax must also be paid by national banks located in Maryland. Such corporations and national banks pay regular taxes on their real estate, and the assessed value of such real estate is deducted from the "fair" aggregate value of their shares in computing the final valuation for purposes of the share tax. The rate of tax in the case of shares of banks and trust companies, casualty, surety, guaranty and fidelity companies, and fire, title, and marine insurance companies is limited to the full State rate (usually about 25 cents per $100) plus $1.00 per $100 for local purposes.

Domestic corporations paying the share tax are also subject to the bonus tax on organization. They do not pay the annual franchise tax on issued capital stock and may or may not fall within the classes of corporations paying a franchise tax on gross receipts." § 191. Taxes payable by domestic finance corporations.— 

Finance corporations include credit, investment banking, investment trust, mortgage, and commercial banking corporations. The term excludes banks and trust companies. 

Domestic finance corporations pay the same taxes as other corporations not within the "ordinary business classification,"8 except that the value of their shares for tax purposes excludes the proportion of their business done outside the State. The ratio of business done within and without the State is presumed 

See the next section. 

7 See § 193, infra. 

See the preceding section for these taxes.

to be the same as the ratio of gross receipts within and without the State, exclusive of income from permanent investments. 

Accordingly, domestic finance corporations pay taxes on their real estate, but not on their personal property; taxes on the value of their shares (for account of their stockholders), excluding Maryland real estate and excluding business done outside the State; and the bonus tax on organization, but no annual franchise tax of any kind, whether measured by capital stock or by gross receipts. The rate of tax on shares of finance corporations is the full State rate (about 25 cents per $100) plus $1.00 per $100 for local purposes. 

If such a corporation does no business in the State, it is classed as an ordinary business corporation and pays all taxes accordingly." § 192. Taxes payable by railroad corporations.-A domestic steam railroad corporation pays county and/or city taxes on its real and personal property, but no State taxes thereon. 

Rolling stock is apportioned according to the amount of trackage in the various counties. The proportion of rolling stock corresponding to trackage outside the State is exempt. The shares of stock of such a corporation are not taxed. It pays no bonus tax on organization (unless its lines are to be wholly outside the State, when it is classed as an ordinary business corporation). Its annual franchise tax is based on its gross receipts, excluding the proportion thereof which its lines outside the State bear to its lines within the State. The tax is at the rate of 14% of gross earnings up to $1,000 per mile, 2% of earnings from $1,000 to $2,000 per mile and 22% of earnings over $2,000 per mile.

A foreign railroad corporation operating in the State pays the same taxes, except that it has no exemption from State taxes on its real and personal property. Its shares of stock (if dividend-paying) are taxed to resident stockholders at the rate of 45 cents per $100. §193. Franchise tax on gross receipts payable by title and trust companies, and by certain transportation, communication, electric, and gas companies.—In addition to taxes on real estate and the share tax paid for account of stockholders 

See § 189, supra.

257 in lieu of personal property taxes, certain public and quasipublic corporations pay an annual franchise tax measured by gross receipts. Such tax in the case of railroads has already been mentioned. 10 The rate is 22% on earnings of telegraph or cable, express or transportation, parlor car, sleeping car, safe deposit and trust¹¹ companies; 2% on earnings of telephone, oil pipe line, and title insurance¹2 companies; 1%% on earnings of gas companies; and 1% on earnings of electric light or power companies. All of the above except safe deposit and trust companies and title insurance companies are granted a deduction for the proportion of their lines or business outside the State. Certain other deductions are granted to trust companies and title insurance companies. 

This tax applies to foreign corporations engaged in the above businesses in the State, as well as to domestic corporations. § 194. Taxes payable by foreign corporations.-Every foreign corporation (except national banks) doing business in the State pays the same taxes as a domestic ordinary business corporation on real estate and tangible personal property within the State, and on intangible property "used in or in connection with its business in the State," as to which it is deemed a "resident" of the county and/or city in which its principal office in the State is located. If the stock pays dividends, stockholders resident in Maryland are taxed thereon at the rate of 45 cents per $100. The annual report must include a list of resident stockholders. Such corporations also pay an annual franchise tax based on the "amount of capital employed in the State" as of January 1. Insurance companies, and corporations paying a franchise tax measured by gross receipts¹³ are exempt from the franchise tax on capital employed.

National banks located in the State pay a tax on their shares for account of their stockholders, and are exempt from taxes on personal property. The definition of foreign corporations, for tax purposes, includes such banks, and they would, therefore, be subject to the same franchise taxes as other foreign

[182-188. Hearings and appeals.] § 196. Rules of construction.- CODE, ARTICLE 81 

1. The provisions of this article, so far as they are substantially the same as existing statutes, shall be construed as continuations thereof, and as intended to make no substantive change in existing laws, except so far as such change shall be clearly manifest; and no implication of a change of intent shall arise by reason of a change in words or phraseology, or by reason of a relocation or rearrangement of sentences, phrases, sections or paragraphs except so far as such change of intent shall be clearly manifest.

L. 1929, Ch. 226, by which Article 81 was revised and reenacted, also provided (Sec. 13) that the unconstitutionality of any portion of that Act should not affect the remainder, and (Sec. 14) that inconsistent Acts, charters, and ordinances should be repealed to the extent of their inconsistency, with appropriate saving clauses as to taxes accrued and as to irrepealable charter exemptions. Such exemptions are discussed in § 65, supra. A leading case on the surrender of tax exemptions is State v. Baltimore & O. R. Co., (1916) 127 Md. 

434, 96 Atl. 636. 

2. As used in this Article: (1) The term "corporation" shall include association or joint stock company. (2) The phrase "organized under the laws" shall mean formed or existing under the statute or common law.

(3) The term "foreign" as applied to a corporation or company shall mean organized under the laws of any State (other than this State), Territory, District, possession or foreign country, or the 

United States.

This definition, which includes national banks, was added to the tax laws in the 1929 revision. (4) The term "domestic" as applied to a corporation shall mean organized under the laws of this State. (5) The word "person" shall include a corporation unless such construction would be unreasonable. (8) The phrase "interest-bearing" or "dividend-paying" shall, as applied to securities, respectively mean actually paying interest or dividends during the twelve months preceding the date of finality; provided that any securities on which interest or dividends are withheld for the purpose of avoiding taxes thereon shall be deemed interest-bearing or dividend-paying, and provided further that newly issued bonds, certificates of indebtedness, and evidences of debt on which no interest is in default shall be deemed interest bearing, and provided further that the declaration of a stock dividend shall be deemed the payment of a dividend within the meaning of this sub-section. (9) The phrase "ordinary business corporation" shall mean any corporation having a capital stock, except railroad companies whose roads are worked by steam, electric or other power, street and passenger railways, steamship and steam-boat companies, and all other common carriers, telegraph, cable, telephone, express, transportation, parlor car, sleeping car, and oil pipe line companies, turnpike companies, bridge companies and sewage disposal companies, safe deposit and trust companies, casualty, surety, guarantee and fidelity companies, insurance companies of all kinds, electric light or power companies, heating, refrigerating, water or gas companies, building or homestead associations, state, national and savings banks, finance corporations, or savings or moneyed corporations; provided that any domestic railroad, railway, street or passenger railway, steamship, steamboat, common carrier, telegraph, cable, telephone, express, transportation, parlor car, sleeping car, oil pipe-line, turnpike, bridge, sewage disposal, electric light and power, heating, refrigerating, gas or water company, which neither owns, maintains nor operates properties, lines or works in this State, or any other domestic corporation having a capital stock which does no part of its business in this State, shall be deemed an ordinary business corporation. 1

(10) The phrase "finance corporation" shall include finance, credit, investment banking, investment trust, mortgage and commercial banking corporations, and any corporation other than banks or trust companies substantially competing with national banks in this State.

See note to Par. (15). (18) A foreign corporation doing business in this State shall in respect to intangible property used in or in connection with its business in this State, including property held in trust for a resident of this State, be deemed a resident of the county and/or city in which its principal office in this State is situated.

(20) The phrase "principal office" as applied to a domestic corporation shall mean the office, if any, in this State from which its business is actually directed and managed, or if there be no such office, then the place in this State where the principal business of the company in this State is transacted, or if there be no such place, then the principal office named in its charter or reported to the State Tax Commission as the case may be. (21) The phrase "principal office in this State" as applied to a foreign corporation shall mean the place at which the principal business or operations of the company in this State are actually carried on. 

3. [Provides for applicability of tax laws to executors, firms and persons in business, tenants and fiduciaries.] 

§ 197. Classification of taxes.- 

4. The taxes imposed by this Article shall be divided into (1) ordinary taxes, and (2) special taxes. Direct taxes imposed in respect of real or personal property shall be ordinary taxes. Special taxes shall include- (a) Tax on deposits of savings banks. (b) Gross receipts tax. (c) Tax on official commissions. (d) Tax on commissions of executors and administrators. (e) Collateral inheritance tax. (f) Bonus tax on corporations. (g) Tax on franchise to be a corporation. (h) Franchise tax on foreign corporations.

§ 198. What shall be taxed and where.— 

6. The following property, except as in the next two succeeding sections provided, shall be subject to assessment to the owner and taxation for ordinary taxes in this State and in the county and/or city specified below: (1) All real properties in this State, by whomsoever owned, in the county and/or city in which the same are situated. 

Occupancy of streets is an easement, not a franchise, and is taxable as real estate. Consolidated Gas Co. v. Baltimore,

267 (1905) 101 Md. 541, 61 Atl. 532, 1 L.R.A. (N.S.) 263, 109 Am. 

St. Rep. 584.

No exemption of easements can be predicated on the payment of a gross receipts tax, which is a franchise and not a property tax. Postal Telegraph Co. v. Harford County, (1917) 

131 Md. 96, 101 Atl. 600. 

But the "Park Tax" (L. 1882, Ch. 229; Balto. Charter, §797) on gross receipts of street railways is in lieu of a direct tax on intangible property, and so excludes a tax on such company's easements in public streets. United Rwys. & Elec. 

Co. v. Baltimore, (1909) 111 Md. 264, 73 Atl. 633.

As to valuation and assessment of easements, see Art. 81, Sec. 11 (§ 200, infra). 

While mortgages on Maryland real estate are not included in the list of taxable property (the real estate itself being taxed), this does not require the value of such mortgages held by a corporation whose shares are taxed to be deducted in computing the value of such shares. State Tax Commission v. Eureka 

Life Ins. Co., (1926) 150 Md. 380, 133 Atl. 63. Deduction for mortgages held by life insurance and fire insurance companies under L. 1924, Ch. 225, not effective until year 1925 (See Art. 81, Sec. 15 (b) (2)). Id.

Though the Federal license and the franchise of a power company are not subject to taxation, the company may be taxed on the actual value of its tangible property, which may be enhanced by such license and franchise. Susquehanna 

Power Co. v. State Tax Commission, (1930) 159 Md. 334, 151 Atl. 

29, aff'd. 283 U. S. 291, 51 Sup. Ct. 434, 75 L. Ed. 1042. (2) All tangible personal properties located in this State, by whomsoever owned, in the county and/or city in which the same are respectively permanently located, (a) provided that rolling stock of railroads worked by steam shall be taxed only as provided in Section 8(d); and (b) provided further that tangible personal property located in this State, but not owned by a domestic ordinary business corporation, and not permanently located in any county or city shall be subject to assessment and taxation in the county and/or city where the owner resides or has his or its principal office or place of business in this State; and (c) provided further that tangible personal property located in this State owned by a domestic ordinary business corporation shall be taxed in the county and/or city in which the stockholders

respectively reside, or if they be non-residents of this State, then in the county and/or city in which the principal office of the corporation is situated.

No exemption of poles and wires by reason of payment of gross receipts tax. Postal Tel. Co. v. Harford County, (1917) 

131 Md. 96, 101 Atl. 600.

Tangible personal property in this State of foreign corporations held taxable though stockholders resident in Maryland are taxed on their shares in such corporation; the fact that taxability of shares of domestic corporation exempts its personal property is immaterial. Williams & Wilkins Co. v. 

Baltimore, (1906) 103 Md. 293, 63 Atl. 562.

Constitutional provision as to place of taxation of personal property of residents is inapplicable to corporations. Baltimore, C. & A. Ry. Co. v. Wicomico County, (1901) 93 Md. 113, 132, 48 Atl. 853. See McLane v. Appeal Tax Court, (1928) 156 

Md. 133, 143 Atl. 656.

As to stock in trade, see Par. (10), infra. (3) All interest-bearing bonds, certificates of indebtedness or evidences of debt, owned by residents of the State, in whatsoever form made or issued by any public or private domestic corporation (other than a county or city of this State), or made or issued by any State (other than this State), territory, district, possession or foreign country, or by any foreign public or private corporation, in the county and/or city in which the owners respectively reside. "Mortgage participation certificates" issued by a corporation are not assignments of the mortgages, but are corporate bonds or evidences of debt and taxable as such. Baltimore v. 

Harper, (1925) 148 Md. 234, 129 Atl. 641; Ray v. Englar, (1925) 148 Md. 246, 129 Atl. 645. The taxation of corporate bonds, secured by mortgage on Maryland realty, is proper, although the real estate has been taxed. Simpson v. Hopkins, (1896) 82 Md. 478, 33 Atl. 714. 

As to limited rate of tax, see Art. 81, Sec. 27(b) (§ 201, infra).

Intangible personal property of partnership taxed at business situs as if legal entity, notwithstanding Md. Const., Art. III., Sec. 51, providing that personal property be taxed at residence of owner. McLane v. Appeal Tax Court, (1928) 

156 Md. 133, 143 Atl. 656.

269 (4) All interest-bearing mortgages, owned by residents of this State on real estate or tangible personal property situated in whole or in part outside of Maryland, in the county and/or city in which such owners respectively reside. 

Mortgages on Maryland real estate are not taxable unless the mortgagor is a corporation, when the debt might be taxable under the preceding paragraph in the hands of a resident holder. Cf. majority opinion by Bond, C. J. with dissenting opinion of Parke, J. in Baltimore v. Harper, (1925) 148 Md. 234, 129 Atl. 641.

As to limited rate of taxation, see Art. 81, Sec. 27(c) (§ 201, infra).

Personal property of banks whose shares are subject to this tax is exempt. See Art. 81, Sec. 7 (15). Both shares and property of national banks cannot be taxed. Frederick

Where a company is incorporated in two states, the situs of its stock for taxation purposes is in both. Northern Cent. 

R. Co. v. Fidelity Trust Co., (1927) 152 Md. 94, 136 Atl. 66, 60 A. L. R. 558. (But see § 206, infra.) As to exemption of shares of domestic railroad companies, see Art. 81, Sec. 7 (16).

The rate of tax is limited in certain cases. See Art. 81, Sec. 27 (c) and (d) (§ 201, infra). 

An exemption of a corporation "from the payment of any and all municipal taxes" does not exempt it from payment of the tax on shares assessed against stockholders. Havre de 

Grace v. Havre de Grace & P. Bridge Co., (1924) 145 Md. 491, 125 Atl. 704.

A corporation engaged in the lending and investment of money, though not a bank, is a "moneyed corporation" and not an ordinary business corporation, and its shares are taxable. Industrial Corp. v. State Tax Commission, (1919) 134 

Md. 379, 106 Atl. 852.

A tax cannot be levied for one county on shares of stock of corporations having principal offices there, applicable to shares owned by residents or non-residents of the county. A local law levying such a tax (L. 1900, Ch. 597) held unconstitutional, under Md. Const., Art. Md. 1, 57 Atl. 632.

Shares of stock of a domestic corporation owned by nonresidents may be taxed, at the principal office of the corporation. Corry v. Baltimore, (1903) 96 Md. 310, 53 Atl. 942, 103 Am. St. 364, (aff'd. 196 U. S. 466, 25 Sup. Ct. 297, 49

The tax on shares being a tax on the stockholders, though collected from the corporation, such corporation is not entitled to have the value of its patent rights (along with that of its real estate) deducted from the whole value of its property in making valuation of the shares, on the ground that a tax on patent rights might violate U. (d) Rolling stock of railroads worked by steam shall, for purposes of county and Baltimore City taxation, be apportioned among the counties of this State and the City of Baltimore in proportion to the mileage of such railroads therein; and whenever the railroads owning, hiring or leasing said rolling stock shall extend beyond the limits of this State, that proportion of the total rolling stock not permanently located in this State which the mileage of such railroad in this State bears to its total mileage, shall be deemed located and taxable in Maryland.

The apportionment of this tax between the various counties according to mileage therein is not in violation of Md. Const., Art. III, Sec. 51, requiring taxes on personal property to be levied at the residence, as that applies only to natural persons.

§ 200. Method of assessment. 

11. Except as hereinafter provided, all property directed in this 

Article to be assessed, shall be assessed at the full cash value thereof on the date of finality. Any assessment existing on June 1, 1929, or thereafter made, shall continue in force from year to year until changed pursuant to the provisions of this Article. 

A valuation arrived at arbitrarily is void. Consolidated 

Gas Co. v. Baltimore, (1905) 101 Md. 541, 61 Atl. 532, 1 L. R. 

A. (N. S.) 263, 109 Am. St. Rep. 584. See also notes to Art. 

81, Sec. 15. The taxing authorities may be examined as to the methods used in arriving at an assessment. Consolidated 

Gas Co. v. Baltimore, (1907) 105 Md. 43, 65 Atl. 628, 121 Am. 

St. Rep. 553; and see notes to Art. 81, Sec. 15(a).

Easements may be valued and taxed as real estate, but bonds issued by a corporation, since they are taxable in the hands of the owners, should not be added to the capital stock in computing the total taxable worth of such corporation for the purpose of assessing easements. Consolidated Gas Co. v. 

Baltimore (supra), 101 Md. 541.

If bonds are included indirectly in the valuation of easements, the assessment is void. Nor is it proper to ascertain

the value of easements by deducting the value of all other property from the total value of the corporation's property. 

Consolidated Gas Co. v. Baltimore (supra), 105 Md. 43. 

For a later case on the valuation of easements for tax purposes, see United Rwys. & Elec. Co. v. Baltimore, (1909) 

111 Md. 264, 73 Atl. 633. As to separate and distinct valuation for rate-making purposes, see Miles v. Public Service 

Comm., (1926) 151 Md. 337, 135 Atl. 579.

As to assessments generally, see Allegany County v. Union 

Mining Co., (1884) 61 Md. 545.

15. (a) In computing the assessable value of shares of stock in any national bank located in this State, or in any domestic corporation (other than finance corporations) having a capital stock divided into shares which are subject to assessment and taxation under this article, the State Tax Commission shall first ascertain the total aggregate value of the shares of capital stock of such corporation by considering (1) the market value, if any, of the shares of such stock, without reference to sales at abnormal prices, rendering market quotations not a fair index of actual value of the shares of stock as a whole; (2) the net earnings or income of such corporation, and (3) the net value of its assets; provided (a) that such aggregate value of the shares of capital stock shall never be ascertained to be less than the fair aggregate value of all the property and assets of such corporation of whatsoever kind and wheresoever situate, less the indebtedness or other liabilities of such corporation, exclusive of the capital stock, but with a fair allowance for contingent liabilities, and (b) that such aggregate value of the shares of the capital stock shall never be ascertained to be less than the total value of the real estate and tangible personal property owned by such corporation in this State. 

Proviso (b) above, as contained in Code 1924, Art. 81, Sec. 

163, is a valid and constitutional provision. Susquehanna

In determining the aggregate value of bank stock, it is improper to add together the amount of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits, and deduct one-fourth of the total; the Commissioner (now Commission) should take the market or intrinsic value, making only such deductions as are reasonable on account of fluctuations and actual conditions.

(c) After making the deductions specified in paragraph (b) of this section from the total value of the capital stock ascertained under paragraph (a), the residue shall be divided by the number of shares outstanding and the quotient shall be the assessable value of each share.

Unissued shares are not assessable. Consumers' Ice Co. v. 

State, (1895) 82 Md. 132, 33 Atl. 427. (d) If two or more classes of stock of such corporation shall be outstanding, the State Tax Commission shall ascertain how much of the total value of the capital stock, after making the deductions specified in paragraph (b) of this section, should fairly be attributed to each class, and the amount so ascertained shall be divided by the number of shares of such class of stock outstanding, and the quotient shall be the assessable value of each share of such class of stock. (e) Shares of stock assessable under this section shall be taxed to the several owners thereof, and the taxes thereon shall be debts of such owners, but may be collected in each case from the bank or other corporation, which shall be bound to pay the same for account of its stockholders whether or not dividends are declared thereon, as if such corporations were the ultimate taxpayer, but may obtain reimbursement therefor from the respective stockholders, and may charge the same in reduction of any amounts due to the several shareholders as dividends or otherwise.

138 Md. 668, 114 Atl. 717.

Susquehanna Power Co. v. State Tax Commission, (1930) 159

16. In computing the assessable value of shares of stock in domestic finance corporations, the State Tax Commission shall proceed in the same manner as prescribed in Section 15, except (1) that the

property and business outside of this State shall be excluded, to the end and intent that so much only of the value of the shares as represents business done in Maryland shall be taxed, and (2) that in apportioning the value of the shares between the business within and without Maryland, it shall be presumed in the absence of clear evidence to the contrary that the value of the property and business within Maryland bears to the value of the total business and property the same ratio which the gross receipts or earnings in Maryland (exclusive of income from permanent investments) bears to the total gross receipts or earnings (exclusive of income from permanent investments). All taxes assessed under this section shall also be subject to the provisions of paragraph (e) of Section 15. 

A corporation, not a bank, engaged in the lending and investment of money, is subject to this tax. Industrial Corp. v. State Tax Comm., (1919) 134 Md. 379, 106 Atl. 852. See also notes to Art. 81, Sec. 15.

28. [This section provides that ordinary State taxes shall be levied for the calendar year; that all State, county and/or city taxes on assessments by the State Tax Commission shall be levied for the calendar year and as of January 1 of such year as the "date of finality"; that, except upon assessments made by the State Tax Commission, all ordinary county and city taxes shall be levied for the same period as prescribed by local law, and all ordinary State, county, and city taxes shall be levied as of the same date of finality" as prescribed by local law; and that counties may change to a levy for the calendar year and as of January

§ 204. Franchise tax on deposits of savings banks.- 

90. [This section provides for an annual franchise tax on the deposits of mutual savings banks, at the rate of 4 of 1% of such deposits. Threefourths of the tax goes to the county-or Baltimore City-in which the bank is situated, and the remaining one-fourth goes to the State. deductions are made, but the personal property of such banks is exempt from taxation under Art. 81, Sec. 7 (20), except for share taxes paid by the corporation in which the bank is a stockholder. For cases dealing with the tax on deposits, see Westminster v. Westminster Savings Bank, (1900) 92 Md. 62, 48 Atl. 34; State v. Sterling, (1864) 20 Md. 502.

Section 90 was amended by L. 1931, Ch. 254, to provide that the tax should be payable on August 1 and that interest should accrue thereafter if the tax is unpaid by that date.] 

§ 205. Gross receipts tax.- 

91. (a) A State tax as a franchise tax is hereby levied annually for the year 1930 and subsequent years measured by the gross receipts for the preceding calendar year, of: (1) All domestic or foreign railroad companies, whose roads are worked by steam, doing business in this State, at the following rates, to wit:

One and one-quarter per centum on the first $1,000 per mile of gross earnings, or on the total earnings if they are less than $1,000 per mile and

Two per centum on all gross earnings above $1,000 and up to $2,000 per mile; and

Two and one-half per centum on all earnings in excess of $2,000 per mile.

Such tax is not open to objection as interfering with interstate commerce, since it is limited to proportion of gross receipts which mileage within Maryland bears to total mileage. 

Cumberland & P. R. Co. v. State, (1901) 92 Md. 668, 48 Atl. 

503, 52 L.R.A. 764. See 1 U. S. Code, Ann., (Const.), pp. 313342.

Charter exemption of Northern Cent. Ry. Co. repealed by imposition of general gross receipts tax. State v. Northern 

Cent. Ry. Co., (1900) 90 Md. 447, 45 Atl. 465, aff'd. 187 U. S. 

258, 23 Sup. Ct. 62, 47 L.Ed. 167.

Irrepealable exemption of "shares" of B. & O. R.R. exempts it from all franchise taxes, including the gross receipts tax. 

But the exemption does not apply to receipts from hotels. 

State v. Baltimore & O. R. Co., (1877) 48 Md. 49. See 

Baltimore v. Baltimore & O. R. Co., (1848) 6 Gill, 288, 292, 48 

Am. Dec. 531.

This tax is not in violation of Article 15 of the Bill of Rights, being a tax on franchises and not on property. An exemption of a constituent company in a consolidation prior to 1851 exempts the consolidated company proportionately. Exemption of "capital stock" includes exemption from gross receipts tax. State v. Philadelphia, W. & B. R. Co., (1876) 45 Md. 

361, 24 Am. Rep. 511.

A tax on gross receipts from passenger fares is a tax on the railroad and not on the passengers, and is not unconstitutional. 

State v. Baltimore & O. R. Co., (1871) 34 Md. 44, aff'd. in 

Baltimore & O. R. Co. v. State, 21 Wall. 456, 22 L.Ed. 678. (2) Every domestic or foreign telegraph or cable, express or transportation, parlor car, sleeping car, safe deposit and trust company doing business in this State, at the rate of two and one-half per centum (22%); provided, however, that the gross receipts tax payable in the year 1932 and in subsequent years, by safe deposit and/or trust companies shall be computed and paid at the rate of two and onehalf per centum (22%) with respect only to their safe deposit and trust business, including all receipts derived from the business of acting in a fiduciary or representative capacity, and at the rate of two per centum (2%) on all receipts derived from the business of insurance or guaranty (if any), without any deductions or credits of any kind whatsoever.

A corporation incorporated by special act to do a banking, trust, safe deposit, and real estate business is subject to the

CORPORATE TAXATION 

287 gross receipts tax. State v. Central Trust Co., (1907) 106 

Md. 268, 67 Atl. 267.

Payment of the gross receipts tax does not exempt a corporation from taxation of its personal property or its easements; the gross receipts tax is a franchise rather than a property tax. Postal Tel. Co. v. Harford County, (1917) 131 Md. 96, 101 

Atl. 600.

The gross receipts tax ("Park Tax") imposed on street railway companies by L. 1882, Ch. 229, is in lieu of a direct tax on intangible property and excludes a tax on their easements in public streets. United Rwys. & Elec. Co. v. Baltimore, (1909) 

111 Md. 264, 73 Atl. 633. (3) All domestic and foreign telephone and oil pipe line companies and title insurance companies doing business in this State at the rate of two per centum (2%); provided, however, that the gross receipts tax payable in the year 1932 and in subsequent years by title insurance companies shall be computed and paid at the rate of two per centum (2%) with respect only to their receipts derived from the business of insurance or guaranty, without any deductions or credits of any kind whatsoever. (4) All domestic and foreign electric light or power companies doing business in this State, at the rate of one (1%) per centum. 

Payment of the gross receipts tax does not relieve a corporation from payment of the tax on its shares, the latter being a tax on the individual stockholders. United States Elec. 

Light & Power Co. v. State, (1894) 79 Md. 63, 28 Atl. 768. 

(5) All domestic and foreign gas companies doing business in this State, at the rate of one and one-half (1½ %) per centum. (b) If any such railroad company has part of its road in this State and part thereof in another State or States, such company shall return a statement of its gross receipts over its whole line of road, together with a statement of the whole length of its line and the length of its line in this State, and such company shall pay to the State, at the said rates herein before prescribed upon such proportion of its gross earnings as the length of its line in this State bears to the whole length of its line; and similar statements shall be made by each oil pipe line company, and each sleeping car, parlor car, express or transportation company, telephone or telegraph or cable company, so that the proportion of the said gross earnings of the said companies, respectively, accruing, coming from their business within this State,

may be accurately ascertained, or said statement may be made in any other mode satisfactory to and required by the State Tax Commission. The said gross receipts tax shall be due and payable at the treasury on or before the first day of July in each year. 

The gross receipts tax is intended to apply only in respect of business done in Maryland. State v. U. S. Fid. & Guar. Co., (1901) 93 Md. 314, 48 Atl. 918. Surety companies are no longer taxed on their gross receipts. (c) [Applicability to partnerships and individuals in same businesses.]

98-100. [These sections provide for a tax on certain official commissions. Sec. 98 was amended by L. 1933, Ch. 242.] § 206. Possibility of inheritance taxes in certain cases on stock of non-resident decedents.— 

101-130. [These sections provide for a tax on commissions of executors and administrators, and for a collateral inheritance tax. The application of the provisions in the case of shares of stock held by resident decedents, in either domestic or foreign corporations, offers no difficulty. 

Shares of stock in domestic corporations held by non-residents pass to the domiciliary executor or administrator without any formality,

under Art. 93, Sec. 78. No inheritance tax can be imposed on stock of non-resident decedents, according to a recent decision of the Supreme Court, since such stock has its situs only at the residence of the owner. 

First National Bank v. Maine, (1932) 284 U. S. 312, 52 Sup. Ct. 174, 76 L. Ed. (Adv. Ops.) 211. This decision would seem to preclude local administration on such stock at suit of residuary legatee, next of kin or creditors under Art. 93, Sec. 79. The little-used procedure provided by that section may, therefore, be regarded as now obsolete. 

Even if such administration were granted, no inheritance tax could be imposed, and under Section 130 of the tax law, providing for “reciprocal exemptions," no tax could be imposed on the commissions of the administrator if the decedent was a resident of any of the nearly forty states having no such tax or offering reciprocal exemption. As to earlier law, (see Citizens' Nat. Bank v. Sharp, (1880) 53 Md. 521; State v. Dalrymple, (1889) 

70 Md. 294, 17 Atl. 82. Sec. 105A was added by L. 1933, Ch. 323.] § 207. Bonus tax.- 

133. Every domestic corporation having capital stock, except (1) railroad corporations authorized to construct, maintain or operate railroads in this State; (2) building or homestead associations, and (3) co-operative associations organized under Article 23 of the Code of Public General Laws (1924), Section 420, shall, at or before the time of incorporation, pay for the use of the State a bonus tax for its authorized capital stock at the following rates, to wit:

Twenty cents for every thousand dollars of the amount of its authorized capital stock, where such authorized capital stock amounts to one million dollars or less, but in no case less than twenty dollars. 

An additional bonus tax of one hundred and fifty dollars for every million dollars or fractional part thereof on the amount of authorized capital stock in excess of one million dollars and not in excess of five million dollars.

An additional bonus tax of twenty dollars for every million dollars or fractional part thereof on the amount of authorized capital stock in excess of five million dollars. 

For purposes of this section stock without par value shall be treated as if it were of the par value of one hundred dollars per share. 

As to liability for bonus tax imposed by prior statutes, see 

Roland Park Co. v. State, (1895) 80 Md. 448, 31 Atl. 298; 

State v. National Bank of Baltimore, (1870) 33 Md. 75.

The effect of payment or non-payment of the bonus tax on the question of corporate existence under the earlier statute is discussed in § 371 (App.), infra. The present statutory provision (Art. 23, Sec. 7) is discussed in §§ 18 and 175, supra. 

See notes to Art. 81, Sec. 135.

1931, CH. 262 

136. Every ordinary business corporation, excluding charitable, benevolent and fraternal institutions, shall pay annually to the State Treasurer for the use of the State on or before the first of August in each year succeeding the date of its incorporation, an annual tax for its franchise to be a corporation (in addition to any other tax imposed by law) at the following rate, that is to say:

On the amount of its capital stock issued, outstanding and/or subscribed for, on the first day of the preceding January, for the first five thousand dollars or less, the sum of ten dollars. 

For every one thousand dollars or fractional part thereof in excess of said five thousand dollars up to and not greater than fifty thousand dollars, the additional sum of one dollar.

For every additional two thousand dollars or fractional part thereof in excess of said fifty thousand dollars up to and not greater than one hundred thousand dollars, the additional sum of one dollar. 

If the amount of such capital stock is more than one hundred thousand dollars, but not greater than two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, there shall be an additional annual franchise tax of twenty dollars.

If the amount of such capital stock is more than two hundred and fifty thousand dollars and not greater than five hundred thousand dollars, there shall be an additional annual franchise tax of twenty dollars.

If the amount of such capital stock is more than five hundred thousand dollars and not greater than one million dollars, there shall be an additional annual franchise tax of thirty dollars. 

If the amount of said capital stock is more than one million dollars and not greater than ten million dollars, there shall be an additional annual franchise tax at the rate of fifty dollars for each additional million dollars or fractional part thereof, and on every five million dollars in excess of ten million dollars, the additional annual franchise tax on such excess shall be at the rate of one hundred dollars for each five million dollars or fractional part thereof. 

Every such corporation which has no part of its capital stock issued, subscribed for or outstanding on the first day of the preceding

CORPORATE TAXATION 

293 January, shall pay for such franchise an annual tax of ten dollars ($10.00).

For purposes of this section stock without par value shall be treated as if it were of the par value of one hundred dollars per share. 

The claim of the State for the franchise tax, though accruing after a State receivership, will be recognized in bankruptcy. 

In re Malko Milling & Lighting Co., (1929) 32 F. (2d) 825 (D. Ct. Md.). 

The amendment (L. 1931, Ch. 262) provides for interest after August 1 instead of after October 1.

The above tax applies only to ordinary business corporations. 

Certain other corporations pay a franchise tax on gross receipts, (see § 205, supra) and are taxed at a limited rate on their shares of stock. Still others (such as insurance companies other than fire, title, and marine insurance companies) pay no franchise tax, but a direct tax at the full State, county, and/or city rate on their shares (see § 201, supra). Casualty, surety, guaranty, and fidelity companies are taxed at a limited rate on their shares (§ 201, supra) and pay no franchise tax (§ 205, supra). The same is true of banks; but trust companies pay also a franchise tax on gross receipts. 

137. For the purpose of Section 136 the entire authorized capital stock of such corporation, as shown by the charter, certificate of incorporation, or any amendment thereof, shall be taken as issued, unless on or before the fifteenth day of March in each and every year the corporation shall file with the State Tax Commission an affidavit of any officer of the corporation, showing the actual number of its issued, outstanding and/or subscribed for shares, if any, of each class, as of the first day of the preceding January; provided, however, if a proper report, under oath, is filed, within fifteen days from the date (as shown by the records of the State Tax Commission) of the mailing of a notification of the amount of such tax due, the annual franchise tax which such corporation shall pay shall be computed upon the amount of its actually issued, outstanding and/or subscribed for capital stock, plus an additional ten per centum (10%) of the amount of its issued, outstanding and/or subscribed for capital stock, said tax, however, not to exceed, in the aggregate, the amount of tax if calculated upon the entire authorized capital stock; and in the event that no part of the capital stock was issued, outstanding or subscribed for, such corporation shall pay an annual franchise tax of twelve dollars and fifty cents ($12.50).

1931, CH. 262 

138. The State Tax Commission shall annually on or before the first day of June ascertain and certify the amount of each such tax to the Comptroller who shall forthwith transmit to such corporations a bill for the amount of the franchise tax, and such tax shall be payable to the Treasurer without interest at any time on or before August first of such year, provided the account is mailed on or before July first; and if the account shall not be mailed until after July first, the same shall be payable without interest at any time within thirty days after the mailing of the account. All corporation franchise taxes not paid on or before August first, or within thirty days after the mailing of the account, as above provided shall thereafter bear interest at the rate of one-half of one per cent for each month or fraction of a month; if such tax shall not be paid before the first day of December following, a penalty of five per cent on the amount thereof shall be added.

The amendment (L. 1931, Ch. 262) provides for interest after August 1 instead of after October 1, and reduces the penalty after December 1 from 10% to 5%.

Franchise tax on foreign corporations.- 

1933, CH. 347 

140. Every foreign corporation, except insurance companies of all classes, charitable and benevolent institutions and corporations subject to a franchise tax measured by gross receipts, which does business or exercises its franchises or maintains an office in this State, shall pay to the State Treasurer, for the use of the State, an annual franchise tax upon the amount of capital employed by it in this State on the preceding first day of January, as determined by the State Tax Commission, at the following rates, that is to say: 

The sum of twenty-five dollars for every fifty thousand dollars, or fractional part thereof of capital employed by it in this State up to five hundred thousand dollars-but in no case less than twenty-five dollars. 

If the amount of such capital is more than five hundred thousand dollars, and not more than five million dollars, then an additional amount equal to one-fortieth of one per cent. on the excess.

295 If more than five million dollars, then an additional amount at the rate of thirty dollars for every million dollars of such last-named excess.

144. (a) If any domestic corporation shall refuse or neglect to pay to the State, or the proper officers thereof, any franchise tax due by it, or any tax on its capital stock or shares thereof due by it, or any gross receipts tax due by it, for a space of two years from the first day of January next after the expiration of the calendar year during which said taxes became due and payable, it shall be the duty of the Comptroller of the State to certify immediately thereafter to the Governor a list of all such corporations, and the Governor shall forthwith issue and publish his proclamation declaring under this section that the charters of such corporations shall be repealed, annulled and forfeited, and that the powers conferred by law upon such corporations shall be inoperative, null and void, upon the expiration of sixty days from the date of the first publication of such proclamation, unless all such taxes, together with all interest and penalties due thereon, are paid before the expiration of said sixty days. 297 all taxes, interest and penalties as aforesaid, after the first publication of said proclamation, shall be omitted from subsequent publications thereof. A charter will not be forfeited for failure to do business for two years and non-payment of franchise tax unless such tax was assessed (prior statute). Murphy v. Wheatley, (1906) 

102 Md. 501, 63 Atl. 62. (b) The Secretary of State is directed to send copies of each of the said proclamations of the Governor to the Comptroller, to the Treasurer and to the State Tax Commission. The Comptroller, Treasurer and State Tax Commission shall note upon their respective records the facts of the repeal, annulment and forfeiture of the charters of all corporations whose charters have been repealed, annulled or forfeited as aforesaid, and the revival of those which have been revived as provided by Section 144½ of this Article. It shall be the duty of the Comptroller, at the time he certifies said corporations to the Governor as aforesaid, also to mail to each corporation so certified, at its address or office as the same appears upon his books, a notice that its charter will be repealed, annulled and forfeited, under the provisions of this section unless all taxes, interest and penalties so due by it are paid as aforesaid, it being the intention hereof that the mailing of such notice shall be sufficient, and that the failure for any reason of any such corporation to receive the notice so mailed to it, shall in no wise affect the repeal, annulment and forfeiture of its charter, in accordance with this section. (c) Whenever it is established to the satisfaction of the Governor that any corporation named in said proclamation has not neglected or refused to pay said tax for two consecutive years, or has been mistakenly reported to the Governor by the Comptroller as refusing or neglecting to pay such taxes as aforesaid, the Governor is authorized to correct such mistake and to make the same known by filing his proclamation to that effect in the office of the Secretary of State who shall send a copy thereof to the Comptroller, to the Treasurer and to the State Tax Commission. The effect of such proclamation shall be to restore to said corporation its charter with the same force and effect and to all intents and purposes as if said charter had at all times remained in full force and effect.

This paragraph was added by the 1931 amendment (L.

1442. The charter of any corporation of this State, heretofore or hereafter forfeited for the non-payment of taxes may, at any time, be revived in the manner following: (a) The last acting president or vice-president and secretary or treasurer of such corporation shall sign and verify under oath articles of revival in which shall be stated: (1) The name of the corporation at the time of the forfeiture of its charter. (2) The name by which the corporation will thereafter be known, which name must be such as could be adopted by a corporation of this State organized or existing at the time of the receipt for record of the articles of revival. (3) The postoffice address of the place at which the principal office of the corporation in this State will be located, which shall be in the same county or city in which its principal office was located at the time of the forfeiture of its charter, and the name or names and postoffice address or addresses of the corporation's resident agent or agents (giving in each case the county and city, town or place and street and number, if number there be). (4) That the articles of revival are for the purpose of procuring the revival of the charter of the corporation. (b) If any or all of the officers required by this section to sign and verify the articles of revival shall be dead, or shall refuse or neglect to sign or verify such articles of revival, any three of the last acting directors of such corporation may sign and verify the articles of revival. In any case where there shall be less than three directors of said corporation living and ready and willing to act as aforesaid, those who were stockholders or members of such corporation at the time of forfeiture, or their assigns, may elect as many directors as may be necessary, together with the surviving directors or those who are ready and willing to act to constitute three directors and such directors may sign and verify the articles of revival. A meeting of the stockholders or members may be called by any director, stock-

CORPORATE TAXATION 

299 holder or member upon ten days' written or printed notice, stating the place, day and hour of such meeting and the purpose thereof, such notice to be given to each stockholder or member, or his assigns, by leaving the same with him or at his residence or usual place of business, or by mailing it, postage prepaid, and addressed to him at his address as it last appeared upon the books of the corporation; at such meeting the stockholders or members, or their assigns, present in person or by proxy may elect directors as aforesaid. 

The directors so elected may take all steps and do all things necessary and proper to be done for the revival of the existence of such corporation as herein before provided with the same validity as if performed and done by the last president, or vice-president and secretary or treasurer or the officers performing the functions of said officers of such corporation. After a revival of the existence of such corporation shall be effected, a meeting of the stockholders of such corporation shall forthwith be called by the president or by a director, upon such notice as is required by law, by the charter, or by the by-laws for an extraordinary meeting thereof, and at such meeting the stockholders or members shall elect a full board of directors which board shall then elect such officers as are provided by law, by the charter, or by the by-laws to conduct and carry on the business and affairs of the corporation. (c) Such articles of revival shall be delivered to the State Tax Commission, which, upon the payment, and not before, of a recording fee of ten dollars and a revival fee of twenty-five dollars, and upon being satisfied, and not before, that all State and local taxes (other than taxes on real estate) and interest and penalties due by the corporation, irrespective of any period of limitation otherwise prescribed by law affecting the collection of any part of such taxes, and an amount equal to all State and local taxes (other than taxes on real estate) and interest and penalties which, irrespective of any period of limitation otherwise prescribed by law affecting the collection of any part of such taxes, would have been payable by the corporation if its charter had not been forfeited, have been paid, shall receive the same for record and indorse thereon the date and time of such receipt and promptly record the same, together with the indorsements thereon, as in the case of a certificate of incorporation. The recording by the State Tax Commission of the articles of revival shall be conclusive evidence of the payment of the fees and taxes required to be paid and of the revival of the charter of the corporation, except in a direct proceeding by the State, county or city entitled to such taxes. After the recording by it of such articles of revival the State Tax Commission shall transmit the copy thereof, duly certified by it, to the Clerk of the Circuit Court or Superior Court (according to the location of the principal office of the corporation), by whom the same shall be again recorded. One-quarter of the recording fees collected shall be paid by the State Tax Commis-

sion for recording such articles of revival to the Clerk of the Circuit or Superior Court, to whom the same are transmitted, and for the balance and for the revival fee it shall account quarterly to the Comptroller and pay the same forthwith to the State Treasurer for the use of the State. A duly certified copy of the articles of revival from the records of the State Tax Commission or the Clerk of the Circuit or Superior Court shall be evidence of the revival of the charter of the corporation and of its right to exercise the powers contained in its charter. (d) The State Tax Commission shall promptly notify the Comptroller and the Treasurer of the receipt for record of all articles of revival. (e) Such revival of the charter of the corporation shall validate all contracts, acts, matters and things made, done and performed within the scope of its charter by such corporation, its officers and agents during the time when such charter was void, with the same force and effect and to all intents and purposes as if said charter had at all times remained in full force and effect; and all real and personal property, rights and credits of said corporation at the time its charter became void, and which were not disposed of prior to the time of such revival shall be vested in such corporation, after such revival, as fully and amply as they were held by said corporation at and before the time its charter became void, and said corporation after such revival shall be as exclusively liable for all contracts, acts, matters and things made, done or performed in its name and on its behalf by its officers and agents prior to such reinstatement, as if its charter had at all times remained in full force and effect.

229. Grounds for appointment of receivers. . 324 324 § 217. Corporate existence can be terminated only by legislative act.-A corporation can in legal theory be created only by the State legislature. Likewise only the State legislature can terminate the existence of a corporation.¹ As the legislature may create corporations by means of general laws, so the legislature may by general laws provide for the termination of corporate existence on the terms and conditions therein stated. 

While the legislature may terminate corporate existence by special act (subject to constitutional limitations), in ordinary practice corporations are terminated, as they are created, by general laws. Courts of equity have no inherent power to 

1 See Du Puy v. Transportation Co., (1896) 82 Md. 408, 436, 33 Atl. 889, 34 Atl. 910. 306

3 dissolve corporations and have only such jurisdiction in that respect as is conferred on them by statute,2 and while they have inherent power to appoint receivers for the property of a corporation where there is fraud or spoliation or imminent danger of the loss of its property, courts of equity cannot, except as permitted by statute, indirectly exercise the power to dissolve a corporation by appointing a receiver to assume control of its property and management and to distribute its property. Loss of all its property and franchises does not dissolve a corporation. Nor does the ownership of all its shares by a single person. In the case of Swift v. Smith, Dixon & Co., an individual purchased all the stock of a corporation, failed to elect officers or otherwise keep up the corporate organization, and subsequently executed a conveyance in his own name of land belonging to it. The court sustained the validity of the deed on the ground that although the corporate existence had not been terminated (overruling an earlier dictum), the corporate life was suspended for the time being and until the reëstablishment of the corporate organization. This case and others in which one man owned all or practically all the corporate stock have been discussed in an earlier chapter.7 Ownership by one person of all the stock of a corporation having capital stock does not of itself and apart from other circumstances justify the courts in ignoring the corporate existence, as previously shown. Nor is the corporation thereby dissolved. The death of all the stockholders of a corporation would not dissolve it, since the shares would pass

658; Howeth v. Coulbourne Bros. Co., (1911) 115 Md. 107, 80 Atl. 916. 

Davis v. U. S. Electric Co. (1893) 77 Md. 35, 40, 25 Atl. 982, and see §§ 138, supra, and 229, infra. 

State v. Bank of Maryland, (1834) 6 G. & J. 205, 230, 26 Am. Dec. 561. (1886) 65 Md. 428, 5 Atl. 534, 57 Am. Rep. 336.

In the case of corporations having no capital stock it has been said that the death of all the members dissolves the corporation. 10 There has been no judicial determination of the point in this State, though it was discussed in Nicolai v. 

Maryland Agricultural & Mechanical Assn.11 The statute now provides:

Whenever it shall happen in the case of any corporation having a definite number of members and no capital stock, that by death or resignation the membership shall be reduced below a majority of the prescribed number, the corporation shall not on that account be dissolved; but it shall be lawful for the surviving or continuing members, so long as the number thereof shall be two or more, to fill vacancies and continue the corporate succession.12 13 As previously pointed out,¹³ the life of a corporation was in early days usually limited to a definite number of years by the statutory authority (special or general) creating it. In such cases, the corporation automatically ceased to exist at the end of the period so fixed. 14 Today there are no such corporations in Maryland except such (if any) as may have been created by special act since June 1, 1908. The statute effective on that date, provides that

Every corporation formed under this Article shall have, until forfeiture, the right of perpetual succession; and all provisions in the charter or certificate of any existing corporation or imposed upon by any act in force at the time of its creation or formation limiting its duration, are hereby annulled and repealed.15 

A similar provision with respect to banking institutions was enacted in 1927.16 It may, therefore, be stated broadly (subject to the exceptions above noted) that corporate existence can be terminated only in accordance with one of the statutory methods presently to be stated.

§ 218. Statutory provisions for dissolution of corporations.- 

The following statutory methods have been provided for the termination of corporate life: (a) Voluntary dissolution by petition filed by the corporation in a court of equity.17 (b) Voluntary dissolution by petition filed by the corporation with the State Tax Commission (applicable only in the case of corporations having no assets and no liabilities). 18 (c) Dissolution by bill in equity filed by a creditor or stockholder (applicable only in the case of an insolvent corporation).19 (d) Forfeiture of charter for abuse or non-use of franchises by suit at law filed by the Attorney General.20 (e) Forfeiture of charter for non-payment of taxes by proclamation of the Governor.21

Termination of corporate life also results from merger or consolidation with another corporation pursuant to statutory authorization.

As previously shown,22 merger or consolidation has the effect of terminating the life of the corporations merged or consolidated and vests all the property and rights of such corporations in the new corporation resulting from such merger or consolidation, which new corporation likewise assumes all liabilities of the merged or consolidated corporations. In the case of merger or consolidation, therefore, it is not necessary that the corporate property should be collected and distributed and the questions of law incident to such collections and distributions discussed in this chapter do not arise. § 219. Voluntary dissolution by petition filed in court of equity.—Sections 88, 89, 90, and 93 of the Corporation Law23 prescribe the manner in which a corporation may voluntarily dissolve by application to a court of equity and the manner in which the distribution of its property is effected. They are as follows:

88. Any corporation of this State may close its affairs and authorize a bill for its dissolution to be filed in the following manner: 

A majority of the whole board of directors shall pass a resolution declaring that dissolution is advisable and calling a meeting of the stockholders or members to take action thereon. The meeting of the stockholders or members shall be duly warned in the manner provided in Section 19 of this Article. If two-thirds of all the shares (or, if two or more classes of shares have been issued, two-thirds of each class), outstanding and entitled to vote, or two-thirds of the members vote in favor of dissolution, a petition for dissolution shall be forthwith filed in the name of the corporation and on its behalf in a Court of Equity of the county or city in which its principal office is located. Whenever all of the stockholders or members shall consent in writing to a dissolution, no meeting of stockholders or members or notice thereof shall be necessary.

Voluntary dissolution of corporations having no assets or liabilities by petition filed with the State Tax Commission.-Section 91 of the Corporation Law prescribes the terms and conditions of dissolution of corporations without assets or liabilities as follows: 

91. In addition to the provisions in the foregoing section, any corporation of this State possessing no assets and owing no debts may close its affairs and authorize a petition for dissolution to be filed with the State Tax Commission by adopting the following procedure: 

If no stock has been issued, a majority of the incorporators or directors named in the certificate of incorporation shall pass a resolution declaring that dissolution is advisable and thereupon a petition shall forthwith be filed in the name of the corporation, with the State Tax Commission of Maryland, such petition to be signed and sworn to by such incorporators or directors, giving their addresses and setting forth therein that the corporation has no outstanding contractual obligations and has no assets or liabilities. Upon the filing of such petition, the State Tax Commission shall pass an order directing all persons interested in the corporation to show cause, if any they have, why it should not be dissolved on another date to be named in said order, which order shall be published by the State Tax Commission once in some newspaper published in the city or county where the principal office of such corporation is located at least fifteen days prior to the date on which the Commission shall take final action, and if no cause is shown, or no sufficient cause, why an order of dissolution should not be passed, the State Tax Commission shall pass such order dissolving such corporation, and a copy thereof for recordation shall be forwarded by the said Commission to the clerk of the Circuit or Superior Court, as the case may be, where the certificate of incorporation is recorded, and a copy thereof for recordation shall also be forwarded to the Secretary of State, if the certificate of incorporation is recorded in the office of said Secretary of State.

If any stock of the corporation has been issued, a resolution authorizing the dissolution shall be passed by a majority of the directors and a majority in amount of stock outstanding at meetings duly warned according to law, and if more than one class of stock, then by a majority of each class, and in such case the petition shall be valid if sworn to and filed by the president and secretary, or by a majority of the directors, provided that in all cases a certified copy of such resolution shall be filed as an exhibit with the petition. 

Accompanying the filing of any petition heretofore referred to with the State Tax Commission, there shall be a fee of fifteen dollars out of which shall be paid the cost of advertising and for the balance, the State Tax Commission shall account quarterly to the Comptroller of the Treasury and pay the same to the Treasurer for the use of the State.

The State Tax Commission shall in no case pass an order of dissolution when it appears that such corporation has assets, liabilities or outstanding contractual obligations.

The commission has no jurisdiction to dissolve a corporation unless the provisions of the statute are exactly complied with.

By Section 77 (previously discussed) it is provided that in the event of the insolvency of a corporation unpaid stock subscriptions "shall be considered as an asset of the corporation." 

Wright v. Lewis31 was a suit brought by a trustee in bankruptcy under this section against a stockholder to collect an unpaid subscription to stock. The defendant demurred to the bill on the ingenious ground that as the unpaid subscriptions were by the section treated as an asset of the corporation and as the total assets of the corporation (including the amount of the unpaid stock subscriptions) were in excess of its liabilities, the corporation was not insolvent within the meaning of the section and the suit was therefore not maintainable. The court held that the corporation was insolvent within the meaning of the section.

98. Whenever the Attorney-General or any State's Attorney shall be authorized by the Governor to institute proceedings against a corporation to determine whether it has been guilty of such misuse, abuse or non-use of its powers and franchises as would by law make proper the forfeiture of its charter, the Attorney-General or State's Attorney so authorized shall file in the Court hereinafter designated a petition in the name of the State setting forth in detail the alleged cause of forfeiture; and thereupon the Court shall lay a rule upon the corporation to show cause within a time named why a judgment of forfeiture should not be entered as prayed; a copy of such rule and of the petition shall be served on the corporation by a day to be therein limited, as other process against the corporation, as hereinafter provided, would be served. By the day named in said order, unless further time is granted by the Court, the corporation shall file its answer, setting forth all its defences and verified by the affirmation or affidavit of one of its officers; such further pleadings, if any, shall be filed within such time as the Court shall direct. 

99. If issues of fact be joined in such proceedings, the same shall stand for trial at such time as the court shall direct and shall be tried by a jury if either party desires it; otherwise they shall be heard and determined by the court. If from the findings of the jury or upon consideration or determination by the court, the court shall be of opinion that legal cause of forfeiture has been shown, and that the public interest requires that a forfeiture should be declared, a judgment of forfeiture shall be entered and the charter of the corporation shall thereby be annulled and vacated; and it shall be ousted of its corporate franchises; and the court shall thereupon appoint a receiver or receivers of the corporate estate and assets. The powers of such receivers and all the consequences of dissolution shall be such as are hereinabove conferred and provided by this article. 

100. If the corporation shall neglect to plead within the times appointed and provided, the court shall proceed to hear the petition ex parte; and if a cause of forfeiture is shown, a judgment shall be entered as is provided in the preceding section. 

101. If the court upon a hearing, ex parte or otherwise shall be of opinion that legal cause of forfeiture has been shown, it may, nevertheless, in its discretion, before passing a final judgment, require the corporation within a time fixed to remedy the grievance complained of and may suspend the entry of a final judgment until the time so fixed, and may afterwards refuse to enter such judgment if the grievance has been remedied.
