the corporation. And from any final judgment or determination of the court in proceedings hereunder, either party may appeal to the Court of Appeals as provided by sections 73 and 74 of article 5 of the annotated code.

The method of forfeiture provided in Section 98 is valid and constitutional; while proceedings for forfeiture of the charter of a corporation may be maintained only by authority of the legislature, no special act is required and the legislature may by general law prescribe the method of forfeiture.35 

When a corporation purchased the railroad of another (which acted ultra vires in making the sale) and operated the road at rates higher than the charter of the vendor road permitted, this did not constitute a violation of the vendee corporation's charter. 36 The habitual sale by an incorporated club of liquor to its members in violation of a local option law is a misuse of its franchise which justifies forfeiture of its charter.37 

Issuance by a corporation of insurance policies in an amount exceeding that permitted by law justifies forfeiture of its charter. 38 While the statute does not provide in terms for a demurrer by the State to the answer, this is a correct mode of pleading.39 Appeal may not be taken from an order overruling a demurrer; the statute's procedure for appeal (that is, only from final judgment) must be followed.40 Petitions filed pursuant to Section 102 are not removable.41 While abuse, misuse, or non-use of corporate franchises may be made the basis of a proceeding by the State for the forfeiture of a corporate charter, they do not constitute a basis for dissolving a corporation in a suit brought for that purpose by a stockholder, creditor or any other private person and cannot be collaterally taken advantage of by any private person.42

This section applies in the case of all corporations dissolved by court decree, whether in a proceeding initiated by the corporation itself pursuant to Section 88,47 or by a creditor or stockholder of an insolvent corporation pursuant to Section 92,48 or by the Attorney General for forfeiture of the corporate franchise pursuant to Sections 98 and 101.49 The winding up of corporations dissolved otherwise than by court proceedings is provided for in Section 95, discussed in the next section. (a) Powers of statutory receiver. It will be observed that by Section 94 the court which has dissolved the corporation collects and distributes its assets through the agency of receivers appointed by the court. The powers of the statutory receiver are greater than those of the ordinary chancery receiver. The statutory receiver is entirely different from the ordinary chancery receiver. 494 The chancery receiver is a mere custodian, having no title to the property in his hands and no powers other than those expressly conferred upon him by the court or derived from its established practice.50 The receiver of a dissolved corporation appointed pursuant to this section is vested with title and has the other powers therein enumerated. In order that he may have these powers, however, the corporation must have been dissolved and the mere appointment of receivers for an admittedly insolvent corporation does not operate to dissolve it.5¹ (b) What property vests in the receiver.-Under the terms of Section 94 all property of the corporation vests in the receiver. The property, however, is subject to liens to which it was subject in the hands of the corporation. The statute

The proper procedure to be followed by the mortgagee is to apply to the court for authority to sell.52 If the corporation has not been dissolved, so that the statute does not apply, its property in the hands of a receiver is subject to existing liens and cannot be sold under a power of sale without permission of the court, but if so sold the sale is valid. 53 The right of the mortgagee to enforce his lien against property in the hands of a receiver is a specific illustration of the broad principle that receivers (in the absence of express statutory provision) have no greater rights in the property of the dissolved corporation than the corporation itself had. In Colton v. Drovers 

Building Assn.,54 the court considered the rights of a receiver of a dissolved banking corporation to recover on a note of a building association which was held by the bank at the time of its dissolution and became due thereafter. At the time of the dissolution the building association had on deposit with the bank an amount less than the amount of the note. On maturity of the note the building association tendered to the receiver in payment of the note the difference between this deposit and the amount of the note. The receiver refused to accept this and demanded payment of the note in full. This was refused and the receiver sued on the note. The court held that the bank could have recovered from the building association only the difference between the amount of the deposit and the amount of the note, since the building association was entitled to set off its deposit against the note, and the receiver, not being a bona fide purchaser for value of the note, took the note subject to the same burdens as it had in the hands of the bank. The fact that the note was not due at the time of the dissolution was held to be irrelevant. While the receiver becomes vested with the property of the corporation, he is not entitled to property which was never an asset of the corporation. Colton v. Mayer55 was a suit by receivers

(c) Right of receiver to set aside preferences.-By the statute, the receiver of a dissolved corporation is, however, given a right which the corporation did not have, the right to set aside fraudulent preferences. The statute provides that "all preferences, conveyances and transfers howsoever made by it [the corporation] or by any of its officers on its behalf, which would be void or fraudulent under the provisions of the insolvency laws of this State, if made by a natural person, shall to a like extent and with like remedies be fraudulent and void; and for the purpose of setting aside such preferences, payments and transfers, the receiver of such corporation shall have all the powers vested in the permanent trustee of an insolvent debtor." Article 4756 contains the "insolvency laws of this State" herein referred to. 

The insolvent laws (which do not apply to corporations) provide that the property of the insolvent shall vest in the permanent trustee created thereby, and he is given broad powers to set aside fraudulent conveyances and transfers constituting preferences under the act. Section 94 of the 

Corporation Law, so far as it operates to invalidate preferences, was first enacted into law by L. 1902, Ch. 198. At common law, preferences by an insolvent corporation were not invalid. 57 

In the case of a corporation, as in the case of an individual insolvent, preferences consist in paying one creditor in preference to another and do not include cash transactions, which are valid. 58 While the statute gives the receiver the powers conferred by the insolvency laws on the trustee of an insolvent debtor, it does not make the insolvency laws otherwise applicable to corporations.59 The authority given by the statute to set aside fraudulent preferences was applied in James Clark Co.

95. Upon the dissolution of any corporation of this State in any manner otherwise than by judicial proceedings, and until other persons shall be appointed as receivers by some court of competent jurisdiction, the directors at the time of dissolution shall become and be trustees for the creditors, stockholders and members of the corporation so dissolved. They shall take title to its assets, real and personal, and shall have full power to wind up and settle its affairs, to sue for and collect its assets and to pay its debts; and they shall divide among the stockholders or members the money and other property that shall remain after the payment of the debts and necessary expenses; and the said trustees shall be jointly and severally liable to the creditors, stockholders and members of such corporation to the extent of its property and effects that shall come into their hands.

Effect of dissolution on pending suits by and against the corporation.-Section 96 of the Corporation Law provides that dissolution shall not "abate any pending suit or proceeding by or against the corporation, and all such suits may be continued with such change of parties, if any, as the court in which the same are pending shall direct."73a § 228. Dissolution of a corporation matures its obligations. 

The dissolution of a corporation renders further performance of its obligations impossible on either side and therefore has the effect of maturing them at once, notwithstanding the absence of any such provision in the instrument creating the obligation. The dissolution of an insurance company operates to put an end to contracts of insurance issued by it and operates as a breach of the contract on its part giving rise to a claim for damages by the insured for the return of unearned premium value.75 But if the insured takes out new insurance in place of that cancelled by the dissolution of the corporation, the measure of damages will be the cost of the substituted insurance.76 § 229. Duties and liabilities imposed on various classes of foreign corporations.-The questions whether a foreign corporation may be sued in Maryland, whether it must qualify and file an annual report, whether it is liable for an annual franchise tax, and whether it must annually file a list of resident stockholders and certain other information as to its stock, are all determined by different tests under the present Maryland statutes. A foreign corporation may be sued by any one for any cause of action if it is "regularly doing business or regularly exercising any of its franchises" in the State;¹ and any such corporation "which shall transact business" in the State may be sued on dealings or transactions therein or on any controversy with a resident thereof." Every foreign corporation (excluding insurance companies) must qualify and report annually if it "has an office or place of 

1 Art. 23, Sec. 118. See § 231, infra.

327 business" in the State or "purposes to engage therein permanently or temporarily in the construction, alteration, erection or repair of any building, bridge, railroad, railway or structure of any kind." The annual franchise tax on capital employed in the State is imposed on "every foreign corporation, except insurance companies of all classes, and corporations subject to a franchise tax measured by gross receipts, which does business or exercises its franchises or maintains an office" in the State. Finally, "every foreign corporation of any kind doing business" in the State or "owning any property therein" must file annually a list of its stockholders, together with information as to the taxability and value of the shares of its stock. Foreign corporations subject to the annual franchise tax are also obliged to file a report by reason of the broad wording of the section of the law under which domestic corporations are required to report. The situation is further complicated by the fact that national banks are excluded from the definition of foreign corporations in the corporation law but included for purposes of the tax law. Thus, national banks located in the State are not required to qualify or report and are not liable to be sued under the provisions of the corporation law, but they must file a report and list of resident stockholders for tax purposes.⁹ § 231. 335 ment of an annual franchise tax based on the amount of capital employed by it in the State as of January 1.60 Until 1929 the tax was imposed only on companies doing business and maintaining an office or place of business in the State.61 The prior law, however, was construed by the Attorney General to apply to corporations doing business in the State though not maintaining an office or usual place of business.62 Thus, it was ruled that a company warehousing goods in Maryland in a public warehouse and employing an agent whose sole duty was to receive orders and fill them was liable for the tax even though all bills were sent from the home office of the company and paid there.63

A foreign corporation whose only business done within the State constitutes interstate commerce need not pay the franchise tax. Thus, a company maintaining an office in the State only for its traveling salesmen and engineers (all orders being accepted outside the State, and installations and repairs made by labor supplied by purchasers) was engaged solely in interstate commerce and was not required to pay the franchise tax.64

The minimum tax is $25, which is payable by every corporation whose capital employed in the State is valued at $50,000 or less. The rate of tax is $25 for each $50,000 or fraction thereof up to $500,000; 40 of 1% on the amount above $500,000 and not exceeding $5,000,000; and $30 additional for every million dollars in excess of $5,000,000.65 

Franchise tax bills are mailed about June 1 and are payable August 1; thereafter interest is charged at the rate of 1½ of 

1%, per month. On December 1 a penalty of 5% is added, and the corporation forfeits the right to do business in the State.66 Its officers are subject to the same penalties for transacting business which would be imposed on them if the corporation had never qualified.67

Corporations required to report for tax purposes and file list of stockholders. The general statute under which domestic business corporations are required to report is sufficiently broad to include foreign corporations. This statute, in part, requires that a report (as of January 1) be filed with the State Tax Commission not later than March 15 by (1) every corporation subject to assessment on its property or any part thereof by the State Tax Commission,69 and (2) any corporation, firm, or individual against whom any tax is to be calculated by the State Tax Commission.70 Under the latter clause foreign corporations subject to the annual franchise tax on capital employed in the State,"¹ or to the franchise tax on gross receipts 72 are included. The report is on a form prepared by the Commission and is to be made "in such manner and containing replies to such interrogatories as may be determined upon by said Commission . . . in order that it may perform any duties imposed upon it."73 The report is to be under oath of such officer or officers as the Commission may determine.74 The Commission requires that the report be sworn to by the president or the treasurer of a foreign corporation, in accordance with the statutory requirements for reports by corporations which must qualify to do business in the State.75 A penalty of $5 is imposed for delay in filing the

Consequences of failure to qualify and report. 

Every officer or agent transacting business in the State for a foreign corporation "which fails to comply with the provisions of Section 119"83 is guilty of a misdemeanor and liable to a fine of $200.84 The section referred to, which has already been discussed, requires qualification by a company which maintains an office or place of business in the State.85 A corporation having no office in the States is not required by Section 119 to qualify and therefore is not in default for failing to do so.

It would seem, therefore, that such a corporation cannot be in the position of "failing to comply" with the provisions of that section. 

Failure to qualify does not "affect the validity of any contract made with such non-complying corporation, but no suit shall be maintained in any of the courts of this State by any such corporation until it has complied."'87 An insurance company which issued a policy in the State but failed to comply with the provisions of the law was denied the right to maintain a suit to collect assessments on such policy.88

Certified copies of documents filed thereunder need not be produced. 92 § 236. Limitations on exercise of powers by foreign corporations. The general rule is that qualification permits the exercise by a foreign corporation of all its charter powers within the State, 93 with the limitation that privileges contrary to the policy of the State and not granted to domestic corporations may likewise not be exercised by foreign corporations.94 

It is expressly provided by the statute that "no foreign corporation shall engage or continue in any kind of business in this State, the transaction of which by domestic corporations is not permitted by the laws thereof."95 This provision has been held to apply where a foreign electric company sought to use the streets of Baltimore City without express permission from the State or the municipal government, though domestic corporations were required to obtain the permission of the city as well as the grant of power from the legislature. The court decided that the foreign corporation was also subject to the restriction, to the extent at least that it would have to obtain the city's permission.96 In the case of the "mortmain" law, however, since the statute prohibiting bequests to religious corporations without legislative sanction refers expressly to domestic corporations, it has been held that foreign religious corporations are not under the same disability." § 237. Evidence of existence, qualification, and powers.— 

In determining the powers of a foreign corporation which has qualified to do business in the State, the charter as filed with the State authorities" for qualification purposes may be relied on notwithstanding the adoption of amendments which have not been so filed." Qualification may be proved by exhibiting the certificate issued by the proper State officials without the necessity of producing certified copies of documents filed at the time of qualification." The existence of a foreign corporation may be proved by the license of such State officials. authorizing it to do business; or by production of a paper from such State office purporting to be its charter and bylaws; or by letters patent issued by the governor of the State in which it claims to be incorporated.10 § 238. Where, however, the majority stockholder of a foreign corporation was its president, secretary, treasurer, a director, and its managing agent, but rendered no accounts as agent, and the corporation, because of improper and fraudulent motives, refused to make him account, it was held that the court would assume jurisdiction of a bill by a minority stockholder to require him to render an account.27 The Maryland courts. seldom appoint receivers for foreign corporations, except as ancillary to a receivership in the state of incorporation. It has been held that the courts have no power to appoint receivers for an insolvent foreign corporation "in the absence of jurisdiction over the subject matter of the suit."'28 The existence of tangible assets to be administered in Maryland is sufficient to warrant the appointment of receivers in event of insolvency, but no Maryland receiver will be appointed if the only assets in the State are debts due by local residents on account of subscriptions or assessments.29 Where the controversy leading to the application for a receivership is one relating to internal management, no receiver will be appointed. In a recent case the corporation and a director were joined as defendants. The bill sought appointment of a receiver and an injunction against interference with the receivership by the defendant director. The object of the bill was to settle quarrels between the directors and defeat efforts of the defendant director to control the corporation. 

This seemed merely a question of internal management and the court declined to uphold jurisdiction.³ 30 In a recent New Jersey case involving a Maryland corporation, the court did not hesitate to take jurisdiction where the only questions involved were the propriety of an investment by the corporation in another corporation controlled by the voting stockholders of the first corporation and the propriety of a reduction of capital stock to permit payment of dividends.

Powers of receiver of foreign corporation appointed in state of incorporation.-Progressive recognition of the rights of foreign receivers appears from the cases decided by the Maryland courts. Originally a foreign receiver was not permitted to sue at all in the courts of the State.32 Later it was held that he might bring an action in the name of the corporation,33 and this was extended, in the case of actions to collect stock subscriptions, to permit suit by the foreign receiver in his own name as receiver.34 The proper practice at the present time is for the foreign receiver to apply for and obtain the permission of the Maryland court before bringing suit.35 If the courts have already assumed jurisdiction of the same subject matter, no suit will be entertained by the foreign receiver.36 In the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia it has been held that payment may be properly made in the District by the United States Government to receivers of a Maryland corporation appointed by a Maryland court, and that such payment cannot be restrained by a New York receiver of such corporation.37 The distinction between "chancery receivers" and "statutory receivers" or liquidators (see Section 224) is important in this connection.

§ 255. Charter powers not to be narrowly construed.— 

The aforegoing enumeration of the purposes, objects and business of the Corporation is made in furtherance, and not in limitation, of the powers conferred upon the Corporation by law, and is not intended, by the mention of any particular purpose, object or business, in any manner to limit or restrict the generality of any other purpose, object or business mentioned, or to limit or restrict any of the powers of the Corporation. The Corporation is formed upon the articles, conditions and provisions herein expressed, and subject in all particulars to the limitations relative to corporations which are contained in the general laws of this State. § 270. (Sec. 2) Special meetings.— 

Special meetings of the stockholders of the corporation may be called at any time by the President or by a majority of the Board of Directors, either by vote or in writing, or by a majority of the Executive Committee (if created pursuant to the By-laws) either by vote or in writing. Upon request in writing, delivered to the President or Secretary or any Director, of the holders of a majority of all the shares outstanding and entitled to vote, it shall be the duty of the President, Secretary or such Director to call forthwith a meeting of stockholders. Such request shall state the purpose of the meeting and notice thereof shall be given as provided in Section 3 of this Article I. If the person to whom such request in writing shall have been delivered shall fail to issue a call for a meeting within three (3) days after the receipt of such request, then the stockholders owning a majority of the voting shares may do so by giving the notice prescribed in Section 3 of this Article I. No business other than that stated in the notice of the meeting shall be transacted at any special meeting of the stockholders, however called. Special meetings of the stockholders shall be held at the principal office of the corporation in (Blank No. 7) Maryland, except in cases in which the notice of the meeting designates some other place; but all meetings shall be held within the State of Maryland.

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 17-20, 27. Text, §§ 68, 77, 108-111.] § 272. (Sec. 4) Quorum.- 

At any meeting of stockholders the presence, in person or by proxy, of the holders of a majority of all shares having voting rights at such meeting shall be necessary and sufficient to constitute a quorum for the election of directors or for the transaction of other business; but, in the absence of a quorum, the stockholders entitled to vote who shall be present in person or by proxy at any meeting (or adjournment thereof) may, by vote of a majority of shares so present and entitled to vote, adjourn the meeting from time to time, but not for a period of over thirty (30) days at any one time, by announcement at the meeting until a quorum shall attend. At any such adjourned meeting at which a quorum shall be present, any business may be transacted which might have been transacted at the meeting as originally notified. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 21. Text, § 112.] § 273. (Sec. 5) Proxies.— 

Stockholders may vote either in person or by proxy, but no proxy which is dated more than three months before the meeting at which it is offered shall be accepted unless such proxy shall on its face name a longer period for which it is to remain in force. Every proxy shall be in writing subscribed by a stockholder, or by his duly authorized

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 23. Text, § 113.] § 274. (Sec. 6) Voting.— 

At every meeting of the stockholders, every stockholder of the corporation shall be entitled to one vote for each share of voting stock registered in his name on the books of the corporation on the date for the determination of voting rights thereat; provided, however, that no share shall be voted by any stockholder if any instalment duly called thereon shall be overdue and unpaid. Upon demand of stockholders holding ten per cent (10%) of the shares present in person or by proxy and entitled to vote, the votes for Directors, or upon any question before a meeting, shall be by ballot; and except in cases in which it is by statute, by the Charter, or by these By-laws otherwise provided, a majority of the votes cast shall be sufficient to elect and pass any measure. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 21, 23. Text, §§ 38, 42, 113-116.] § 275. (Sec. 7) Inspectors.- 

Two inspectors may be elected by the stockholders at any meeting, and, if so elected, such inspectors shall open and close the polls, shall receive and take charge of the proxies and ballots and decide all questions as to the qualifications of voters, the validity of proxies and the acceptance or rejection of votes.

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 15, 27. Text, §§ 69, 120.] § 284. (Sec. 7) Quorum.- 

A majority of the Board of Directors shall be necessary and sufficient to constitute a quorum for the transaction of business at every meeting of the Board of Directors; but if at any meeting there be less than a quorum present, a majority of those present may adjourn the meeting from time to time, but not for a period of over ten days at any one time, without notice other than by announcement at the meeting until a quorum shall attend. At any such adjourned meeting at which a quorum shall be present, any business may be transacted which might have been transacted at the meeting as originally notified. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 10, 15. Text, §§ 69, 117, 120. By-laws may provide for quorum of not less than two, nor less than one-third of Board.]

§ 285. (Sec. 8) Removal.— 

At any meeting of the stockholders called for the purpose, any director may, by the vote of a majority of all the shares of stock outstanding and entitled to vote, be removed from office, with or without cause, and another may be appointed in the place of the person so removed, to serve for the remainder of his term. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 20. Text, §§ 110, 111, 115, 116.] § 286. (Sec. 9) Vacancies.- 

If any director shall die or resign, or if the stockholders shall remove any director without appointing another in his place, a majority of the remaining directors (although such majority is less than a quorum) may elect a successor to hold office for the unexpired portion of the term of the director whose place shall so become vacant, and until his successor shall have been duly chosen and qualified. Vacancies in the Board of Directors created by an increase in the number of directors may be filled by the vote of a majority of the entire Board as constituted prior to such increase, and directors so elected by the Board to fill such vacancies shall hold office until the next succeeding annual meeting of stockholders and thereafter until their successors shall be elected and qualified. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 69, 118, 120.] § 287. (Sec. 10) Compensation.- 

Directors, as such, shall not receive any stated compensation for their services, but by resolution of the Board of Directors a fixed sum and expenses of attendance, if any, may be allowed for attendance at any regular or special meeting thereof. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to preclude a director from serving the corporation in any other capacity and receiving compensation therefor. 

[Text, § 131.] Article III. Officers § 288. (Sec. 1) Executive officers.- 

The executive officers of the corporation shall be a President, a Vice-President, a Secretary and a Treasurer, and such other officers as the Board from time to time considers necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the corporation. The executive officers shall be elected annually by the Board of Directors at its first meeting

BY-LAWS 

367 following the annual meeting of stockholders. Each such officer shall hold office for a term of one year, and thereafter until his successor is elected and qualified or until his death, resignation or removal. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 12. Text, §§ 71, 123.] § 289. (Sec. 2) President.- 

The President shall be a director of the corporation. He shall be the chief executive officer of the corporation. He shall, when present, preside at all meetings of the stockholders and directors; he shall have general management and direction of the business of the corporation and all powers ordinarily exercised by the President of a corporation; he shall have authority to sign and execute, in the name of the corporation, all authorized deeds, mortgages, bonds, contracts or other instruments; he shall annually prepare a full and true statement of the affairs of the corporation which shall be submitted at the annual meeting of the stockholders; and shall be filed within twenty (20) days thereafter at the principal office of the corporation in the 

State of Maryland. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15, 86. Text, §§ 71, 124.] § 290. (Sec. 3) Vice-President.- 

In the absence of the President, the Vice-President shall perform all the duties of the President, and when so acting shall have the powers of the President. The Vice-President shall (if provided by resolution of the Board of Directors) have authority to sign and execute in the name of the corporation all authorized deeds, mortgages, bonds, contracts or other instruments, and shall also have such additional powers and duties as may be assigned to him by the Board of Directors. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 71, 124.] § 291. (Sec. 4) Secretary.- 

The Secretary shall keep the minutes of the meetings of the stockholders, of the Board of Directors and of the Executive Committee, in books provided for the purpose; he shall see that all notices are duly given in accordance with the provisions of the By-laws or as required by law; he shall be the custodian of the records and of the corporate seal or seals of the corporation; he shall see that the corporate seal is affixed to all documents, the execution of which on behalf of the corporation under its seal is duly authorized, and when

so affixed may attest the same; he may sign, with the President or a 

Vice-President, certificates of stock of the corporation; and, in general, he shall perform all duties ordinarily incident to the office of a Secretary of a corporation, and such other duties as, from time to time, may be assigned to him by the Board of Directors, or by the President. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 71, 124.] § 292. (Sec. 5) Treasurer.- 

The Treasurer shall have charge of and be responsible for all funds, securities, receipts and disbursements of the corporation, and shall deposit, or cause to be deposited, in the name of the corporation al moneys or other valuable effects in such banks, trust companies, or other depositories as shall, from time to time, be selected by the Board of Directors; he shall render to the President and to the Board of Directors, whenever requested, an account of the financial condition of the corporation; he may sign, with the President or a Vice- 

President, certificates of stock of the corporation; and, in general, shall perform all the duties ordinarily incident to the office of a treasurer of a corporation, and such other duties as may be assigned to him by the Board of Directors or by the President. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 71, 124.] § 293. (Sec. 6) Assistant officers.- 

The Board of Directors may elect one or more Assistant Secretaries and one or more Assistant Treasurers. Each such Assistant Secretary and Assistant Treasurer shall hold office for such period and shall have such authority and perform such duties as the Board of Directors may prescribe. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 71, 124.] § 294. (Sec. 7) Subordinate officers.— 

The Board of Directors may elect such subordinate officers as it may deem desirable. Each such officer shall hold office for such period, and shall have such authority and perform such duties, as the Board of Directors may prescribe. The Board of Directors may, from time to time, authorize any officer to appoint subordinate officers and to prescribe the powers and duties thereof. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 12, 15. Text, §§ 71, 124.]

BY-LAWS 

369 

§ 295. (Sec. 8) Compensation.- 

The Board of Directors shall have power to fix the compensation of all officers of the corporation. It may authorize any officer upon whom the power of appointing subordinate officers may have been conferred to fix the compensation of such subordinate officers. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 13. Text, §§ 79, 131.] 

§ 296. (Sec. 9) Officers holding more than one office.—

Two or more offices (except that of President and Vice-President) may be held by the same person, but no officer shall execute, acknowledge or verify any instrument in more than one capacity. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 12. Text, §§ 71, 123.] § 297. (Sec. 10) Removal.- 

The Board of Directors shall have power at any regular or special meeting to remove any officer with or without cause, and such action shall be conclusive on the officer so removed. The Board may authorize any officer to remove subordinate officers. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 15. Text, §§ 123, 133.] § 298. (Sec. 11) Vacancies.- 

The Board of Directors at any regular or special meeting shall have power to fill a vacancy occurring in any office for the unexpired portion of the term. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 15. Text, §§ 118, 123.] Article IV. 

Committees 

§ 299. (Sec. 1) Executive Committee.— 

The Board of Directors, by vote of a majority of the entire Board, may provide for an Executive Committee of three or more directors. 

If provision be made for an Executive Committee, the Board of Directors shall elect the members thereof to serve during the pleasure of the Board and may designate one of such members to act as chairman. Vacancies in the Committee shall be filled by the Board. 

During the intervals between the meetings of the Board of Directors, the Executive Committee shall possess and may exercise any or all of the powers of the Board of Directors in the management of the business and affairs of the corporation, to the extent authorized by

resolution adopted by a majority of the entire Board of Directors. 

The Executive Committee shall keep full and fair accounts of its transactions. All actions shall be reported to the Board of Directors at its meeting next succeeding such action, and shall be subject to revision and alteration by the Board of Directors; provided that no rights of third persons shall be affected by any such revision or alteration. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 13. Text, § 70.] § 300. (Sec. 2) Meetings of the Executive Committee.- 

A Majority of the Executive Committee shall be necessary and sufficient to constitute a quorum. The Executive Committee may determine its rules of procedure and the notice to be given of its meetings. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 13. Text, § 70.] § 301. (Sec. 3) Other committees.- 

The Board of Directors, by resolution, may provide for such other standing or special committees of three or more directors as it deems desirable, and discontinue the same at pleasure. Each such committee shall have such powers and perform such duties, not inconsistent with law, as may be assigned to it by the Board of Directors. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 13. Text, §§ 69, 70, 118.] Article V. Stock § 302. (Sec. 1) Certificates.- 

Each stockholder shall be entitled to a stock certificate or certificates certifying the number and kind of shares owned by him. Said certificate shall be signed by the President or a Vice-President and by the Secretary or an Assistant Secretary, or the Treasurer or an Assistant Treasurer, and shall thereafter be sealed with the seal of the corporation. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 37. Text, § 96.] § 303. (Sec. 2) Transfer of shares.- 

Shares of stock shall be transferable only on the books of the corporation by the holder thereof in person or by his duly authorized

BY-LAWS 

371 attorney, and on surrender of the certificate or certificates duly endorsed. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 51ff. Text, §§ 72, 80, 142–145.] § 304. (Sec. 3) Transfer agents and registrars.— 

The Board of Directors may appoint one or more transfer agents and/or one or more registrars of its stock, and may from time to time define their respective duties. No certificate of stock shall be valid until countersigned by a transfer agent, if the corporation have a transfer agent, or until registered by a registrar, if the corporation have a registrar. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 51ff. Text, §§ 72, 80, 142–145.] 

§ 305. (Sec. 4) Closing books of the corporation against transfer of stock; record dates.—

The Board of Directors may fix a time not exceeding twenty (20) days preceding the date of any meeting of stockholders, any dividend payment date, or any date for the allotment of rights, during which the books of the corporation shall be closed against the transfer of stock. In lieu of providing for the closing of the books against transfers of stock as aforesaid, the Board of Directors may fix in advance a time not exceeding thirty (30) days preceding the date of any meeting of stockholders, any dividend payment date, or any date for the allotment of rights, as record date for the determination of the stockholders entitled to notice of, and to vote at such meeting, or entitled to receive such dividends or rights, as the case may be, and, in that event, only stockholders of record on such date shall be entitled to notice of, or to vote at, such meeting, or to receive such dividends or rights, as the case may be. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 15. Text, §§ 72, 142–143.] 

§ 306. (Sec. 5) Mutilated, lost or destroyed certificates.—

The holder of any certificate representing shares of stock of the corporation shall immediately notify the corporation of any mutilation, loss or destruction thereof, and the Board of Directors may, in its discretion, cause one or more new certificates, for the same number of shares in the aggregate, to be issued to such holder upon the surrender of the mutilated certificate; or in case of the loss or destruction of the certificate, upon satisfactory proof of such loss or destruction and the deposit of indemnity by way of bond or other-

wise, in such form and amount and with such sureties or securities as the Board of Directors may require, to indemnify the corporation against loss or liability by reason of the issuance of such new certificates; but the Board of Directors may, in its discretion, refuse to issue such new certificates, save upon the order of some court having jurisdiction. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 15, 78–79. Text, §§ 69, 72, 118.] Article VI. Sundry Provisions § 307. (Sec. 1) Dividends.- 

Subject to the applicable provisions of law and of the Charter, the Board of Directors may in its discretion declare what, if any, dividends shall be paid from the surplus or from the net profits of the corporation, or upon any class of such stock, and the dates when such dividends shall be payable. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 87 (L. 1931, Ch. 480). Text, § 119.]

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 13. Text, § 90.] § 309. (Sec. 3) Fiscal year.— 

The fiscal year of the corporation shall be the calendar year, unless otherwise provided by the Board of Directors. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 13, 15. Text, § 78.] § 310. (Sec. 4) Seal.- 

The seal of the corporation shall be circular in form, with the name of the corporation inscribed around the outer edge, and in the center shall be inscribed the words "Incorporated Maryland (Blank No. 17)."

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 85. Text, §§ 179–181.] § 312. (Sec. 6) Bonds.- 

The Board of Directors may require any officer, agent or employee of the corporation to give a bond to the corporation for the faithful discharge of his duties, in such amount, on such conditions, and with such surety or sureties, as may be required by the Board. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 13, 15. Text, §§ 73, 118.] § 313. (Sec. 7) Stock of other corporations.— 

Shares of stock in other corporations owned or held by the corporation may be voted by the corporation by such officer, agent or proxy as the Board of Directors may from time to time appoint, and, in the absence of such appointment, may be voted by the President or a Vice-President, or by proxy or proxies appointed by the President or a Vice-President. Any and all proxies, waivers, consents and other instruments may be executed and any and all other action may be taken by the corporation as owner or holder of shares of stock in other corporations by such officer, agent or proxy as the Board of Directors may appoint, or, in the absence of such appointment, by the President or a Vice-President. 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 22 (L. 1981, Ch. 480). Text, § 124.] § 314. (Sec. 8) Amendments.- 

These by-laws, or any of them, or any additional or supplementary by-laws, may be altered or repealed and new by-laws may be adopted at any annual meeting of the stockholders without notice, or at any special meeting the notice of which shall set forth the terms of the proposed amendment, by the vote of the holders of a majority of the shares represented in person or by proxy and entitled to vote at such annual or special meeting as the case may be. The Board of Directors may exercise the power to make, alter and repeal by-laws if there are no shares of stock outstanding entitled to vote thereon;

and at any time may make, alter and repeal additional and supplementary by-laws not inconsistent with these by-laws and any by-law adopted by the stockholders; but any such additional or supplemental by-laws may be altered or repealed by the stockholders as provided in this Section.

§ 354. Par value stock, one class.

The total amount of the authorized capital stock of the corporation is Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($500,000), divided into Ten thousand (10,000) shares of the par value of Fifty Dollars ($50.) each, all of which shares are Common Stock.² 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 4, 38. Text, § 34.] 

§ 355. Preferences and qualifications of preferred stock and common stock.

The preferences, voting powers, restrictions and qualifications of each class of stock are as follows:

PREFERRED STOCK 

(a) Dividends.-The holders of the Preferred Stock shall be entitled to receive from the surplus or net profits of the Corporation, when and as declared by its Board of Directors, dividends at the rate of six per cent. (6%) per annum upon the par value thereof, payable quarterly on the first days of January, April, July and October in each year. Such dividends shall be cumulative, accounting from the date of issue of each share of stock, and shall be payable for the current and all previous years before any dividends shall be paid or set apart on the Common Stock. The Preferred Stock shall not be entitled to participate in or receive any dividend or share of profits, whether payable in cash, stock or property, in excess of the aforesaid cumulative dividends. No dividends on any outstanding stock of the Corporation shall be declared out of paid-in surplus. (b) Preferences Upon Liquidation, etc.-In the event of liquidation, dissolution or winding up of the Corporation (whether voluntary or involuntary) the holders of the issued and outstanding Preferred Stock shall be entitled to receive out of the assets before any distribution to the holders of any other class of stock a sum equal to one hundred and five per cent. (105%) of the par value of each share plus all accumulated and unpaid dividends thereon. 

A consolidation or merger of the Corporation with any other corporation or corporations shall not be deemed to be a liquidation, dissolution, or winding up within the meaning of this clause. supra) follow immediately after the above clause in the charter of this corporation. As to formalities required for issuance of any of the stock authorized by the charter, see Chap. XI, supra. Forms, §§ 324-328; 359-360. 

1 For a clause combining Preferred Stock having a par value with Common Stock having no par value, see the complete form of charter printed supra, at § 257.

As to issuance of stock, see Chap. XI, supra; forms, §§ 324-328, 359-360. 

1 This clause should be preceded by a clause like that in § 257 or § 354.

(c) Voting Rights.-Except as herein provided, or otherwise provided by law, the holders of the Preferred Stock shall not be entitled to vote under any circumstances, or in connection with any action taken by the Corporation. However, if and whenever four consecutive quarterly dividends on the Preferred Stock shall have accrued and be unpaid in whole or in part, then so long as there shall be any such accrued unpaid dividends thereon each share of the Preferred Stock shall entitle the holder of record to one vote in respect thereof in all proceedings in which action shall be taken by Stockholders of the Corporation, on an equal basis, share for share, with the holders of the Common Stock. If all such accrued unpaid dividends shall be paid by the Corporation at any time, then and thereupon all power of the Preferred Stock to vote as in this paragraph provided shall cease; subject, however, to being revived again upon any subsequent default by the Corporation in the payment of four consecutive quarterly dividends as provided above; (d) Redemption.-At the option of the Board of Directors, the whole or any part of the Preferred Stock outstanding at any time may be redeemed on any of the respective dates fixed for the payment of dividends thereon, at one hundred and five per cent. (105%) of its par value, together with all unpaid dividends accrued thereon to the date of redemption, upon not less than thirty (30) days previous notice given by mail to the holders of record of the Preferred Stock. 

In the event that less than all of the outstanding Preferred Stock is to be redeemed, the redemption may be effected either by lot or pro rata, in such manner as may be prescribed by resolution of the Board of Directors. After any of the outstanding Preferred Stock shall have been called for redemption and the holders thereof duly notified and the funds necessary to effect such redemption have been set aside by the Board of Directors, the holders thereof shall have no further rights as stockholders of the Corporation but shall be entitled only upon presentation of the certificates properly endorsed to receive the redemption value thereof, as above set forth. Notice of redemption shall be deemed to have been given when addressed to such Preferred Stockholders at the addresses recorded on the books of the Corporation and mailed at the City of Baltimore, State of Maryland. 

COMMON STOCK² 

(a) Dividends.—After all accumulated dividends on the outstanding Preferred Stock shall have been declared, and the Corporation 2 Frequently two classes of so-called Common Stock" are provided for, which are treated in all respects on the same basis except that the voting power is exclusively vested in one such class.

CHARTER PROVISIONS AS TO CAPITAL STOCK 389 

shall have paid the same or shall have set apart a sum sufficient therefor, the holders of the outstanding Common Stock shall be entitled to receive out of the remaining surplus or net profits, such dividends as may from time to time be declared by the Board of Directors. No dividends on any outstanding stock of the Corporation shall be declared out of paid-in surplus. (b) Preferences Upon Liquidation, etc.-In the event of the liquidation, dissolution or winding up of the Corporation, whether voluntary or involuntary, the holders of the outstanding Common Stock after the payments hereinabove provided for have been made to the holders of the outstanding Preferred Stock, shall be entitled to share equally, share for share, in all remaining assets available for distribution.

A consolidation or merger of the Corporation with any other corporation or corporations shall not be deemed to be a liquidation or winding up within the meaning of this clause. 

(c) Voting Rights.-Each share of Common Stock shall entitle the holder of record thereof to one (1) vote in all proceedings in which action shall be taken by Stockholders of the Corporation. 

[Code, Art. 23, Secs. 4, 38. Text, Chap. V. (§§ 34-40.)] 

§ 356. Provision for participation by preferred stock in earnings over and above amount needed to pay fixed dividends on preferred and on common stock.— 

After quarterly dividends at the rate of One Dollar ($1.00) per share have been declared on the Common Stock of the Corporation, out of surplus or net profits remaining after declaration of fixed dividends as above provided on the Preferred Stock, the holders of the outstanding Preferred Stock and of the outstanding Common Stock shall be entitled to receive on an equal basis, share for share, out of the remaining surplus or net profits, such dividends as may from time to time be declared by the Board of Directors. If there shall be an increase in the authorized capital stock of the Corporation, and Common Stock shall at any time be issued and outstanding in excess of the number of shares now authorized by this Certificate of Incorporation, then in lieu of the above provision, after quarterly dividends to the Common Stock amounting in the aggregate to One Dollar ($1.00), multiplied by the number of shares of Common 

Stock now authorized by this Certificate of Incorporation, shall have been declared, out of surplus or net profits remaining after declaration of the fixed dividends on the Preferred Stock, the holders 1

of the outstanding Preferred Stock and of the outstanding Common Stock shall be entitled to receive equally, class for class, and not share for share, out of the remaining surplus or net profits, such dividends as may from time to time be declared by the Board of Directors. Upon liquidation or dissolution (but not upon consolidation or merger) of the Corporation, the holders of the outstanding 

Preferred Stock and of the outstanding Common Stock, shall, after payment of the fixed preferences to such Preferred Stock hereinabove provided, and, thereafter, after payment of the sum of Twelve Dollars ($12.00) per share to the holders of the outstanding Common 

Stock, be entitled to receive, equally, share for share, the remaining assets available for distribution. If there shall be an increase in the authorized capital stock of the Corporation and shares of Common Stock shall then be outstanding in excess of the number of shares thereof now authorized by this Certificate of Incorporation, then in lieu of the above provision, after payment of the fixed preferences to such Preferred Stock, and, thereafter, after payment to the holders of the outstanding Common Stock of liquidating dividends amounting in the aggregate to Twelve Dollars ($12.00), multiplied by the number of shares of Common Stock now authorized by this Certificate of Incorporation, the holders of the outstanding Preferred 

Stock and of the outstanding Common Stock shall be entitled to receive equally, class for class, and not share for share, the remaining assets available for distribution.¹ 

[Code, Art. 23, Sec. 38. Text, § 37.]

G. Capital Stock. The amount of the authorized capital stock of each of said consolidating corporations is as follows: 

The Southeast Trust Company has an authorized capital stock of twenty thousand (20,000) shares of the par value of fifty dollars ($50.00) per share, all issued and outstanding, to wit: An aggregate capital of $1,000,000. It also has a surplus of $2,000,000. 

The Southern Tristate Bank and Trust Company has an authorized capital stock of forty thousand (40,000) shares of the par value of fifty dollars ($50.00) per share, all issued and outstanding, to wit: An aggregate capital of $2,000,000. It also has a surplus of $2,000,000.

The total amount of authorized capital stock of the new consolidated corporation hereby formed shall be $3,500,000, divided into seventy thousand (70,000) shares of the par value of fifty dollars ($50.00)' per share. In addition thereto said corporation will have a paid-in surplus of $3,500,000. 

H. The total amount of capital stock of the new corporation to be issued for stock of the consolidating corporations is seventy thousand (70,000) shares of the par value of fifty dollars ($50.00) per share. 

I. There are no restrictions imposed upon the transfer of the shares or of any of them, except as may be provided in the by-laws. 

J. All of the capital stock of the new consolidated corporation shall be of one class.

K. The manner of converting the capital stock of each of the consolidating corporations into stock of the new corporation shall be 

1. All of the stock of The Southeast Trust Company (Con solidating Corporation) shall be surrendered to the new corporation and in lieu thereof, there shall be issued to the stockholders of the said The Southeast Trust Company thirty thousand (30,000) shares of the stock of the new corporation, the holder of each share of the stock of The Southeast Trust Company (Consolidating Corporation) being entitled to receive one and one-half shares of the stock of the new corporation. The new corporation shall issue script for fractional parts of shares where the number of shares of stock of The Southeast Trust Company (Consolidating Corporation) held by any stockholder does not entitle him to an even number of shares of the stock of the new corporation; but said script when issued shall not entitle the

holder to any dividends which may hereafter be declared by the new corporation unless and until the said script shall be converted by the holder at any time into capital stock of the new corporation by surrender of such script in amounts calling for a full share or shares of stock of the new corporation. 

2. All of the stock of The Southern Tristate Bank and Trust 

Company shall be surrendered to the new corporation and in lieu thereof there shall be issued to the stockholders of The Southern Tristate Bank and Trust Company forty thousand (40,000) shares of the stock of the new corporation, the holder of each share of the stock of The Southern Tristate Bank and Trust Company being entitled to receive one share of stock of the new corporation.

L. All other provisions and details to perfect the consolidation shall be as follows: 

1. By-Laws. The Board of Directors of the consolidated corporation, consisting of the persons heretofore named, shall meet at the call of the President on twenty-four hours' written notice mailed to their respective addresses after the receipt for record of this agreement by the State Tax Commission, at the time and place designated in said notice, and among other things shall have power¹ at such meeting to adopt by-laws for the corporation and subsequently to repeal, amend or add to the same. 

Among other things, provision shall be made in the by-laws so to be adopted by the Directors, subject to subsequent repeal or modification by the directors, for the selection from among the Board of Directors of an Executive Committee consisting of not more than twelve members; the Chairman of the Board of 

Directors, Vice-Chairman of the Board of Directors, and the President of the corporation to be ex officio three members of the said Committee. The duties of this Executive Committee shall be defined in the by-laws. 

The original by-laws shall also provide for the following other 

Committees: 

a. Discount Committee. b. Investment Committee. c. Trust Committee. 'It may be questioned whether under the present statute this power can be lawfully conferred upon directors while there is stock outstanding. See § 67, supra. As to applicability of corporation law to banking institutions, see § 4, supra.

CONSOLIDATION 

407 2. Directors. The Directors of the corporation for the first year shall be thirty in number, and thereafter shall be such number as may be lawfully fixed by the by-laws. The Directors shall be elected each year at the annual meeting of the stockholders to be held at the principal office of the corporation which shall be in Baltimore City on the second Monday in January; and all elections shall be by ballot, and at such elections and all other meetings of the stockholders each stockholder shall be entitled to one vote for every share of stock standing in his name but stockholders may vote either in person or by proxy; and no person shall be eligible as a director who is not a stockholder to the amount of ten shares of stock standing in his name. 

3. Seal. The form of the seal of the corporation shall be "The Southeast Trust Company-Seal-Maryland, 1882–19----”; subject to subsequent change by the by-laws. 

4. Form of certificates of the capital stock of the corporation shall be as prescribed by the Board of Directors. 

5. Surplus. The assets of the new consolidated corporation as hereinabove provided include at the present time a paid-in surplus over and above capital stock in the amount of three million five hundred thousand dollars ($3,500,000); but it is distinctly understood and provided that said surplus fund shall in no sense constitute or be considered capital stock or fixed capital of the said new consolidated corporation, and the Board of Directors of the said corporation as herein constituted or as the same may from time to time hereafter be constituted by successive elections, shall have full and ample power from time to time to reduce such surplus fund by distribution among the stockholders, by dividends or otherwise; provided, however, that no dividend shall be declared from such surplus which would reduce the amount thereof to a sum less than twenty per cent. of the aggregate amount of capital stock. 

6. Rights, powers and liabilities. The consolidated corporation is hereby given all the property and assets belonging to said former separate corporations of whatsoever kind, nature and description, and all the powers and rights and all the debts and liabilities of said former separate corporations of whatsoever nature and description, are hereby devolved upon said new consolidated corporation, which is hereby substituted by operation of law in the room and stead of said consolidating corporations. 

And in accordance therewith all of the property and assets belonging to said consolidating corporations, whether real, personal or mixed, of whatsoever nature or description, including

all trust estates and all property held under any agreement of trust or in accordance with any testamentary disposition, or by virtue of the order of any court of the State of Maryland, of the United States, or of any other State or territory of the United States, or of any foreign country, and all and singular the powers, rights, privileges and franchises of the consolidating corporations, including all powers conferred upon or vested in either of them by contract, agreement or testamentary disposition or order of any court, as aforesaid, are to be taken and deemed, upon and after the execution and recording of this agreement, to be vested in the consolidated corporation hereby established without further action or deed, and all such property and assets shall be the property and assets of the consolidated corporation, and all powers, rights, privileges and franchises of the consolidating corporations shall be exercisable by the consolidated corporation to the same extent as heretofore exercisable by either of the consolidating corporations, so that the said consolidated corporation shall be hereby substituted for all purposes whatsoever in the room and stead of said former separate corporations. 

All rights, duties and powers conferred upon either of said consolidating corporations by will or deed of trust or other legal instrument heretofore executed but not yet effective in the appointment of either of said consolidating corporations as executor, trustee, or guardian or in any other fiduciary capacity, may be assumed and discharged by the said new consolidated corporation as the legal successor of both of said consolidating corporations.

And it is further provided and agreed that in all cases where either of said consolidating corporations is now acting in the capacity of trustee under any contract or deed of trust securing bonds or otherwise, or in the capacity of syndicate manager or agent or as receiver, guardian, executor, administrator, committee, depository, assignee, transfer agent or registrar of stocks or bonds, or in any other fiduciary capacity whatever, under any contract, agreement, deed of trust, will or appointment of any court as aforesaid, the duties and powers of said fiduciary capacity shall be devolved upon and are hereby expressly assumed by and shall be in all respects performed by the said consolidated corporation in the same manner, to the same extent, under the same rights, powers and liabilities as heretofore existed with respect to the said consolidating corporations respectively.

CONSTITUTION ARTICLE III LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT 

33. 

*The General Assembly shall pass no special law for any case for which provision has been made by an existing general law ** 

[Text, § 6.] 39. The General Assembly shall grant no charter for banking purposes, nor renew any banking corporation now in existence, except upon the condition that the stockholders shall be liable to the amount of their respective share or shares of stock in such banking institution, for all its debts and liabilities upon note, bill or otherwise; the books, papers and accounts of all banks shall be open to inspection under such regulations as may be prescribed by law. 

[Text, § 9.] 

48. Corporations may be formed under general laws, but shall not be created by special act, except for municipal purposes and except in cases where no General Laws exist, providing for the creation of corporations of the same general character as the corporation proposed to be created, and any act of incorporation passed in violation of this section shall be void; all charters granted or adopted in pursuance of this section, and all charters heretofore granted and created subject to repeal or modification, may be altered from time to time, or be repealed; provided, nothing herein contained shall be construed to extend to banks or the incorporation thereof; the General Assembly shall not alter or amend the charter of any corporation existing at the time of the adoption of this article, or pass any other general or special law for the benefit of such corporation except upon the condition that such corporation shall surrender all claim to exemption from taxation or from the repeal or modification of its charter, and that such corporation shall thereafter hold its charter sub- 417

ject to the provisions of this Constitution; and any corporation chartered by this State which shall accept, use, enjoy or in anywise avail itself of any rights, privileges, or advantages that may hereafter be granted or conferred by any general or special act, shall be conclusively presumed to have thereby surrendered any exemption from taxation to which it may be entitled under its charter, and shall be thereafter subject to taxation as if no such exemption has been granted by its charter. 

[Text, §§ 6, 9, 64–66.] 

58. The Legislature, at its first session after the ratification of this Constitution, shall provide by Law for State and municipal taxation upon the revenues accruing from business done in the State by all foreign corporations.
